lawyer:
Dr Md Zahir with Shah Md Ezaz Rahman, Advocates—For the Petitioners. 
Akhtar Imam with MM Nuruzzaman, Advocates—For Respondent Nos. 1-3. 
M Moniruzzaman Khan with Morshed Ahmed Khan and ASM Abdur Razzaque, Advocates—For Respondent No. 6.
parties:
Anwar Hossain (Md) & another ------ Petitioners 
Vs 
Uttara Valley Ltd and other ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
This is an application under section 233 of the Companies Act. The application is contested by the respondent Nos. 1-3 jointly and by the respondent No. 6 separately.

2. The petitioners are amongst the subscriber share-holders of the Company. On incorporation of the Company the subscriber share-holders, six (6) in number subscribed 300 shares, of which the petitioner No. 1 subscribed 54 shares and petitioner No. 2 subscribed 48 shares and thus the petitioners acquired more than 30% of the subscribed shares in the Company. The petitioner No.1 was appointed as the first Managing Director of the company. The Company was incorporated on 28-11-94. The tenure of the petitioner as Managing Director, as per Articles of Association of the Company was for 3 years and subsequently the period was extended. The respondent-company purchased 25-08 acres of land vide registered sale deed and its name was duly mutated in the records of right in respect of 23.38 acres, as at the time of mutation 1.7 acres of land, out of the purchased 25.08 acres of land, was found to have been recorded as khas land. The petitioners were ousted from the management of the Company by the respondent Nos. 2-5, who conspired to grab the company's property. On 8-12-2002 petitioners received notice from the Upazila Land Office, Sylhet Sadar, (respondent No. 9) in connection with a mutation case in respect of the company's landed property and on query it was revealed that beyond the knowledge of the petitioners the respondent No. 3, who has been appointed as the Executive Director, sold company's landed property to the respondent Nos. 6-8 through six separate registered sale deeds and the said respondent Nos. 6-8 filed the mutation case in the office of the respondent No. 9 and on 12-12-02 the petitioner No. 1 filed objection there-against the office of the respondent No. 9 and accordingly, the proceeding was stayed. It was revealed from the copy of the sale deeds, procured subsequently, that the respondent No.3 without any authority from the Board of Directors of the Company illegally claiming his authority under Article 82 of the Articles of Association sold the company's land in reference and executed and registered the sale deeds for and on behalf of the Company in favour of the respondents Nos. 6-8 and that 22 acres of land were sold for Taka 6,70,000 and that the sale proceeds have not been deposited in the company's account. One of the purchasers is the respondent No. 7, who is the son of respondent No. 2; and another purchaser is respondent No. 8 who is the wife of the respondent No. 3, the executant of the sale deeds; and the other purchaser is respondent No. 6, who is a nephew of the respondent No. 2. The respondent Nos. 2-8 misappropriated the company's property in the aforesaid manner and that the affairs of the Company are being carried on to the prejudice and disregard of the interest of the petitioners and that petitioners could not move the Board of Directors or any General Meeting for taking any resolution against the fraudulent transaction of the respondents and that affairs of the Company were being managed by the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 to the exclusion of the petitioner No. 1, though he is the Managing Director, and that the tenure of the petitioner as Managing Director has been extended for 5 years with effect from 20-11-02. The respondent No.3 is a practicing Advocate of Sylhet Judges Court and he drafted and prepared the Memorandum and Articles of Association of the Company and included Article 82 providing all powers of the Managing Director to the Executive Director and the respondent No. 3 is the named Executive Director in the Articles of Association for a period of 3 years and his tenure has not been extended further. The respondent No.3 bears bad reputation, he is involved in two (2) criminal cases, and that there was no resolution of the Board of Directors, as required under Article 82 (Kha) of the Articles of Association, authorising the respondent No. 3, as Executive Director, to exercise the authority given under Article 82 of the Articles of Association of the Company to execute and register any deed of sale for and on behalf of the company and that the Company never required or intended to sell the land in question and the land in question is alleged to have been sold by the Executive Director, (respondent No. 3) illegally in collusion with the Chairman (respondent No. 2) to the respondent Nos. 6-8 showing a very low price only because respondent No. 6 is the nephew of the respondent No. 2, (Chairman of the Company and respondent No. 7 is the son of the respondent No.2 and respondent No. 8 is the wife of the respondent No. 3(the executant) and that the sale of the land in question through respondent No. 3 in favour of the respondent Nos. 6-8 being without the required resolution of the Board of Directors, the whole transaction as to said sales is illegal and hence no legal right, title and interest has accrued in favour of the respondent Nos. 6-8 on the land in question and in order to stop delivery of possession of the land in question, the petitioner No. 1 made a General Diary at the Kotwali PS Sylhet, on 10-12-02 and that the purchasers being close relations of the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 there is no reason to believe that they had no knowledge about the internal disputes amongst the Directors of the Company and that for protection of the minority share-holders interest this Company can pass such orders as it deems fit including cancellation of any sale deed fraudulently made by any Director of the Company without obtaining authority from the Company and that the petitioner No. 1 did not write any letter to the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms, alleged to have been received on 18-12-02, for supply of certified copy of documents and did not submit any resolution book of the Board of Directors and of the General Meeting of the Company, and that in the record of the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Sylhet Sadar, relating to the mutation case for recording names, the respondent Nos. 6-8 against the land in reference, there is a noting to the effect that papers showing that Managing Director has handed over the charge of his office to the Executive Director (respondent No. 3), and a copy of the resolution of the Board of Directors authorising the Executive Director to exercise the powers under Article 82 of the Articles of Association were submitted but those papers however are not available in the said case record; and that the respondent No. 3, being a family lawyer and a trusted friend of the petitioners and the respondent Directors of the Company, was in possession of the title deeds of the Company's properties and he exploited his fiducial position to misappropriate Company's property and that the petitioners do not possess the proceeding books of the Directors' meetings and of the share-holders' meetings and that the copy of the papers and document, which they have in their possession, have been annexed with the affidavit. The petitioners have no other papers and documents of the Company. The petitioners filed this application to safeguard their interest as well as Company's interest in the Company's landed properties covered by the sale-deeds, evidenced by the Annexures F to F-5 to the application.

3. The respondent Nos. 1-3 in their affidavit-in-opposition stated, amongst others, that the lands were purchased in the name of the respondent-company for setting up poultry, apiculture and agriculture farms, through registered sale deeds, and that the petitioner No. 1, Managing Director of the Company, is in control of the management, affairs and business of the Company and that the land in question has been purchased by the respondent No. 6, a reputed physician and also the Managing Partner of the Partnership Firm namely, Nurjahan Poly Clinic and General Hospital at Sylhet, and that land was purchased for setting up a Modern Charitable Hospital and that Board of Directors of the Company decided to sell the company land to the respondent Nos. 6-8 and the Board resolution was taken in presence of the petitioner No. 1 and that the resolution books are in the custody of the petitioner No. 1 and that the consideration money against the sale of the land was duly paid to respondent-company with which the income tax and land development tax were paid and costs of construction of boundary wall around the Company's land was met and the petitioner No.1 also utilised money out of the sale proceeds of the land and that the petitioner No.1 earlier sold valuable trees from the company's land valued around Taka 20,00,000 which amount was not credited in the account of the company and that the petitioner No.1 submitted his objection in the mutation case on 10-12-02 and 12-12-02 and the respondent No. 9, the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Sylhet Sadar, asked the petitioner No.1 to produce Company's resolution book and the petitioner No. 1 took time up to 19-1-03 for compliance and that the petitioner No.1 removed all the records of the Company and has fabricated new records, which he fraudulently submitted to the office of the Registrar, Joint Stock Companies and Firms on 17-12-02 and took back those on 19-12-02, against which the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 submitted objection petition and the petitioner No.1 accordingly was asked to submit the relevant papers and documents vide memo No. 155 dated 1-2-03 and memo No. 450 dated 17-3-03 but the petitioner No. 1 till date did not comply and that the petitioner filed an affidavit dated 19-8-03 stating that he did not have any document, which he was asked to produce by .Court's order dated 17-3-03 and that the sale proceeds of 16.26 acres of land, evidenced by Annexures F-I (5) to the application, were shared by Mina Uddin and others and as well as the respondent-company (Uttara Valley Limited) and that Minauddin and others received Taka 3,70,000 and the respondent-company received Taka 3,00,000, with which the Company paid income tax and land development tax and that the petitioner No. 1 himself executed two sale deeds in respect of land sold by the Company in favour of one Abdul Hamid Chowdhury and one Lokman Hakim for Taka 60,000, which amount he did not deposit in the Company's account and that Miner Uddin and Sayma, co-owners of the land in the same khatian sold together with Company's land, and they appointed the respondent No. 3 as their attorney to execute and register the impugned sale deeds on their behalf and that the respondent No. 3 was authorised to sell land of the Company by the same resolution, by which the petitioner No. 1 was authorised to execute and register the sale deeds in favour of said Abdul Hamid Chowdhury and Lokman Hakim, and that the resolution book containing the said resolution is in custody of the petitioner No. 1 and that the petitioner No. 1 has filed this petition malafide, inasmuch as the petitioner No. 1 as Managing Director was the Chief Executive of the Company at the relevant time and he was in the management of the Company and, as such, he was in custody of all the books and records of the Company and that on the land sold a Charitable Hospital is to be constructed and that no meeting of the Board of Directors was held on 25-11-97 and 20-11-02 to appoint Managing Director of the Company and that there is no evidence as alleged that any fraud has been practiced on the minority shareholder or that the affairs of the Company were being managed in a manner prejudicial to the interest of the members or to the exclusion of the petitioner No.1; and that in view of the existing provisions of the Articles of Association of the Company there is no necessity for passing an order by this Court further empowering the Managing Director to participate in the management of the Company and that the office of the Company was used by the petitioner No.1 for his Travel Agency business during the period 1994-2002 AD; and that the petitioner No.1 and his son were responsible for filing false case against the respondent No. 3, which was dismissed being found to be false and baseless on investigation, and that there is no necessity for amending the powers of the Executive Director of the respondent-company by amendment of Article 82 of the Articles of Association of the respondent-company, as prayed for, and that there being disputed questions of fact as to the genuineness and or forgery of the documents, the resolution of the Board of Directors and others and as those cannot be resolved in a summary proceeding, and need be decided by taking evidences in appropriate civil suit, the instant application under section 233 of the Companies Act, 1994, is not maintainable and that this Company Court cannot and will not cancel the registered sale deeds in an application under section 233 of the Companies Act and that the petition is also not maintainable on the ground that it will affect the right, title and interest of the innocent 3rd party, who are bonafide purchasers; and that the transaction complained of is an isolated transaction of the Company and there being no continuity of the allegation complained of at the time of filing of the instant application, the application under section 233 of the Companies Act is not maintainable.

4. The respondent No. 6 in his affidavit in opposition, amongst others, stated that the application under section 233 of the Companies Act, 1994 with the prayers as made is not maintainable, inasmuch as the Company Court cannot affect the interest of a 3rd party and that the application under section 233 of the Companies Act does not disclose series of acts of the respondents which are oppressive in nature and that, in fact, the petitioners disclosed only a single transaction relating to transfer of Company's property hence not maintainable and that the respondent No. 6 was aware about the fact that the land in question was not owned by the respondent No. 3 but by the respondent company and that the petitioners, having been excluded from management of the Company, cannot maintain the application under section 233 of the Companies Act and that the petitioners were totally excluded from taking part in affairs of the Company and that the statements made in paragraph 15 of the petitioners' application to the effect that the petitioner's tenure as Managing Director has been extended for a period of 5 years with effect from 20-11-02 is contradictory to the statement that no Board Meeting or Share-holder Meeting was held and that the respondent No. 6 is a physician by profession and passed MBBS in 1984 and in order to set up a Modern Charitable Hospital he purchased the land in question measuring 10.505 acres and that the respondent No. 6 being an outsider had no knowledge about any internal affair of the Company and as per provision of section 126 of the Companies Act a contract on behalf of the Company may be signed by any person acting under its authority, express or implied, and the same shall bind the Company and its successors; and this respondent was not supposed to know whether the Executive Director was authorised or not and that pursuant to Article 82 of the Articles of Association of the Company the Executive Director (respondent No. 3) is authorised to execute any deed on behalf of the Company and that whatever may be the blood relationship between the respondent No. 6 and respondent No. 2 but there was no relationship of the respondent No. 6 with the respondent-company and that because of internal dispute amongst the share-holders of the respondent-company the right, title and interest of the respondent No. 6 in the lands of the Company acquired by purchase cannot be affected and that since purchase the respondent No. 6 is in possession thereof; and that the dispute as to the possession in the land being a question of fact inasmuch as the petitioner claimed possession of the Company on the land in reference, the same cannot be decided in a summary proceeding; and that the respondent No. 6 being a bonafide purchaser of the land in question for valuable consideration, through duly executed and registered sale deeds, and in view of the provisions of section 126 of the Companies Act, the petitioners cannot dispute the purchase of the land in reference by the respondent Nos.6-8 and that registered deeds of sale can only be cancelled by a competent Court as per provisions of section 39 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 and hence for proper remedy, the petitioners are to file civil suit for cancellation of the deeds relating to the land in reference (Annexure-F to F-5) and that the sale of the lands in reference being closed and past transaction and as the cause of action was not continuing on the date of filing of the application, this application under section 233 is not maintainable.

5. Dr M Zahir, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that the petitioners have come up with this application under section 233 of the Companies Act to protect their interest in the property, business and affairs of the Company, in particular on the immovable property of the Company. The learned Advocate submitted that the petitioner No. 1 though appointed Managing Director of the Company, taking advantage of his residing both in London and in Bangladesh, the respondent Nos. 2-5, having majority share-holding in the Company, took over the management and control of the business and affairs of the Company and the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 are managing the affairs and business of the Company and that the respondent No. 3 being a family lawyer and relation of the respondents, taking advantage of such capacity, masterminded the transfer of the land in reference by way of sale to the respondent Nos. 6-8, who are close relations of the respondent Nos. 2 and 3, and that, in fact, the alleged sale transaction is a paper-transaction without any consideration inasmuch as no consideration money has been passed and deposited in the account of the Company and that the petitioners denied to have received any money out of the consideration money as alleged by the respondent Nos.2 and 3. The learned Advocate taking me through the copy of the sale deeds annexed to the application (Annexure-F to F-5) submitted that the respondent No. 3 himself cunningly and fraudulently prepared and executed the sale deeds in favour of the respondent Nos. 6-8, describing himself both as authorised person of the Company to exercise authority under Article 82 of the Articles of Association of the company and also as attorney for and on behalf of the other co-owners named in the sale deeds; and that there is no reference as to the amount payable to the Company and to the other alleged co-owners out of the total consideration money. The learned Advocate submitted that there is no denial to the statements made in the affidavit filed by the petitioners to the effect that the respondent Nos. 6-8 are close relations of the respondent Nos. 2 and 3. Respondent No. 6 is the nephew of the respondent No.2 and respondent No. 7 is the son of the respondent No. 2 and respondent No. 8 is the wife of the respondent No. 3. The learned Advocate submitted that it appears from the affidavit of the respondent No. 6 that the respondent No. 6 was aware about the provisions of Article 82 of the Articles of Association of the Company and, as such, the respondent No. 6 was aware that in order to have proper authority to sign and execute any sale deed on behalf of the Company in respect of any property of the Company a proper resolution of the Board of Directors authorising the respondent No. 3 to exercise his power and authority under the Article 82 was necessary and no such Board resolution could be produced before this Court. The learned Advocate submitted that an attempt has been made to confuse the Court showing a letter addressed to the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies alleged to have been written by the petitioner No. 1 praying for supply of certified copies and with the said letter the resolution book of the Company was enclosed, the learned Advocate taking me through the copy of the said letter, as has been produced by the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies, who has been examined in this case, referred to the endorsement appearing in the said letter to the effect that the resolution book and other documents have been taken back, and submitted that the endorsement has been made by some interested person in the name of the petitioner No.1 and that even on an examination by bare eyes in appears that the two signatures in the name of Anwar Hossain as appearing in the said letter are not of the same hand and are of different style and nature and those are not the signatures of the petitioner No.1. The learned Advocate submitted that it is unusual to submit resolution book and other documents to the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies while praying for supply of certified copies of any document filed with the Registrar, inasmuch as the certified copies were to be supplied from the records lying in the office of the Register of Joint Stock Companies and hence question of submission of the Resolution Book does not arise and that the resolution book and other documents were lying with the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 as it is evident from the noting made in the records of the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Sylhet Sadar, relating to the mutation case filed by the respondent No. 6 for recording his name on the basis of sale deeds (Annexure-F to F-5) of the alleged transfer of land. It appears from the said mutation case record that the papers relating to alleged handing over charge of the office of the Managing Director and copy of the relevant resolution authorising Executive Director to exercise power under Article 82 has been submitted to the said office of the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Sylhet Sadar, but for obvious reasons those are not available in the records. The learned Advocate further submitted that neither there was any necessity nor there was any decision for sale of the land in reference by the respondent-Company and hence in the facts and circumstance the sale of the land in reference to the respondent Nos. 6-8 cannot said to be bonafide and the purchaser-respondent Nos. 6-8 are not stranger purchasers and that by such alleged sale of land the interest of the share-holders of the Company and for that matter the petitioners interest have been prejudiced, inasmuch as property of the Company is being tried to be disposed of illegally, collusively and without lawful authority and thus the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 are guilty for attempt to misappropriate properties of the Company and thus prejudiced the interest of the respondent-company and its share-holders.

6. Dr M Zahir, taking me through the provisions of section 233 of the Companies Act and those of section 397 of the Indian Companies Act, submitted that those are not same although much of the contents of the said sections are similar. The learned Advocate submitted that section 397 of the Indian Companies Act provides that on an application with allegation that the company's affairs are being conducted in a manner pre-judicial to public interest or in a manner oppressive to any member or members such necessary order may be passed "to bring an end to allegations complained of. But in section 233 of our Companies Act, such provision "with a view to bringing to an end the matter complained of" is absent. Rather section 233 provides that on an application with allegation that the affairs of the Company are being conducted or the power of the Director are being exercised in a manner per-judicial to one or more of its members or in disregard of his or their interest and with prayer for necessary orders for safeguarding his or their interest and also the interest of any other member, the Court shall, after hearing the parties, if satisfied that the interest of the applicant or applicants has been or is being or is likely to be prejudicially affected, may make such order as prayed for or such other order as may be deemed fit including direction to cancel or modify any resolution or transaction or regulate the conduct of the Company's affairs in future in such manner or to amend any provision of the Memorandum of Association of the Company; therefore, it is clear that the provision of section 397 of the Indian Law is applicable "for putting an end to the matter complained of" and that means that the act of oppression was, at the time of filing of the application, continuing and nor a past act of oppression. But the provisions of section 233 of our Companies Act is not limited for application only in the case of continuous act prejudicial to the interest of any share-holder but also applicable to remedy any past or present or any intended future transaction affecting any interest of the Company and or its share-holders(s). The learned Advocate submitted that no material could be produced before the Court to show that there was necessity for sale of the Company's land and that there was any Board resolution for such sale and authorising the respondent No. 3 to exercise the authority of the Managing Director provided in Article 82 of the Articles of Association and there being no authority given to the respondent No. 3 to execute and register any sale deed or to enter into any transaction for sale of Company's land, the alleged sales of the Company's land in favour of the respondent Nos. 6-8 by the respondent No. 3 are illegal, without lawful authority and not binding on the Company and the Company has and maintains all right, title and interest as owners on the land in reference. The learned Advocate also submitted that if the petitioner No. 1 is in control of the management and affairs of the respondent Company, as claimed by the respondent Nos. 1 to 3, then what necessitated execution and registration of the sale deeds in reference by the respondent No. 3 and not by the petitioner No. 1 and the malafide and fraud practiced in the transaction is proved, and that by such illegal sale the right, title and interest of the respondent Company on the lands converted by the sale deed (Annexure-F to F-5) have not been affected and the Company is still the lawful owner and possessor of said land and the respondents No. 6 to 8 have not acquired any valid right, title and interest on the said land by such purchase through the said sale deeds and hence, the respondent Company should be directed to take legal steps against such illegal sale deeds.

7. Mr M Moniruzzaman Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 6, submitted that the transaction between the Company and the respondent No. 6 being the transaction of the Company with a 3rd party cannot be challenged by any share-holder inasmuch as, the respondent No. 6 is a bonafide purchaser without notice and against valuable consideration. The learned Advocate submits that no matter there is relationship amongst the respondent Nos. 2, 3 and 6 to 8, such relationship will have no bearing in the transaction between the Company and the respondent Nos. 6-8 and that the respondent No. 3 having authority under the provisions of Article 82 of the Articles of Association duly executed and registered the sale deeds in accordance with the provisions of law against valuable consideration therefore, such transaction cannot be defeated and this Court under section 233 of the Act cannot set aside such sale, inasmuch as this Court cannot nullify any registered deed of sale, which can only be done in a properly framed suit in a Civil Court in accordance with law. The learned Advocate referred to several decisions of the Indian Jurisdiction namely, in the case of Suresh Kumar Sanghi vs Supreme Motors Ltd of Delhi High Court reported in (1983) 54 Company Cases 235; and in the case of CP Gnanasambanbam vs Tamil Nadu Transport Private Limited and others of Madras High Court reported in (1971) 41 Company Cases 26; and in the case of Raj Sahhab Vishwamita vs Amar Nath Mehrotra of Allahabad High Court reported in (1986) 59 Company Cases, 854; and in the case of Sheth Mohanlal Ganpatram vs Shri Sayaji Jubilee Cotton and Jute Mills Co Ltd and others of the Gujarat High Court reported in (1964) 34 Company Cases 777; and in the case of Shanti Prashad Jain vs Kalinga Tubes Ltd of the Supreme Court of India reported in (1965) 35 Company Cases 351, in support of his contention that no application under section 233 of the Act is maintainable unless the allegation complained of as to prejudicial act is continuing on the date of filing of the petition. The learned Advocate submitted that provision of section 233 of the Act is a new provision provided for safeguarding the interest of the minority share-holder since earlier the minority holders had to abide by the acts and decisions of the majority share-holders, who controlled the management and affairs of the Company, no matter whether beneficial to or against the interest of the minority share-holders and that as per wish of the majority share-holders the Board of Directors is formed. The share-holders, however, have the right to go for action against the Directors for their wrongdoings but cannot get any relief against the wrong acts done favouring any third party by the Directors even if exercised in a manner prejudicial to the interest of the members of the Company. In the Indian Companies Act section 153 C was added in 1956 which was based on section 210 of the English Companies Act, 1948. The purpose of the added section was to give an alternative remedy to winding up in case of mismanagement or oppression, keeping the Company alive. Since it was felt that though it might be just and equitable for ordering winding up of a Company but it was not fair for winding up of a Company when the Company was otherwise solvent and could do its business profitably providing benefits to its share-holders through proper management in the business and affairs of the Company, by changing the management. The Indian Companies Act subsequently subdivided the section 153C into sections 397 and 398 in the new Indian Companies Act.

8. The learned Advocate then in the words of his Lordship in the case of Shanti Prashad Jain reported in (1965) 35 Company Cases (SC) 351 (366) submitted that "it is not enough to show that there is just and equitable case for winding up the Company, though that must be shown as preliminary to the application of section 397. It must further be shown that the conduct of the majority share-holders was oppressive to the minority as members and this requires that events have to be considered not in isolation but as a part of a consecutive story. There must be continuous acts on the part of the majority share-holders, continuing up to the date of petition, showing that the affairs of the company were being conducted in a manner oppressive to some part of the members. The conduct must be burdensome, harsh and wrongful and mere lack of confidence between the majority share-holders and the minority share-holders would not be enough unless the lack of confidence springs from oppression of a minority by a majority in the management of the Company's affairs, and such oppression must involve at least an element of lack of probity or fair dealing to a member in the matter of his proprietary rights as a share-holder."

9. The learned Advocate, in support of his contention states that the purpose of section 233 is to restrain or stop the majority share-holder from continuing with their prejudicial acts disregarding the interest of the share-holder or any one of them and that the stopping of any prejudicial act leads one to presume that a prejudicial act is continuing or is in existence, inasmuch as in a case of past act, question of stoppage or order of restrainment does not arise and the section thus provides wide power on the Court and the Court can pass such order as it may think necessary " for putting an end" to the oppression or mismanagement, prejudice to the interest of the share-holder(s), by the controlling majority share-holders and, as such, the provision is preventive in nature and accordingly, this section cannot come to the aid for any relief in respect of any past act or closed transaction between the Company and a 3rd party. The learned Advocate in the language of Justice Bhegwati in the case of Sheth Mohanlal Ganpatram reported in (1964) 34 Company Cases 777(807) submitted that "Apart from the plain dictate of the language of sections 397 and 398 there are other considerations which with me in taking the view that a past and concluded transaction between a company and a third party cannot be set aside on an application under sections 397 and 398. Let us see what are the consequences to which the other construction must logically and inevitably lead and then consider whether the legislature could have possibly intended such consequences. The effect of accepting that construction would be that if a transaction has been entered into between a Company and a third party as part of a continuous and continuing course of oppressive or prejudicial conduct, any share-holders who are aggrieved by such conduct would be entitled to ask the court to set aside such transaction. Now such transaction may not come within any of the three recognised exceptions to the rule in Foss vs Harbottle and yet the aggrieved share-holders would be entitled to challenge such transaction by taking proceedings in their own right under sections 397 and 398. The result would be enlarged beyond the three well recognised exceptions and whenever any transaction is entered into by a company with a third party which is part of oppressive or prejudicial conduct on the part of those in management of the affairs of the company, it would be liable to be challenged at the instance of the aggrieved share-holders. Now could the legislature have intended to bring about such a result which would have the effect of almost abrogating the rule in Foss vs Harbottle so far as transactions with third parties are concerned? Could the legislature have intended to strike a death-blow to the rule in Foss vs Harbottle which has held the field now for well-nigh over hundred years and that too in this indirect manner? 1 should be certainly slow to accept a construction which would have the effect of producing this consequence." The learned Advocate submits that otherwise the result would be that even when a company may have no cause of action to sue a third party, any share-holder, being opposed to such a transaction between the company and third party, may move the court for setting aside such transaction. There may be cases that the transaction between the company and a third party, which is bonafide and beneficial for the majority of the share-holders, to which some of the share-holders objects and in such case the minority share-holders) are not entitled to any relief under section 233 of the Act.

10. The legislature cannot be said to have intended to confer such cause of action on individual or minority share-holder (s) against the third party or the company so as to entitle him/them to set aside a bonafide and beneficial transaction of the company, otherwise it would make it impossible for any outsider to deal with a Company or a person advancing the interest of the Company and that will clearly be detrimental to the interest of the Company, for it would scare away the person dealing with the Company.

11. The learned Advocate then submits that in the instant case the respondent No. 6 has purchased the land for setting up a Charitable Hospital and in the meantime the respondent No. 6 has invested a large amount of money, for developing the land and also in arranging procurement of the hospital equipment, and that the Company having got its money against the sale of the land in reference the petitioner share-holders have also been benefited there from. The learned Advocate submitted that in order to succeed in an application under section 233 of the Companies Act the petitioners require to show that the transaction complained of is of prejudicial nature and has affected the interest of the share-holders, which is absent in the instant case, inasmuch as no material has been produced before this Court to show that by the sale transactions the petitioners have been affected or their interest have been prejudiced, in any way.

12. Mr Akhtar Imam, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent Nos.1- 3, submitted that the Company has sold the land as per provisions of law and there is no legal bar in selling Company's property in favour of any relation of the share-holder(s) and or Director(s) of the Company. The Company has sold the land against valuable consideration and with the sale proceeds the outstanding dues of the Company has been paid and the boundary wall has been erected, and those acts are beneficial for the Company as well as for the share-holders. The learned Advocate submitted that under Article 82 of the Articles of Association of the Company the Executive Director has been authorised to execute and register sale deeds in respect of any property of the Company sold in favour of the purchaser (s) and that the petitioner No. 1 as Managing Director has also earlier sold Company's landed property through registered sale deeds and that by the same resolution both the Managing Director and the Executive Director were given the authority to exercise their powers under the authority of the Articles of Association of the Company for completing any transaction in respect of immovable property through execution and registration of the required sale deeds. The learned Advocate further submitted that the petitioner No.1 is still the Managing Director of the Company and both, in fact and in law, he is the Chief Executive of the Company and is in control of the management of the Company. The respondent No. 3, Executive Director, has acted in accordance with Article 82 with consent and within the knowledge of the petitioner No. 1 and therefore the petitioner No.1 is now stopped from raising any objection being barred by the principle of waiver, estoppel and acquiescence. The learned Advocate submitted that the land in reference has been transferred for a noble cause for setting up a Charitable Hospital but that too is not without consideration but against valuable consideration as per market value and that the main object for setting up the respondent company is to purchase and sell movable and immovable properties and therefore, the impugned sale is in accordance with the business of the Company and therefore, the petitioners cannot challenge the transaction in question. The learned Advocate also adopted the submission made by the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No.6 on the point of maintainability of the instant application under section 233 of the Companies Act, 1994, inasmuch as the transaction in reference is a past transaction, whereas, according to him, the provision of section 233 requires that an application can be filed only when the action complained of is still continuing, and the relief to be given is of preventive nature and that if a transaction between the Company and a 3rd party, who has no connection with the Company, is allowed to be nullified by the share-holder(s), then all such transactions will be opened to and subjected to challenge by any share-holder, resulting in creating a source for chaos and stoppage in the dealings and business of the Company. The instant application is malafide and for which instead of raising any objection at the time of the sale-transaction, the petitioners have come up with this application at this later stage. In view of the admitted fact that internal dispute has arisen amongst the petitioner share-holders and the respondent share-holders of the respondent-company, the instant application is ex facie an act of malafide on the part of the petitioner and the application is liable to be rejected.

13. I have perused the application and the affidavits filed by the petitioners, the affidavits-in-opposition filed separately by the respondent Nos. 1-3 and the respondent No. 6. I have considered the submissions made by the learned Advocates for the respective parties. I have also perused the decisions cited by the learned Advocate of the respondent No. 6.

14. The learned Advocate for the petitioner in reply has referred to an unreported decision in the case of Nurul Huq Chowdhury vs Mr M Mahjabin Chowdhury (Matter No. 2 of 2002 disposed of by the judgment and order dated 18-11-02 in support of his contention that through introduction of section 233 of the Companies Act provisions have been made to safeguard the interest of the minority share-holder and that if the conduct on the other side is both prejudicial and unfair, there is no independent or overriding requirement that it should be just and equitable to grant relief only when the petitioner comes to the court with clean hands. The combined effect of introducing such provision in our Companies Act to empower the Court to make such order as it thinks fit for giving relief, if it is first satisfied that the affairs of the Company are being or have been conducted in a manner which is unfairly prejudicial to the interest of the Company or some part of the members and therefore, even if it is found that the petitioners have not come up with clean hands but the respondents acted illegally and prejudicially to the interest of the Company or its share-holders, the Court is empowered to give relief under section 233 of the Act. I find substance in the submission and therefore, the instant application is not liable to be rejected even if it is found that the petitioners have not come with clean hands and the action complained of is against the interest of the Company and or the share-holders.

15. It appears that the petitioners have challenged the authority of the respondent No.3, the Executive Director, in transferring the lands of the Company through execution and registration of the sale deeds (Annexures-F to F-5) on behalf of the Company in favour of the respondent Nos. 6-8 and, for that matter, it has been asserted that the said action of the respondent No. 3 is prejudicial to the interest of the company and its share-holders. The allegation is that though Article 82 has given an authority enabling the Executive Director to sign and execute any sale deed on behalf of the Company in respect of the Company's property jointly with the Managing Director or singly by himself only upon a resolution of he Board of Directors giving an approval for exercising such authority, but in the instant case no such approval was given i.e. no such resolution was adopted by the Board of Directors allowing the Executive Director to exercise his authority as provided under Article 82. I have perused the sale deeds in reference executed by the respondent No. 3 in favour of the respondent Nos. 6-8, copies of which have been annexed as Annexures F to F-5 to the application. It appears from the said copies of the sale deeds that the Executive Director has executed the sale deeds asserting his authority under Article 82 of the Articles of Association. But no resolution empowering the Executive Director for exercising such authority under Article 82 could be produced before this Court. It further appears that the sale deeds have been made in favour of the nephew and wife of the respondent No. 2 and son of the respondent No. 3 and no proof or any material has been placed before this Court to show that the sale proceeds have been received by the Company or the sale proceeds have been deposited in the bank account of the Company. Further, neither any Board resolution, nor any material has been produced before the Court to show that there was any necessity on the part of the Company for sale of the lands in reference. It is true that there is no bar in transferring any property belonging to a Company by way of sale by the Directors in favour of the near relations but in such case the Director or the Management is required to be much more cautious to avoid any allegation of malafide or favouritism and it is natural that in case of sale of immovable property of any Company by the Director, the share-holders of the Company do take resolution for sale of such immovable property and further, through a resolution the Company gives authority to the Managing Director or any other Director, in spite of provisions giving such authority to the Managing Director is in existence in the Articles of Association, for concluding any such transaction relating to the immovable property and to execute and register the required sale deed(s). In the instant case such authority is absent. In view of the facts and circumstance of the case that respondent Nos. 1-3 could not produce any material to show that Executive Director has been duly authorised by the Board of Directors through any resolution to exercise his authority under Article 82 of the Articles of Association. 1 find merit in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the respondent No.3 acted illegally and without lawful authority in executing and registering the sale deeds (Annexure-F to F-5) in favour of the respondent Nos.6 to 8 for the alleged sale of immovable property of the Company and thus the right, title and interest of the Company in the lands in reference as owners have not been affected at all and the company continues to be the lawful owner. The disposal of any immovable property in the absence of proof of any necessity of the Company cannot be said to be a bonafide transaction and moreso, when in the instant case the transfers have been made in favour of the close relations of the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 and when admittedly, internal disputes exist amongst the petitioner share-holders and the respondent-share-holders of the Company and the sale proceeds have not been deposited in the account of the Company. In the facts and circumstances, there is reason to believe that the respondent-share-holders, being majority, have acted malafide to deprive and to cause prejudice to the interest of the petitioner made sham-transaction of sale. Even if it may not be possible to annul any sale deed executed and registered under the Registration Act, on an application under section 233 of the Companies Act, yet in the instant case, I am of the view that the petitioner's challenge is not for declaring the sale deeds to be illegal and not genuine but to declare the action of the Executive Director in disposing of the Company's property without lawful authority and to declare the sales in reference to be illegal and unauthorised transaction being made by an unauthorised person and without lawful authority. A lawful owner cannot be divested from his property by any illegal action of any unauthorized person through executing and registering a purported sale deed. Thus the alleged transaction of the Company's property in favour of the respondent Nos. 6 to 8 by the unauthorised respondent No. 3 cannot disentitle the Company to own and possess the land in reference and the Company continues to have its right, title and interest in the land in reference and such unauthorised action of sales by the respondent No. 3 is of no legal effect. Further, purchasers (respondent Nos. 6-8) being near relations of the respondent Nos. 2 and 3, particularly respondents No. 6, should have been more cautious in purchasing Company's land and should have retained a copy of the resolution, if there had been any, authorising the respondent No.3 to exercise his authority under Article 82 of the Articles of Association, when he appears to have knowledge about the provisions of said Article 82 as has been referred to in his affidavit-in-opposition. The bonafide purchasers have some obligations to perform in purchasing immovable property to ensure proper purchase.

16. The provisions of law as to section 397 of the Indian Companies Act and those of section 233 of our Companies Act though appears to be similar but are not same. It has been rightly pointed out by Dr M Zahir that the relief under section 397 of the Indian Act is for "bringing to an end the matter complained of refers to an action which is continuing otherwise, question of "bringing to an end" cannot arise. The words "with a view to bringing to an end the matter complained of" is absent in section 233 of our Companies Act. Sub-section 3 of section 233 of the Companies Act, 1994, which runs as under:

Section 233(3) "If after hearing the parties present on the date fixed, the Court is of opinion that the interest of the application or applicants has been or is being or is likely to be prejudicially affected for reasons specified in the application, it may make such order as prayed for or such other order as it deems fit including the direction;

(a) to cancel or modify any resolution or transaction;

or

(b) .........................

(c) .........................

17. The words "has been" relate to a past act and the words "is being" relate to the present transaction and the words "is likely to be" relate to the future transaction and reading, as such, 1 am of the view that the section 233 of the Act provides for remedy to one or more share-holder(s), subject to his/their qualification as per section-233 (1) of the Act, and he/they may move a Company Court against any action of any Director or Directors, if exercised in a manner prejudicial to or in disregard of interest of any of such share-holder(s) and in such case such share-holder (s) may pray for such order as would be necessary for safeguarding his/their interest in the Company or its property. The word "transaction" as appearing in section 233 (3) of the Act is absent in section 397 of the Indian Companies Act and the word "transaction" includes any deal by the Company. The provisions of section 233 of our Companies Act is much more wider than those of section 397 of the Indian Companies Act. It need be considered that section 233 of the Act has been provided to safeguard the interest of the share-holders in general but it is to be noted that the said provision cannot be allowed to be exercised by any of the share-holders against any valid action or transaction of the Company or its Director(s) which may affect his individual interest but benefits the company. There may be cases where transaction of the Company is beneficial for the majority of the share-holders but prejudicial to the interest of minority share-holder say, for instance, there being need for raising money for implementation of a new project of the Company, there being no consensus, the majority of the share-holders passed a resolution for sale of certain properties of the Company and sold the same in due course and though such resolution and the sale may not be liked by some share-holders who were minority in the meeting and they considered the same as against their interest and, as such, is oppressive, in such case relief under the provision of section 233 cannot be available. It is to be seen that whether transaction in question has been made bonafide and in the interest of the Company in general and is beneficial for the majority of the share-holders, and if the answer is in the affirmative, then in spite of such transaction being prejudicial to the interest of some share-holder it cannot be questioned under provisions of section 233 of the Companies Act. The cases cited by the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 6 and also adopted by the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent Nos. 1-3, no doubt, have propounded sound principle of law with which I am in respectful agreement and in those decisions it has been settled that an application 'under section 397 of the Indian Companies Act has to be filed during the continuity of the action complained of. By the said provision the Court has been given power to pass orders within a limited scope i.e. "with a view to bringing to an end the matters complained of "which provision is absent in section 233 of our Companies Act. The provisions of section 397 of the Indian Companies Act are preventive in nature, whereas section 233 of out Companies Act are remedial is nature, as such, the decisions cited by the learned Advocate for respondent No. 6 are not applicable in the instant case.

18. It has been submitted that the petitioners have not come up with clean hands before this Court, inasmuch as in his application the petitioner categorically stated that no meetings of the Board of Directors or of share-holders have taken place and no resolution has been adopted by the Company, but in the supplementary affidavit as well as in the main application the petitioner has claimed that his tenure of office as managing director has been extended for five years, which supports the claim of the respondents that the meetings of the Board of Directors have been held; and thus, it is proved that on oath the petitioners have made false statements and, in view of above, it was submitted on behalf of the respondents that this application should be rejected inasmuch as this is an equitable relief. But having regard to the fact that the purpose of section 233 of the Companies Act is to empower the court to make such order as it thinks fit if it is satisfied that the affairs of the Company has been or is being or likely to be conducted in unfair or prejudicial manner and against interest of some of the share-holders, if not against all the share-holders, and it has been found in the instant case that the respondent No. 3 by his action has tried not only to injure the interest of the petitioner-share-holders but, in fact, has caused prejudice to the interest of the Company in attempting to sell land of the Company unauthorisedly, although there was no necessity to dispose of the property of the Company and the land can be used or utilised for the benefit of the Company and its share-holders in future and, as such, though the petitioner appears to have come not with clean hands but relief should not be denied having regard to the fact that prejudice has been caused to the company itself. Therefore, although the petitioner has moved this application not with clean hand, but the petition cannot be rejected in the fact and circumstances of the case and on the basis of the decision in the case of Nurul Huq Chowdhury referred to above.

<u>19. In the facts and circumstances, I am of the view that the respondent No. 3 with the aid of respondent No. 2 has acted illegally and unauthorisedly in executing and registering the sale deeds, evidenced by Annexure-F to F-5 to the application under section 233 of the Act, purportedly for and on behalf of the Company, claiming exercise of his authority under Article 82 of Articles of Association of the Company. There being no resolution authorising the respondent No. 3, the Executive Director, to exercise the authority under Article 82 of the Articles of Association of the Company and there being no necessity for such sale, it cannot be said to be bonafide and the respondent No. 3 has acted illegally and without lawful authority and by such illegal and unlawful action of respondent No. 3, the right, title and interest of the Company on its property have not been affected in any way and the respondent Nos. 6-8 have not acquired any right, title and interest on the land of company. The sales have no validity and effect in the eye of law.</u>

20. Accordingly, the application is allowed without any order as to costs.

(a) The alleged sales of Company's land in favour of defendant Nos. 6 to 8 through registered sale deeds evidenced by Annexure-F to F-5 to the application, are declared to be illegal, without lawful authority and of no legal effect and by such sales the right, title and interest of the Company in the lands, detailed in the schedules of the sale deeds evidenced by Annexure-F to F-5 to the application, have not been affected, and the respondent Nos. 6 to 8 have not acquired any lawful right, title and interest in the land in reference detailed in the schedule of the sale deeds evidenced by Annexure-F to F-5 to the application.

(b) The respondent-company should take necessary steps to safeguard its right, title and interest in the lands in reference, if necessary, by taking legal steps for cancellation of the sale deeds in reference as evidenced by Annexure-F to F-5 to the main application; and

(c) The petitioner No.1, subject to his tenure as Managing Director, should be allowed to discharge his function as per Articles of Association, and in case it is not possible for the petitioner to function as such with the respondent share-holders, then the petitioners should offer their shares in the Company for sale to the respondent-share-holders and the respondent-share-holders, in their discretion, may purchase the shares of the petitioner-share-holders and in case the respondent-share-holders decline to purchase the shares of the petitioner; then the Company should purchase the shares of the petitioner-share-holders as per market value and the value of the shares should be reassessed and fixed by the Chartered Auditors of the Company having regard to the assets and liability of the respondent company and the paid up share capital be adjusted and the share register be corrected accordingly.

The costs and fees to be borne by the respondent-Company.

End.
