case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 10th January, 2004 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 29 of 1996).
full_judgment:
Mohammad Fazlul Karim J: The defendant No.5 petitioner seeks leave to appeal against the judgment and decree dated 10.01.2004 passed by the High Court Division in Appeal from Original Decree No. 29 of 1996 dismissing the appeal affirming those dated 3.9.1995 of the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Khulna in Title Suit No. 26 of 1992.

<u>2. The plaintiff-respondent filed the suit impleading the petitioner as defendant No.5 and others as the defendants praying for decree declaring the deed of agreement between the parties cancelled and for recovery of compensation to the tune of Tk. 25 lac stating, inter alia, that in terms of Asian Development Bank Loan No. 329 Bangladesh Krishi Bank was entrusted to establish three Ice Plants in Bangladesh and in terms thereof the plaintiff decided to establish Ice Plant and Cold Storage on the supplying of the necessary machinery by the defendant No.5- Krishi Bank out of its fund and being approached the agreement No. 25 was executed on 15.06.1985 between the concerned parties including the plaintiff and the defendant No.5 and the plaintiff was granted sanction letter in 1985 on condition that the Krishi Bank would supply the machinery on payment of fund in foreign currency and the plaintiff would purchase land and construct factory building for establishment of the Ice Plant and cold storage. It was agreed upon that the loan would be sanctioned in foreign currency and not in Bangladeshi currency. A tripartite contract was entered into between M/s. Jain Enterprise on 16.5.1985 for supplying of machinery and other materials and in the said contract Frick Company of USA rep-resented by its local agent Messers Eastern Trading Agency Limited was the first party and in the 2nd agreement Covington Diesel of USA represented by local agent Messers Eastern Trading Company was the first party and in both the agreements 2nd and 3rd parties were Bangladesh Krishi Bank and the plaintiff's company respectively. The plaintiff in terms of the agreement deposited 10% of Letter of Credit margin with Bangladesh Krishi Bank, Labonchora Branch and also opened Letter of Credit on 18.6.1985 with the Principal Office of Janata Bank, Dilkusha Commercial Area. In terms of the first agreement it was decided that a compressor would be supplied to the plaintiff and as there were some mistakes committed by the Krishi Bank at the time of opening of the Letter of Credit the machinery had not been reached and the Letter of Credit stood can-celled and the plaintiff had no latches or inaction in the matter but it was caused due to negligence and mistake of the Krishi Bank which led the plaintiff to suffer irreparable loss and injury and also a loss of time of about 1½ years. Bangladesh Krishi Bank regretted not to supply the imported Compressor and the Generator and advised the plaintiff to import the Compressor and the Generator at his own initiative. Consequently, agreement was executed on 05.11.1986 for importing of the Compressor and the Generator and the first party to the said contract was Sunita Textile and Engineering, Calcutta represented by their local agent Kingsook Limited, Dhaka and for the 2nd agreement Ward Power Limited. Stamford, UK represented by its local agent Messers Kingsook Limited was the first party and in the said agreement 3rd and 4th parties were the plaintiff's company and the Bangladesh Krishi Bank respectively. In terms of the said agreement the plaintiff opened Letter of Credit with Janata Bank on 23.11.1986 of importing a Generator through Chittagong Port. It is further alleged that for the establishment of the project there was a tripartite contract executed between the concerned parties for supplying of other machinery and one Messers Jain Enterprise, Bombay represented by local agent M/s. Eastern Trading Limited was the first party and Bangladesh Krishi Bank and the plaintiff were the 2nd  party and 310 party respectively. In terms of the said agreement Air Blower and Amonia Gas along with 26 other items were to be sup-plied and the foreign currency for those materials were lying with the Krishi Bank and in terms of the advice of Krishi Bank the plaintiff opened Letter of Credit with Janata Bank on 18.6.1985 which was valid up to 31.12.1985 and the plaintiff deposited 10% of the Letter of Credit which was opened on 18.6.1985 in terms of the agreement No. 25. A portion of the machinery arrived at Benapol port but having several reminders Bangladesh Krishi Bank and insurance company did not make any inspection and also did not take any step to release the machinery which were lying at the Benapol port uncared for and ultimately the plaintiff had to release the said part machinery on payment of huge salami and demurrage on 27.10.1986. The supplier did not fulfill the contract in supplying the entire machinery and the 2nd installment of the machinery arrived at Benapol port on 09.5.1987 without Air Blower and Amonia Gas. The plaintiff further alleged that the defendant No.5 Bangladesh Krishi Bank has not yet arranged to import of Air Blower and Amonia Gas, without which the project in question, is not able to go into operation. The 2nd installment of the machinery were kept lying at Benopol port and the machinery were mostly damaged by woodworms and also destroyed by insects and the plaintiff got the said materials inspected through "The Finds" who did the inspection work from 19.9.1987 to 12.1.1987 and submitted their report on 19.10.1987. From the report it appears that Bombay office transmitted 82 packets of machinery but only 80 packets arrived at Benopol port and most of the machinery were infested by insects, woodworms and damaged causing unusable. The plaintiff wrote letter to the defendant No.5 and also submitted the aforesaid report to defendant No.5 on 26.10.1987 but without any result. In 1985 when the plaintiff took up the project for establishment of ice Plant and Cold Storage, there was huge demand for such plant and shortage in the country and the plaintiff could earn profit if project could go into operation in 1986-87 but due to latches and inaction of the defendant No.5 the project could not go into operation. The plaintiff subsequently applied for additional loan and asked the defendant No.5 to import Air Blower and Amonia Gas for the project but those were not attended to and meanwhile the project cost increased by 35%. Meanwhile, the plaintiff acquired .16½ decimals of land in commercial area and constructed a factory building and thereby invested about Tk.13,00,000/-. The plaintiff further requested the defendant No.5 for loan of Tk. 35,00,000/- and subsequently asked for at least Tk. 18,97.075/- but the defendant No.5 informed the plaintiff to apply in the relevant form to which the plaintiff submitted form on 12.12.1987 but the said prayer remained unattended. On the other hand, without supplying Air Blower and Amonia Gas and other necessary machinery defendant No.5 by letter dated 17.7.1988 wanted to know as to when the plaintiff would go in operation with the project and subsequently the then General Manager of the Krishi Bank made inspection of the factory building constructed by the plaintiff and assured the plaintiff with financial help but ultimately did nothing and at the time of approaching the plaintiff was asked to supply lay out plan to defendant No.5 by letter dated 15.8.1988 and the plaintiff accordingly deposited the lay out plan and other necessary documents on 29.8.1988 but the Krishi Bank did not take any action in the matter and ultimately the plaintiff sent a notice through his learned Advocate on 09.05.1989 to the District General Manager of Krishi Bank intimating clearly that, the non-supplying of Air Blower and Amonia Gas and for non-performance of other terms of the contract, the agreement between the parties stood cancelled and it was further intimated that for non-performance of the contract by the Krishi Bank the plaintiff is entitled to compensation of Tk. 25,00,000/- Thus, the correspondence continued between the parties and the defendant No.5 having done nothing the plaintiff was compelled to institute the suit.</u>

3. The defendant No.5 Bangladesh Krishi Bank contested the suit by filing a written statement contending that in terms of the contract dated 15.6.1985 between M/s. Jain Enterprise through its agent, Eastern Trading being the first party and Bangladesh Krishi Bank being the 2nd party and M/s. Dadajee Ice, Plant and Storage Limited being the 3rd party, the plaintiff opened Letter of Credit on 28.6.1984 and the plaintiff received the first installment of the machinery on 06.10.1986. It was also alleged that the period of Letter of Credit was extended up to 31.12.1986 and M/s. Jain Enterprise supplied all other machinery excluding Amonia Gas and Air Blower and the defendant No.5 made part payment for the part machinery to the supplier. The defendant alleged that the goods were damaged due to latches and negligence of the plaintiff who did not take delivery of the goods in time in spite of advice of defendant No.5. The defendant No.5 further alleged that by letter dated 29.10.1988 the plaintiff was directed to deposit the lay out plan and other documents but those were not deposited by the plaintiff and his prayer for additional loan could not be considered. According to the defendant they co-operated with the plaintiff in all respects for speedy establishment of Ice Plant and Cold Storage project and the defendant No.5 is not guilty of any latches or inaction but performed their part of the contract fully and the plaintiff is not entitled to the compensation of Tk.25,00,000/-, as alleged in the plaint. According to the contesting defendant, the agreement with the plaintiff is not liable to be cancelled as the defendant performed his part of the contract and the plaintiff failed to perform his part of the contract and therefore the defendant No.5 was not guilty of any latches or inaction in the matter. It was further alleged that in the contract there was a clause for arbitration and the suit was not therefore maintainable. The defendant also alleged that Air Blower and Amoina Gas was not essential for commission for Ice Plan and Cold Storage project. The contesting defendant also alleged that the plaintiff had sold out almost all the Ice cans and also let out the building with machinery to one wood merchant at a monthly rent of Tk. 5,000/-and the machinery was kept uncared for and prayed for dismissal of the suit.

4. The trial Court framed necessary issues and on consideration of the evidence on record came to the finding that the defendant no.5 did not perform his part of the contract by supplying all the machinery including Air Blower and Amonia Gas which were mandatory for commission of the project and thereby the plaintiff was put to sustain huge loss and injury and the contract in question is liable to be cancelled in terms of Sections 51 and 53 of the contract Act. The trial Court further considered the evidence and concluded that the plaintiff is entitled to compensation of Tk. 25,00,000/-. Accordingly, by judgment and decree dated 04.9.1995 the trial Court decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff with cost.

5. An appeal therefrom was, however, dismissed.

6. Dr. Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner submitted that both the Courts below failed to comprehend that admittedly there was a tripartite agreement and it was not disputed and the present petitioner as per contract opened the Letter of Credit for all equipment required for the implementation of the project of Ice Plant and it is also on record that the supplier M/s. Jain Enterprise, 1st Party failed to supply two items of the Letter of Credit namely 'Air Blower' and `Amonia Gas' and it is also on record that before releasing the shipment and making the payment of Letter of Credit the present petitioner sought permission from the plaintiff-respondent (Exhibit Nos. 36 and 37) and after obtaining their consent accepted the shipment and made payment thereon, which, in no way, came within the mischief of sections 51,53 and 54 of the Contract Act. The learned Counsel further submitted that the learned Courts below also failed to take notice that there is a tripartite agreement and the present petitioner is not the supplier but financier, who is only responsible to facilitate finance for necessary equipment for setting up an 'Ice Plant' and there is noting to show that the present petitioner did not supply necessary funds for purchasing the equipment, rather it is admitted in the plaint that "বাদীপক্ষ উক্ত মালামালের ব্যাপারে সম্পূর্ন অনভিজ্ঞ থাকায় ঐ সময় মালামাল বুঝিয়া পাইতে পারেন নাই তাছাড়া কাষ্টমের চাপের মুখে তাহারা উক্ত মালামালের কাগজপত্র না দেখেই সই করিতে বাধ্য হন। ১৯৮৫ ইং সালে যখন প্রকল্পটি হাতে নেওয়া হয় তখন আইস প্লান্ট ও স্টোরেজ এর চাহিদা দেশে ছিল। এবং ১৯৮৬-৮৭ সালের ভিতর উৎপাদনে যাইতে পারিলে উহার ফিজিবিলিটি এবং প্রকল্প হাতে নেওয়ার উদ্দেশ্য সফল হইত। এবং উহা একটি লাভজনক ব্যবসা হইত।" clearly shows that plaintiff's lack of knowledge prevented implementation of the contract and under apprehension of non-profitability, the plaintiff filed the suit and as such the Courts below erred in law in decreeing the suit. The learned Counsel lastly submitted that the Courts below have also failed to construe the impugned agreements in its true perspective and wrongly treated the petitioner as a supplier and applied Sections 51,53 and 54 of the Contract Act, and as such the impugned judgment and decree are liable to be set aside.

7. On materials it is to be found that under the Asian Development Bank 3 Ice Plants were to be established in Bangladesh and the Bangladesh Krishi Bank was entrusted with the same. It is not disputed that the Bangladesh Krishi Bank invited tenders on 18.2.1982 for importing of machinery and M/s. Jain Enterprise participated to supply the machinery through its local agent and entered into an agreement No. 125 dated 17.3.1983. It is also admitted that out of 3 projects the plaintiff decided to establish one Ice Plant and Cold Storage and the Bangladesh Krishi Bank agreed to finance the plaintiff in foreign currency and also to import machinery for the plaintiff’s project and accordingly an agreement No.124 dated 15.6.1985 was executed. It is also admitted that a sanction letter was issued in favour of the plaintiff in 1985 with the assurance that the defendant Bank would supply machinery at the cost to be paid in foreign currency.

8. The evidence of D.W.1 supports that as per terms of the agreement the defendant No.5 was duty bound to supply Air blower and Amonia gas on importation of the same but the plaintiff did not get the supplying of Air blower and Amonia gas. Admittedly as per terms of the conteract flowing out of the contract agreement No.125 dated 17.3.1983 and subsequent amendment thereto it was the duty of defendant No.5 to supply Amonia gas including air blower and the defendant failed to perform their contract entered into between the parties. The High Court Division considered the provision of Section 53 of the Contract Act providing reciprocal promises that when one party for the contract prevented other party to perform his promise to perform, is entitled to realize the compensation from the other party to any loss as has been sustained in consequence of the non-performance of the contract. The plaintiff has laid evidence to show that non-performance of the promise i.e. the defendant No.5 did not supply air blower and Amonia gas, lack of which the plaintiff could not set up the Ice Plant and cold storage. Section 54 of the Contract Act also provides that when the contract consists of reciprocal promises and one of them could not perform the same or that his performance cannot be claimed till the other has performed and the promisor failed to perform it, such promisor cannot claim the perform of reciprocal promises, must make compensation to the other party to the contract for any loss that party may have sustained by the non-performance of the contract.

<u>9. In the instant case, the Courts below have considered Sections 53 and 54 of the Contract Act and arrived at a finding on material on record that the defendant No.5-petitioner is guilty of non-performance of his part of the contract resulting in causing huge loss to the plaintiff-respondent. It is on record that the plaintiff has repeatedly requested the defendant No. 5 petitioner to provide him the required fund and to supply the wanting air blower and Amonia gas for commissioning the project to which the defendant No.5-petitioner has left a deaf ear, for which the plaintiff has suffered substantial loss and the trial Court has assessed the compensation at Tk.25 lac which the Court of appeal below as a final Court of fact has refused to interfere.</u>

10. In view of the above, the submissions of the learned Counsel for the petitioner have no substance.

11. The petition is dismissed.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 16th August1999 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 400 of 1997)
full_judgment:
Mohammad Fazlul Karim, J.:- This appeal by leave at the instance of the writ petitioner appellants is directed against the judgment and order dated 16.8.1999 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 400 of 1997 discharging, the rule that was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why Rule 5(1) and 5(3A) and rule 8(2) of Bangladesh Civil Service (Examination and Promotion) Rules, 1986 as published by Respondent No. 1 under S.R.O. No./54-L/86/ME (Rule-5) RR-12/86 dated 13th February, 1986 and the S.R.O. No. 117-Law/94 Sha Ma: (Rule-4)-RR-39/88 dated 11.4.1994 vide Annexure-I and L respectively and Rule 8(e) of the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules as published by SRO No. 130-Law/93-Sha:Ma: (Rule-4) RR-60/93 dated 4th July, 1993 vide Annexure 'K' and the minutes dated 11.12.96 of the Departmental promotion committee headed by respondent No. 2 and the decisions taken thereon and signed on 14.12.96 appearing at 3.5 of the said minutes selecting and recommending some 46 (Forty Six) officers who are junior to the appellants for promotion to the posts equivalent to the District level officers of the Livestock Directorate in the scale of Taka 4800/7250/- vide Annexure 'P' should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and are of no legal effect.

2. That the appellant No. 1 was appointed temporarily on ad hoc basis as Thana Livestock Officer vide Notification No. See-1-6A/330/140 dated 29th July, 1970 by the Directorate of Livestock services and joined the said post on 12.8.1970 and that he was temporarily appointed on regular basis in the Bangladesh Livestock Service (Junior) Cadre with effect from 21.10.1975 under Notification No. 6/Admn/LS-29/78/213 dated 18.3.1978. The appellant No. 2 was also appointed temporarily on ad hoc basis in the Bangladesh Livestock Service (Junior) as Thana Livestock officer under notification No. See.1-6A/330/1021 dated 1.8.74 issued by the then Director of livestock services and he joined his service on 7.9.74 and the appellant Nos. 3 and 4 were appointed were appointed temporarily on ad-hoc basis in the Bangladesh Livestock Service (Junior) as Thana Livestock Officers under notification No. 8/Admn-110/76-347 dated 12.6.76. Subsequently upon the recommendation of Public Service commission the appellant Nos. 2 and 3 were regularized in their services under Notification dated 15.1.81 and that the appellant No. 4 was regularized in his service under Notification dated 16.1.1981. The services (Re-organization and conditions) Act, 1975 was enacted to provide for the re-organization of the services by prescribing unified grads and scales of pay and other conditions of service employed in such services and all the appellants during their long service career successfully completed departmental foundation training departmental administrative and management training and also received training from foreign countries and the appellants successfully passed the Departmental examinations conducted by the Public Service Commission and were confirmed to their services with effect from 1.9.80 vide Notification dated 11.8.1991. The 28 Service cadres including B.C.S. (Agriculture Livestock were created by the Bangladesh Civil Services (Re-organization) Order 1980 as contained in S.R.O. 286-L/80/Ed/(IC)S 11-92/80-98 dated 1.9.1980 by the Notification as contained in S.R.O. 310-L/80/ED/(IC) S11-6/80-101 dated 1.9.1980 Bangladesh Civil Service (Agriculture: Livestock) composition and cadre Rules, 1980 came into being. Thereafter the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 was notified and published in the official Gazette vide No. SRO.1-L/81/ED/R-11/70/80 dated 1st January, 1981 and in schedule-1 of the said Recruitment Rules, 28 (Twenty eight) Cadre service were declared in the service of the Republic and in Schedule- II of the said Department Rules 1981 various posts of 28 Cadre services including B.C.S (Agriculture Livestock) were specified. The Bangladesh Civil Service (Examination for Promotion) Rules, 1986 was published and notified by respondent No. 1 vide S.R.O./54-L/86/ME/(Rule-5)RR-12/86 dated 13th February, 1986 by the order of the President allegedly framed the rules. The appellants herein challenged and impugned Rules 5(1) and sub-Rule(2) of Rule 8 as those being discriminatory and affects the fundamental rights of the appellants guaranteed under Article 26, 27 and 29 of the Constitution and the appellants also challenged and impugned clause (e) of Rule 8 of Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 as the same is violative of Articles 26, 27, 29(1) and 31 of the Constitution. Subsequently respondent No. 1 by Notification as obtained in S.R.O. No. 117/-Law/94, Sha: Ma (Rule-4) RR-39/88 dated 11th April 1994 made amendments in Rule 5 of Bangladesh Civil Service (Examination or Promotion) Rules 1986 (Annexure-D) substituting Sub-Rules (3) and (3A) and abolishing sub-Rules (4) and (5) and the appellants also challenged the aforesaid amendment of sub-Rule (3A) of Bangladesh Civil Service (Examination for Promotion Rules 1986) as the same is violative of the fundamental rights of the appellants guaranteed under Articles 27, 29 (1) of the Constitution. In 1994 the respondent No. 2 prepared a draft gradation list of B.C.S. (Livestock) Cadre Officers and in that gradation list the names of the appellants appeared at serial Nos. 154, 175, 209 and 211. All the appellants along with others sere promoted to 6th Grade of National Pay Scale at Taka 4800-7250/- (Senior Scale) vide Notification No. Ma. Shaa: Ma/ Pasha -I/Kha-4/94 (Part-I) 756 dated 7.12.1996 issued by the office of respondent No. 2 under Presidents order and while processing the sonority of the appellants on hearing that some persons junior to the appellants were in process of promotions, submitted representations on 16.9.1996 and 21.9.1996 to respondent No. 2 praying for making promotions and postings as per seniority. The departmental promotion committee headed by respondent No. 2 in total defiance of laws, rules and the. representations held a meeting dated 11.12.1996 under notice dated 7.12.1996, without any specific agenda dated 11.12.1996 under notice dated 7.12.1996 without any specific agenda under heading miscellaneous selected and recommended the names of some 46 officers all whom are junior to the appellants as per the gradation list for promotion to the posts of District Level Officers with the scale of TK. 4800-7250/- and sent the said list for approval of the Prime Minister which is still pending and may be approved at moment and thus the rights of the appellants have been grossly violated. The appellants also challenge the minutes dated 11.12.1996 of the Departmental Promotion Committee signed on 14.12.1996. The case of the appellant is that the impugned Sub Rule(1) and the amended Sub-Rule (3A) of Rule 5 and Sub-Rule (2) of Rule 8 of the Bangladesh Civil Service Examination for Promotional Rules, 1986 are highly discriminatory and violative of the appellant's fundamental rights as guaranteed under Article 26, 27, 29(1) and 31 of the constitution and required to be declared ultra vires the Constitution and be struck down. The further case of the appellants is that the impugned amendment in Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 adding clause (e) (f) and (g) after clause (d) of Rule 8 of the aforesaid Rules is discriminatory being violative of Article 27 and 29(1) of the Constitution affecting the fundamental rights of the appellants and required to be declared ultra vires and is liable to be struck down. The further case of the appellant is that the departmental promotion committee headed by respondent No. 1 acted illegally, malafide and arbitrarily in violation of Constitution in selecting and recommending the names of the persons who are junior to the appellants as per Annexure-P to the writ petition.

3. The respondents entered appearance and filed affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations made in the petition and contended that the appellants have challenged the selections of 46 of their colleagues by the Annexure-P to the writ petition in preference to them for promotion. Thus their cause of grievance essentially relates to the terms and conditions of their service for which the Administrative Tribunal Constituted pursuant to Article 117 of the Constitution is the appropriate and only forum to agitate. It has further been stated that the appellants have not been adversely affected by Sub-Rule 3A of Rule 5 and Sub-Rule 2 of Rule 8 of the Bangladesh Civil Service (Examination and Promotion) Rules, 1986 and they challenged the vires of the Rules as a camouflage to invoke the extra ordinary jurisdiction of the High Court Division conferred upon it under Article 102 of the Constitution. It has further been stated that these rules are not ultra vires the Articles 26, 27, 29, 31 and 44 of the Constitution, It has further been stated that the appellants have not been adversely affected by clause (e) of the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 and it has no relevance to the issue raised in the present writ petition, that is whether the departmental promotion committee headed by the respondent No. 2 was right in promoting the 46 officers, in preference to the appellants, for promotion on the basis of seniority-cum-merit. The further case of the respondents is that the departmental promotion committee headed by the respondent No. 2, has committed no illegality in their selection and recommendation of the 46 officers, in preference to the appellants as the selection was done on the basis of merit-cum-seniority, and furthermore, the appellants cause of grievance relates to their terms and conditions of service and the Administrative Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction in such matter. It has further been stated that the Bangladesh Civil Service (Examination for Promotion) Rules, 1986 was framed by the President in exercise of power conferred upon him by the martial Law Proclamation dated 24.3.1982 in which it is stated that by the said Proclamation dated 24.3.1982 the Constitution was suspended and the Chief Martial Law Administrator assumed all the power of the Government of the Republic. Though the then President came to power staging a coup delete as it was successful, the validity of the law subsequently made by the regime is to be judged by reference to the said Proclamation dated 24.3.1982 and not the Constitution which had been suspended. The said Rule 5(1) and 8(2) are not contrary to the letters and spirits of Article 26, 27 and 29 of the Constitution. It has further been stated that the restriction comes into play only when and against the persons who has taken the benefit under Sub-Rule (1) of the said Rule 8. It has further been stated that the benefit conferred by the Sub-Rule(1) is qualified by the limit set out in the said Sub-Rule (2). The appellants were unsuccessful in the departmental examination for promotion, but were given the promotion under the concessionary Rule 8(1) of the Bangladesh Civil Service (Examination for Promotion) Rules, 1986 and the appellants now could not complaint of Rules from which they derived benefit for themselves to which they are not otherwise entitled to as per terms of Rule 5 of Bangladesh BCS Recruitment Rules, 1981. It has further been stated that the appellants were not at all affected by Rule 8(e) and the same is not violative of the Constitution. It has further been stated that Sub-Rule (3A) was added and the appellants have not been adversely affected thereby as they got their promotion under the concession of Sub-Rule (1) of Rule 8 of the Bangladesh Civil Service (Examination for Promotion) Rules, 1986. It has further been stated that the Sub-Rule (3A) is not ultra vires the Article 27 and 29(1) of the Constitution. The further case of the respondent is that the selection and recommendation of the 46 officers were properly made in a properly held meeting of the departmental promotion committee on the basis merit-cum seniority. The dispute essentially relates to the terms and conditions of their service and the proper and only forum to agitate their grievance is the Administrative Tribunal and as such the writ petition is not maintainable. The said 46 officers have been recommended for promotion as they passed all the departmental examinations, which the appellants did not, the appellants have been promoted to their present grade under the concessionary Rule 8(1) of the Bangladesh Civil Service (Examination for Promotion) Rule 1986 and the appellants themselves, being beneficiaries of the Bangladesh Civil Service (Examination for Promotion) Rules, 1986 have challenged its vires merely as a camouflage to invoked the extra ordinary jurisdiction of this High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. The question of promotion has not bee unrecognised by our Constitution as a fundamental right and it cannot be claimed solely on the basis of their seniority. Even if the Rules, the vires of which have been challenged by the writ petition, are declared ultra vires, their case for promotion will not be advanced thereby and as such the writ petition is misconceived.

4. The rule was discharged. The appellant, thereafter, obtained the leave to appeal to consider the ground, which runs as under:

For that their Lordships of the High Court Division are not justified in holding that me petitioners are beneficiaries of Sub-Rule (2) of rule 8, which is a condition of Sub-Rule (1) of the above said Rule, it may be pointed out that the last portion of Sub-Rule (2) of Rule 8 such as “কিন্তু তিনি অধিকতর পদন্নতির জন্য যোগ্য হইবেন না” has seriously affected the petitioner and it cannot be said that they are benefices by the above said portions of the Rule in question, Besides, the above aid to Sub-Rule 8 relates to the officers who failed to pass the Examination in question within 14 years from their entry in ten Service. But the petitioner cannot be said to have "failed" such Examination until 8.11.1991 as they could no sit for such Examination for want of notification in respect of confirmation in the service.

5. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel for the appellants has submitted that the appellants having been appointed vide Notification dated 27.9.1970 on ad-hoc basis and though regularized with effect from 21.10.1975 but having been confirmed on 11.1.1991 with effect from 1.9.1980 when BCS Livestock as Cadre, was created as such and had little chance to sit for the examination for confirmation whereas the members of the other Cadres had ample chance to sit for the examination for good many years, the provision in exception in Rule 8(2) i. e. কিন্তু তিনি অধিকতর পদোন্নতির জন্য যোগ্য হইবে না।” for further promotion is violative of the provision of Article 102, 31 and 32 of the Constitution and the amendment to BCS (Examination for Promotion) Rules 1986 to that extent is void. The learned Counsel has further submitted that the foundation training having been started in 1989, 6 (Six) other Cadres having been given exemption, the members of the Agriculture Livestock being similarly situated like those 6 (six) Cadres, to provision of Rule 8(2) of the Bangladesh Civil Service Examination for Promotion Rules 1986 providing "but he shall not be eligible for further promotion" is contrary to the exemption that have been given to other Cadres who were similarly situated inasmuch as relaxation as contemplated in Rule 8 of the BCS Recruitment Rules, 1981 has been given to other 6 (six) Cader's was clearly discriminatory furthermore, the delay in holding examination for confirmation for which the appellant could not appear should not make him liable to suffer and the respondent should not be allowed to have double standard for members of the different Cadre Services.

6. Mr. Fida M. Kamal, the Additional Attorney General for the respondents has submitted that the classification being reasonable as there is a reasonable nexus to the object sought to be achieved but the appellants were given benefit under Rule 8(1) and (2) inasmuch as they have never qualified at the foundation examination required for promotion.

7. Bangladesh Civil Service (Agriculture: Livestock) was constituted vide S.R.O. No. 310-L/80/ED(IC)S11-6/80-101 dated 1.9.1980 under the rules called the Bangladesh Civil Service (Agriculture: Livestock) composition and Cadre Rules, 1980 providing in Rule 8 as to probation and confirmation that no person shall be confirmed in the service unless he has served the prescribed period of probation, has successfully completed such training and passed such departmental examination as may be prescribed by the Government and unless his conduct and work has been found satisfactory.

BCS Recruited Rules 1981 provides further in Rule 7 for confirmation that:

(1) A person initially appointed in Service shall be required to undergo-

(a) fundamental training for a period not less than 4 months at the Civil Officers Training Academy in the fields of Agriculture, Fisheries, Livestock and Mass Mobilization and also in such other fields as may be determined from time to time by the Government; and

(b) .........

(2) No person shall be confirmed in the concerned Service unless he has successfully completed the training under sub-rule 9(1), passed such departmental examination as may be prescribed, by order, by the Government and also has served the period of probation under rule 6.”

8. Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules 1981 in Rule 8 thereof provides provision for relaxation inter alia, that the President may, on the recommendation of the Council Committee on promotion constituted by the Government, relax in exceptional cases the condition of length of service for promotion specified in Schedule II thereof.

9. It appears from notification No. See-1-6A/330/140 dated 29th July 1970 that the appellants were temporarily appointed on ad hoc basis under the Directorate of Livestock Services and that by notification No. 6/Admn. 39/8/213 dated 18.3.1978 the appellants were appointed on ad-hoc basis on the Bangladesh Livestock Service (Junior) as Thana Livestock Officers under Notification No. 8/Admn-110/76-347 dated 12.6.76. Subsequently upon the recommendation of Public Service Commission the appellant Nos. 2 and 3 were regularized in their services under Notification dated 15.1.81. The Services (Re-organization and Conditions) Act, 1975 was enacted to provide for the Re-organization of the Services of the Republic by prescribing unified grades and scales of pay and other conditions of services. The 28 service cadres including B.C.S (Agriculture-Livestock) were created by the Bangladesh Civil Services (Re-Organization) Order 1980 vide notification dated 1.9.1980 on which Bangladesh Civil Service (Agriculture Livestock) composition and cadre Rules, 1980 came into force. Thereafter the Bangladesh Civil Service Rules, 1981 was notified and published in the Gazette on 1st January, 1981 with 28 Cadre services in Schedule 1 of the said recruitment Rules. The Bangladesh Civil Service (Examination for Promotion) Rules, 1986 was published and notified by respondent No. 1 on 13th February, 1986 and the appellants have challenged the impugned Rules 5(1) and Sub Rule (2) of Rule 8 as those being discriminatory and affects their fundamental rights requiring to be declared ultra vires to the Constitution and be struck down.

10. Rule 5(1) of Bangladesh Civil Service (Examination for Promotion) Rules, 1986 reads as “কোন অফিসারই পরীক্ষায় অংশগ্রহণের জন্য যোগ্য বিবেচীত হইবেন না, যদি না তাহারা নিজস্ব ক্যাডারে স্থায়ী হইয়া থাকেন, এবং পূর্ণ চার বছর চাকুরী করিয়া থাকেন।”

11. The appellants who were confirmed with effect from 1.9.1980 and have served in the Cadre for above the period of 4 years could not take exception of Rule 5(1) above challenging its virus as it has not affected them in any way inasmuch as the appellants derived benefit for themselves to which they are not otherwise entitled to a per said rule.

Rule 8(2) thereof reads as (২) উপাবিধি (১) এর অধীনে পদোন্নতির প্রতি কোন অফিসার উক্ত উপবিধি (১) এর অধিনে যে বেতন স্কেলের পদে পদোন্নতি পাইয়াছেন উহাতে পাঁচ বছর চাকুরী সম্পূর্ণ হইলে তাহাকে সংশোধীতে নতুন স্কেলভূক্ত টাকা ৩৭০০-৪৮২৫/- বেতন স্কেলের পদে পুনরায় পদোন্নতি দেওয়া যাউতে পারে কিন্তু তিনি অধিকতর পদোন্নতির জন্য যোগ্য হইবে না।

12. Before we embark upon to consider the provision কিন্তু তিনি অধিকতর পদোন্নতির জন্য যোগ্য হইবেনা না।” is violative of the Articles 26, 27 and 29 of the Constitution or not certain facts need to be stated i. e. the appellants (writ-petitioners) were admittedly unsuccessful in their departmental examination for promotion but were given promotion under Rule 8(1) which is a concessionary rule under Bangladesh Civil Service (Examination for Promotion) Rules, 1986 and the respondents were beneficiaries under the said rules. The grievance against the 46 officers who have already passed the departmental examinations were properly selected and recommended for promotion on the basis of merit-cum-seniority but the writ petitioner-appellants did not pass the departmental examination but were promoted to their present grade under the aforesaid concessionary Rule 8(1) and could not equate themselves with others who qualified at the departmental examination alleging the virus of the said provision, for had there been no such provision they would not have been in the existing grade inasmuch as under our scheme of service seniority devoid of merit could not be the sole basis of promotion.

13. The Ministry of Establishment has issued notification dated 1.10.1992 forming a review committee for recommendation for exemption of examination for promotion to senior scale. In one of such meeting in which the BCS Livestock was represented, where in the question of appellants were considered as under:

‘মৎস্য ও পশু সম্পদ মন্ত্রণালয়ের সংশ্লিষ্ট যুগ্মসচিব কমিটিকে জানান যে, বিসিএস (পশুসম্পদ) ক্যাডার ১৩৭৫ টি পদ বিশিষ্ট একটি ক্যাডার। এই ক্যাডারের ৮৯০ জন কর্মকর্তা ক্যাডার পদে স্থায়ী এবং বাকী কর্মকর্তাগণ এখনো স্থায়ী হন নাই। উক্ত প্রতিনিধি আরো জানান যে, এই ক্যাডারে বর্তমানে সিনিয়র স্কেলের কোন পদ খালী নাই। তাহাছাড়া এই ক্যাডারের কর্মকর্তাগণ সিনিয়র স্কেল পরীক্ষায় নিয়মিত অংশ গ্রহণ করিতেছেন। এই অবস্থার প্রেক্ষাপটে এই ক্যাডারের কর্মকর্তাদের সিনিয়র স্কেল পরীক্ষা থেকে অব্যাহতি প্রদানের কোন প্রয়োজন আছে বলিয়া কমিটি মনে করেন না।’

Upon consideration of the said note the decision was taken as under:

সুপারিশ:-

বিস্তারিত আলোচনা এবং কাগজপত্র ও তথ্যাদি পর্যালোচনান্তে কমিটি নিম্ন সুপারিশ করিতেছে।:

(১) বিসিএস (প্রশাসন), বিসিএস (কৃষি) বিসিএস, (আনসার), বিসিএস (নিরীক্ষা ও হিসাব), বিসিএস (বহিঃ শুল্ক ও আবগারী) বিসিএস (অর্থনীতি), বিসিএস (মৎস্য, বিসিএস (খাদ্য), বিসিএস (পররাষ্ট্র বিষয়ক), বিসিএস (বন), বিসিএস (তথ্য), বিসিএস (বিচার), বিসিএস (পশু পালন), বিসিএস (পুলিশ), বিসিএস (ডাক), বিসিএস (প্রকৌশলী), বিসিএস (রেলপথ পরিবহন ও বাণিজ্যিক), বিসিএস (বাণিজ্য), বিসিএস (কর), বিসিএস (টেলিযোগাযোগ) মোট ২০ টি ক্যাডারের কর্মকর্তাদেরকে সিনিয়র স্কেলে পদোন্নতির পরীক্ষা হইতে এককালীন অব্যহতি দানের প্রয়োজন নাই।

(২) বিসিএস (কারিগরী শিক্ষা), বিসিএস (সমবায়), বিসিএস (গণপূর্ত), বিসিএস (স্বাস্থ্য), বিসিএস (সড়ক ও জনপদ), বিসিএস (পরিসংখ্যান), বিসিএস (জনস্বাস্থ্য প্রকৌশণ) ও বিসিএস (পরিবার পরিকল্পনা) মোট ৮টি ক্যাডার বর্তমানে শুন্য পদসহ ৩১-১২-৯২ইং পর্যন্ত সিনিয়র স্কেলে যে সকল পদ শূন্য হইবে শুধুমাত্র সেইগুলোতেই পদোন্নতির জন্য এই সকল ক্যাডারের কর্মকর্তাদের বুনিয়াদি প্রশিক্ষণ বিভাগীয় পরীক্ষা এবং সিনিযর স্কেল পদোন্নতি পরীক্ষা এবং সিনিয়র স্কেল পদোন্নতি পরীক্ষা হইতে অব্যাহতি দেওয়া যাইতে পারে।”

<u>14. The appellants have taken exception in respect of the exemption in respect of 8 Cadres mentioned therein. But for the reasons stated therein, the recommendation was made pursuant to the provision of Rule 8(1) of the Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981. The said rule 8(1) provides that;</u>

<u>Notwithstanding anything contained in these rules:(a) the President may, on the recommendation of the Council Committee on promotion constituted by the Government, relax in exceptional cases the condition of length of experience specified Schedule 11.</u>

15. The appellants have relied much on Annexure-U which states as below:

২। উল্লেখ্য যে, ১৯৮১ সনের পূর্বে চাকুরীতে যোগদানকৃত বিসিএস (পশু সম্পদ ক্যাডারের ২৭৬ জন কর্মকর্তা বর্তমানে ৭২০০-১০,৮৪০/- টাকা স্কেলে কর্মরত, ১৯৮৯ সনে বুনিয়াদি প্রশিক্ষণে অংশগ্রহণের সুযোগ প্রাপ্তির প্রেক্ষিতে ১৯৯১ সনে স্থায়ী হয়। উক্ত কর্মকর্তাদের মধ্যে অধিকাংশ কর্মকর্তার চাকুরী বয়স ঐ সময়ের মধ্যে ১৪ বছর উত্তীর্ণ হওয়ায় সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রণালয়ের বিশেষ বিবেচনায়, ১৯৯২ সনের সিনিয়র স্কেলে পদোন্নতি পরীক্ষায় অংশগ্রহণ করার সুযোগ পান। যদিও কতিপয় কর্মকর্তা ২/১ বার পরীক্ষায় অংশ গ্রহণের সুযোগ পেলেও সব বিষয়ে উত্তীর্ণ হতে ব্যর্থ হন। কিন্তু বর্তমানে সংশোধীত পরীক্ষা বিধির আওতায় সমস্ত শর্ত পূরণ সাপেক্ষে চাকুরীর বয়স ৫-১৪ পর্যন্ত একাধারে ১০ বার প্রত্যেক কর্মকর্তাই পরীক্ষায় অংশগ্রহণ করার সুযোগ পাচ্ছেন অথচ, পশুসম্পদ ক্যাডারের বর্ণিত ২৭৬ জন কর্মকর্তা উক্ত সুযোগ থেকে বঞ্চিত হয়েছেন।”

16. But the Ministry of Establishment in reply in its memo intimated as under:

(খ) তবে উপরোল্লিখিত ২৭৬ জন কর্মকর্তার মধ্যে যারা বিসিএস (পদোন্নতির জন্য পরীক্ষা) বিধিমালা, ১৯৮৬ এর ৮(১) উপ বিধির বিধান অনুযায়ী ১৫ বছর চাকুরি পুর্তিকে সিনিয়র স্কেল পদে পদোন্নতির ক্ষেত্রে বিসিএস নিয়োগ বিধিমালা, ১৯৮১ এর ৫(খ) দফায় বর্ণিত সিনিয়র স্কেল পরীক্ষা হতে অব্যাহতির মাধ্যমে পদোন্নতি পেয়েছেন তাদেরকে বিসিএস (পদোন্নতির জন্য পরীক্ষা), বিধিমালা ১৯৮৬ এর ৮(২) উপ বিধির বিধান অনুযায়ী এমএসএস এর পঞ্চম গ্রেডে ৩৭০০-৪৮২০/- টাকা পদে (১৯৯৯ সনের জাতীয় বেতন স্কেল টাকা ৬০০০-৮০০০/- বর্তমান ১৯৯ ৭ সনের জাতীয় বেতন স্কেল টাকা ৯৫০০-১২,১০০/-) পদোন্নতির জন্য ৫(পাঁচ) বছর অপেক্ষা করতে হবে এবং অতঃপর তারা আর কোন পদোন্নতি পাবেন না।

(গ) উপরের (খ) উপ অনুচ্ছেদে বর্ণিত কর্মকর্তাগণ যেহেতু একটি অব্যাহতির সুবাদে সিনিয়র স্কেল পদে পদোন্নতি পেয়েছেন সেহেতু তাদেরকে সিনিয়র স্কেল পদ পদোন্নতি পেয়েছেন সেহেতু তাদেরকে সিনিয়র পদোন্নাতির ক্ষেত্রে অধিকতর সুবিধাজনক অন্য কোন অব্যাহতি প্রদানের আইন সম্মত কোন সুযোগ নেই।

17. In view of the fact that they have already been promoted to the post of Senior Scale, the appellants has sought to avail the right of equal opportunity for employment in the service of the Republic by extending the scope for relaxation to them as has been done in respect of other 8 Cadres.

<u>18. It is to be borne in mind that each Cadre is an independent Cardre by itself and that the appellants could not allege any discrimination to them simply because the member of other Cadres were given relaxation considering their respective position as they are not similarly situated with that of the appellants.</u>

<u>19. In the case of Bangladesh Vs. Md. Azizur Rahman reported in 46 DLR AD 19 on equality before law it has been held that:</u>

<u>The term "equality before law" should not be interrelated in its absolute sense to hold that all persons are equal in all respects disregarding different conditions and circumstances in which they are placed or special quality and characteristics which some of them may possess but which are lacking in others. In fact, this term means that all persons are not equal in a respects and that persons similarly situated should be treated alike. Equal protection of law is a guarantee that similar people should be dealt with in a similar way and that people of different circumstance will not be treated as if they were the same.</u>

20. The appellants could not show any discrimination among the members of the Cardre BCS (Agriculture: Livestock) so as to invoke the equality clause alleging discrimination. The appellants though did not pass the foundation training and other training for promotion within the period specified in the Civil Service (Examination for Promotion) Rules 1986 but were given relaxation twice pursuant to Rule 8(1) and (2) which they duly availed of. But by availing the benefit under those Rules could not now be allowed to allege that a portion of the Rule 8(2) i.e., "but he shall not be eligible for further promotion" is unconstitutional and liable to be struck down on ground of being discriminatory and void.

<u>21. In the case of Ram Krishna Dalmia and others vs. S. R. Tendolkar and others reported in 1958 S.C. Appeals 754 it has been held that:</u>

<u>It is now well established that while article 14 forbids class legislation, it does not forbid reasonable classification for the purpose of legislation. In order, however, to pass the test of permissible classification two conditions must be fulfilled, namely, (i) that the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statue in question. The classification may be founded on different bases, namely, geographical, or according to object or occupations or the like. What is necessary is that there must be a nexus between the basis of classification and the object of the Act under consideration. It is also well established by the decisions of this Court that article 14 condemns discrimination not only by substantive law but also by a law of procedure.</u>

<u>The principle enunciated above has been consistently adopted and applied in subsequent cases. The decisions of this Court further establish</u>

<u>(a) that a law may be constitutional even though it relates to a single individual, if on account of some special circumstances or reasons applicable to him and not applicable to others, that single individual may be treated as a class by himself:</u>

<u>(b) that there is always a presumption in favour of the constitutionality of an enactment and the burden is upon him who attacks it to show that there has been a clear transgression of the constitutional principles;</u>

<u>(c) that it must be presumed that the legislature understands and correctly appreciates the need of its own people, that its laws are directed to problems made manifest by experience and that its discriminations are based on adequate grounds;</u>

<u>(d) that the legislature is free to recognise degrees of harm and may confine its restrictions to those cases where the need is deemed to be the clearest;</u>

<u>(e) that in order to sustain the presumption of constitutionality the Court may take into consideration matters of common knowledge, matters of common report, the history of the times and may assume every state of facts which can be conceived existing at the time of legislation and</u>

<u>(f) that while good faith and knowledge of the existing conditions on the part of a legislature are to be presumed, if there is nothing on the face of the law or the surrounding circumstances brought to the notice of the court on which the classification may reasonably be regarded as based, the presumption of Constitutionality cannot be carried to the extent of always holding that there must be some undisclosed and unknown reasons for subjecting certain individuals or corporations to hostile or discriminating legislation.</u>

22. Similarly by sub-rule 3A of Rule 5 of the said Rule of 1986 the appellants have not been adversely affected in any way as they availed their promotion under the concessionaire rule 8(1) thereof and as such the said rules could not be in any way violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution for the simple reason that they availing the opportunity could not approbate and reprobate at the same time.

23. The appellants are also not entitled to any benefit of doubt as has been given in Director General NIS vs Md Sultan Ahmed 1996 BLD (AD) 76= 1 BLC (AD) 71 i. e. given to one any denying the benefit to others as the facts and circumstances are not the same and the statute has not directed the provision against one giving benefit to the other of the same class or the same Cadre members with naked discrimination and as such there was no arbitrary classification so as to make it not sustainable under the Constitution on the principle of equality clause for equal treatment.

<u>24. As regards the exemption that has been given to certain other Cadres, the submission of the learned Additional Attorney General that the administrative requirement of particular service necessitated the provisions regarding relaxation in rule 8 in order to meet the circumstance inherent in certain Cadres or the exigencies because of their particular situation arising therein need to be addressed and has referred to clause (M) and (N) of the Recommendations mentioned above of the Ministry of Establishment.</u>

25. Thus the selections of 46 officers was properly made by the departmental promotion Committee on the basis of merit cum seniority and were recommended for promotion as they all have passed the departmental examinations which the appellant has failed to pass but were promoted to the present Grade under the concessionaire rule 8(1) of BCS (Examination for Promotion) Rules, 1986 and the appellant being the beneficiaries of the said rules as they derived the benefit for themselves to which they are not otherwise entitled to under rule 5 including rule 5(3A) of the Bangladesh Civil Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1981 and the appellants as well were not at all affected by rule 8(e) and as such the impugned rules are not violative of the fundamental rights guaranteed under Article 26, 27, 29 (1) and 31 of the Constitution.

<u>26. From the above, the appellants themselves being beneficiaries of the BCS Examination for Promotion) rules, 1980 they could not as well challenge virus of the rule 8(2) merely as a come fledge to invoke the jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution.</u>

27. We do not find any substance in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellants. Accordingly, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division do not suffer from any illegality or infirmity for our interference.

In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.
