full_judgment:
This Rule issued under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, at the instance of the plaintiff/respondent/petitioner, Fazlul Haque Mallik, is directed against the judgment and decree dated 23-11-1994 passed by the Additional District Judge, Naogaon in Title Appeal No. 171 of 1986 reversing that of the Subordinate Judge, Naogaon in Other Class Suit No. 188 of 1983 decreeing the suit in part by the judgment and decree dated 31-7-1986.

2. The brief statement of the case, as revealed from the revisional application, is that the plaintiff/respondent/petitioner instituted Other Class Suit No. 188 of 1983 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Naogaon praying for cancellation of two registered deeds of Heba-bil-ewaj being No. 6440 dated 14-7-1965 and No.152 dated 3-1-1978 purported to have been executed by the father of the plaintiff/ respondent/petitioner, Hafizuddin Mallik, in favour of his 2nd wife defendant/ appellant/ opposite party No.1, Nurjahan Begum, and also praying for partition of the suit property by granting a share in favour of the plaintiff/ respondent/petitioner to the extent of 14 annas from the lot Nos. 1-14 in 'B' schedule, 7 annas from the lot Nos.15-20 of the said schedule, 3 annas 10 gondas from the lot No.21 of the said schedule and 4 annas 13 gandas, 1 kara 1 kranti from the lot No.22 of the said schedule B, alleging inter alia, that the father of the plaintiff /respondent/petitioner namely, Hafizuddin Mallik, exclusively owned the lot Nos.1-14. The lot Nos. 15-20 was owned by the mother of Hafizuddin Mallik, Asiron Bewa and the lot No. 21 jointly belonged to Hafizuddin Mallik and the defendant-opposite party Nos.7 and 9 who got the same by auction purchase jointly. The lot No. 22 also belonged to Hafizuddin Mallik and the defendant-opposite party Nos. 7 and 9. The mother of Hafizuddin Mallik filed a Partition Suit being Partition Suit No.83 of 1956 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Rajshahi in respect of the present suit lands and other lands which was disposed of amicably on the basis of compromise decree and thereby Hafizuddin Mallik, the father of the plaintiff/respondent/petitioner got lot Nos.1-11 and his mother got lot Nos.15-20 of the present suit. The lot Nos. 12-14 are the self-acquired property of Hafizuddin Mallik. The mother of Hafizuddin Mallik died leaving one son Hafizuddin Mallik and two daughters Romesha Bibi who was the predecessor of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 3-6 and Osimon Bibi, the defendant-opposite party No.2. Thereafter, Hafizuddin Mallik died on 24th Baisakh, 1383 BS leaving behind one son, the plaintiff/respondent/petitioner and the defendant/appellant/opposite party No.1, Nurjahan Begum, who is his 2nd wife as his heir. The mother of the plaintiff/respondent / petitioner having been divorced by Hafizuddin Mallik while the petitioner was a child of 10/11 months, the petitioner was brought up under supervision and nursing of his father Hafizuddin Mallik who was a long time patient of Tuberculosis and was fully dependent on the nursing and care of his second wife, defendant-opposite party No.1. Taking this advantage, the defendant/ appellant/opposite parties No.1 obtained the signature of Hafizuddin Mallik in the impugned deeds of Heba-bil-ewaj in collusion with others to which Hafizuddin Mallik had no knowledge of its contents. At the relevant time of the purported execution of the second deed Hafizuddin Mallik was in death bed and was taken to Naogaon town for the purpose of treatment and he was made to put his signature in the impugned deed of gift dated 3-1-1978 without understanding the fact of gift which is a fraudulent deed having no consideration and it was never acted upon. The plaintiff-petitioner came to know about the disputed deed of Heba-bil-ewaj from the defendant-opposite party No.1 on 25th Baisakh 1385 BS when he approached her requesting her to make partition of the suit properties which was refused by her and hence he filed this suit.

3. The suit was contested by the defendant/appellant/opposite party No.1 Nurjahan Begum by filing written statement alleging, inter alia, that the mother of the plaintiff-petitioner was divorced by Hafizuddin Mallik and the petitioner having been born after the said divorce in the house of his maternal grandfather situated at Pathakata, he was brought up there and practically Hafizuddin Mallik did not supervise him in any manner. Hafizuddin Mallik was a TB patient and was fully dependent on his loving 2nd wife defendant/respondent/opposite party No.1 for nursing and having been satisfied with her nursing made the impugned gifts by executing two deeds of Heba-bil-ewaj at different times and it is not a fact that those were obtained fraudulently. The defendant/ appellant/opposite party No.1 also denied that Hafizuddin Mallik had an intention to transfer two bighas of land only in 1965 and fraudulently the first deed of Heba-bil-ewaj has been obtained by inclusion of a land measuring 4.07 acres. Hence he prayed for dismissal of the suit.

4. At the trial the plaintiff/respondent/ petitioner examined 5 witnesses and exhibited some documents which were marked as exhibits. On the other hand, the defendant/appellant/opposite party examined 4 witnesses and also exhibited some documents. The trial Court, on assessing the evidence on record and the facts and circumstances of the case, decreed the suit in part only in respect as to the cancellation of the Heba-bil-ewaj deeds and dismissed the other part of the prayer as to the partition of the suit property.

5. As against the said judgment and decree, the defendant/appellant/opposite party No.1 preferred the appeal before the Court of District Judge, Naogaon, being Title Appeal No.17 of 1986 which was transferred to the Court of Additional District Judge, Naogaon, for disposal, who on hearing the parties allowed the appeal reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

6. Against the said reversal of the trial Court's judgment in appeal, the plaintiff/ respondent/petitioner preferred this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the instant Rule.

7. The Rule has been properly served upon the defendant/appellant/opposite party and the learned Senior Counsel Mr Mahbubey Alam along with Samarendra Nath Biswas appeared on behalf of the defendant /appellant/opposite party No.1, Nurjahan Begum. But as Nurjahan Begum died during the pendency of this revision her heirs have been substituted duly and the learned Advocate Mr Samarendra Nath Biswas filed power on behalf of the defendant/ appellant/ opposite party Nos.1(a) to 1(c) and learned Senior Counsel Mr Mahbubey Alam on their behalf conducted the case before this Court. On the other hand, Mr Md Oziullah along with Mrs Hosne Ara Sultana have appeared on behalf of the plaintiff/respondent/petitioner and conducted the case before this Court.

8. Mr Md Oziullah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff/ respondent/petitioner, has firstly submitted that the impugned judgment passed by the appellate Court below is not a proper judgment of reversal, inasmuch as the learned appellate Court came to an erroneous finding that both the deed of Heba-bil-ewaj dated 14-7-1965 and 3-1-1978 were genuinely executed by the donor and, as such, lawful, although the Holy Quran was admittedly handed over to the donor as consideration of the Heba-bil-ewaj after 4 days. He contends that to constitute a valid Heba-bil-ewaj the consideration must pass from the donee to the donor simultaneously with the offer and acceptance of the gift.

9. His has next submitted that on the admitted fact of nonpayment of consideration simultaneously with the gift the false narration as to the passing of the consideration stated in the registered deed of Heba-bil-ewaj dated 14-7-1965 made the deed invalid. The admitted fact of non-payment of consideration since ipsofacto proved that the deed of Heba-bil-ewaj was illegal, the appellate Court ought to have affirmed the finding of the trial Court that the deed of Heba-bil-ewaj was obtained fraudulently exercising undue influence upon the sick and dependent husband.

10. The third contention, which Mr Oziullah meticulously argued, is that the impugned judgment passed in appeal since not a proper judgment of reversalas such, this Court is empowered to reassess the evidence on record and come to its own finding as to the genuineness of the deeds of the Heba-bil-ewaj which was categorically proved by the witnesses as obtained by practising undue influence and fraud upon the executant.

11. On the other hand, the learned Advocate Mr Samarendra Nath Biswas appearing on behalf of the defendant/ appellant/ opposite party, by referring to section 168 of Mullah's Mohamadan Law, argued that there being no time limit for payment of consideration for Heba-bil-ewaj as defined in the section, the handing over of consideration after 4 days did not invalidate the deed of Heba-bil-ewaj. He further submits that the two essential elements of Heba-bil-ewaj are the payment of consideration and the intention of the donor to divest itself from the title of the property. Having been satisfied in this case, despite the handing over of the materials of consideration after 4 days, the deeds of Heba-bil-ewaj are valid documents which the trial Court wrongly considered and the appellate Court after considering the true aspect of the facts and circumstances of the case and on correct appraisal of law and the evidence of the witnesses, correctly reversed the Judgment and decree of the trial Court. The impugned Judgment, since does not suffer from any infirmity, it cannot be interfered with by this Court.

12. I have heard the learned Advocates on behalf of the parties including the Senior Counsel Mr Mahbubey Alam who advanced argument in aid to his learned friend Mr Samarendra Nath Biswas. I have perused the Lower Court Record and the exhibits filed by the parties. I have engaged my considered view to the arguments advanced at the Bar.

13. Addressing the 3rd argument of Mr Oziullah first as to the ability of this Court to reassess the evidence on record, it transpires that long line of decisions of this Court approved this proposition that in the case of reversal of judgment and decree of the trial Court by the appellate Court, the revisional Court under the provision of section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, in order to apprise itself as to the error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by the Courts below, can reassess the evidence on record and may come to its own finding about the case on wholesale basis. Reference may be made in this context to the case of Anwara Khatoon vs Md Abdul Hye reported in 5 BLC (AD) 14.

14. From the pleading of the parties it transpires that the plaintiff/respondent/ petitioner framed the suit under section 39 of the Specific Relief Act and challenged two deeds of Heba-bil-ewaj one executed and registered as deed No. 6440 on 14-7-1965 for a quantum of land of 4.07 acres and the other was executed and registered as deed No. 152 on 3-1-1978. The parties have adduced evidence separately in respect of both the deeds as the alleged transaction took place at an interval of about 13 years. But, unfortunately, Courts below did not apprise the evidence on record separately for coming to a correct conclusion about the genuineness of both the deeds of Heba-bil-ewaj and on sweeping and slipshod consideration of the evidence on record the trial Court decreed the suit in part and conversely the appellate Court reversed the decree of the trial Court. Such a practice is deplorable and always depreciated by this Court. The trial Court should have framed separate issues as to the genuineness of both the deeds of Heba-bil-ewaj and should apprise the evidence on record separately. Since the suit has been framed under section 39 of the Specific Relief Act praying for cancellation of registered instrument the Civil Judgment delivery system should not be floated in the manner which has been done in the present case and a strong note of caution must be addressed against such practice by the subordinate judiciary.

15. The pertinent question raised in the first line of argument by the plaintiff/ respondent/petitioner is, whether the decision regarding time of payment of consideration in case of Heba-bil-ewaj arrived at by the Courts below is correct.

16. Before adverting to the question of time of payment of consideration in Heba-bil-ewaj it will be profitable to examine the status of Heba-bil-ewaj as a means of transfer of property by the Muslims as enunciated in section 168 of Mullah's Principles of Mohamadan Law, which is considered as an authentic compilation of the principles of Muslim Law which explained different provision of law, relying upon decisions of the superior Court of this subcontinent.

17. Heba-bil-ewaj has been explained in section 168 in Mullah's Principles of Mohamadan Law in the following manner:

"A Heba-bil-ewaj, as distinguished from a heba or simple gift, is a gift for a consideration. It is, in reality, a sale, and has all the ingredients of a contract of sale. Accordingly, possession is not required to complete the transfer as it is in the case of a heba, and an undivided share (mushaa) in property capable of division may be lawfully transferred by it, though this cannot be done in the case of a heba. Two conditions, however, must concur to make the transaction valid, namely, (1) actual payment of consideration (ewaj) on the part of the donee, and (2) a bonafide intention on the part of the donor to divest himself in praesenti of the property and to confer it upon the donee, the adequacy of consideration is not material; but, whatever its amount, it must be actually and bonafide paid. Such a transaction is called the heba-bil-ewaj of India as distinguished from "true" heba-bil-ewaj dealt with in the notes below. It was introduced by the Muslim lawyers of India as a device for effecting a gift of mushaa in property capable of division."

18. From the above explanation it appears that the two essential elements of Heba-bil-ewaj are the (1) payment of consideration and (2) the intention of the donor to divest itself from the title of the property and to confer it upon the donee. This definition is silent about the actual time of payment of consideration for which question arose before this Court, whether the appellate Court was correct in holding the following opinion:

“বিবাদীপক্ষের সাক্ষী নূরজাহান (১ নং বিবাদী) বলে যে দলিল সম্পাদনের ৪ দিন পর পবিত্র কোরান শরীফ দেওয়া হয়। এই ব্যাপারে প্রধান যে বিবেচ্য বিষয় তাহা হইল এই যে হাফিজ উদ্দিন পবিত্র কোরান শরীফ গ্রহণ করেছে কি না। বিবাদী পক্ষে ১ নং সাক্ষী তাহার সাক্ষে বলেন যে প্রদত্ত কোরান শরীফের মধ্যে একটি মসজিদে আছে এবং অপরটি বাড়িতে আছে। তাই উহা দেখা যায় যে, হাফিজ উদ্দিন (১নংবিবাদী) বরাবর সম্পত্তি দান করিয়া দিয়া উহার বিনিময়ে পবিত্র কোরাণ শরীফ গ্রহণ করিয়াছিল। পবিত্র কোরাণ শরীফ ৪ দিন পর গ্রহণ করিলেও উহাতে কিছু যায় আসে না।”

19. As section 168 of the Mulla's Principles of Mohamadan Law is silent about the time of payment of consideration in a case of Heba-bil-ewaj, this Court with a view to find out a decisive explanation about the question of time of payment of consideration, which being a question of public importance, has examined the points in the long standing precedents of this Sub-continent.

20. In the case of Kanchanmala vs Renu Mian and another reported in 12 DLR 479 their Lordships held— that the recital in the deed goes to show that petitioner Kanchanmala, the donee, was living in her father's house with her husband at the request of her father Ali Akbar. It further shows that the donee (Kanchanmala) is the first child of the donor (Ali Akbar) and the donor was satisfied by the affection and care bestowed upon him by her. The donee gave Rs. 200 to the donor previously for his passage expenses to Mecca and that in consideration of the same and also being satisfied with the nursing and care of the donee, he gifted away the properties in dispute to her for her maintenance. In this backdrop of the case and on the advance payment of consideration of Rs. 200 it was held that the deed of gift executed and registered is a valid deed of Heba-bil-ewaj. It appears in this case that the advance payment of consideration could be treated as valid consideration, paid for a Heba-bil-ewaj to be valid.

21. In the case of Asghar Ali alias Zafar Alam and another vs Naseem Akhtar reported in 1969 PLD Lahore 467 it was held that consideration of Heba-bil-ewaj need not be by money only....Promise to marry, a valid consideration Heba-bil-ewaj in contemplation of marriage—Valid and irrevocable on solemnisation of marriage—by performance of marriage subsequently donor obtains a return of his gift—Such consideration not subject to further condition that donor and donee will continue to live as man and wife.

<u>22. From the decision of these two cases it appears that the payment of consideration in advance and payment of consideration subsequently could constitute valid Heba-bil-ewaj if the other two essential elements i.e. actual payment of consideration and the intention of the donor to divest itself from the title really exist. Although section 168 of Mulla's Principles of Mohamadan Law is silent on the point of actual time of payment of consideration in order to make a valid Heba-bil-ewaj yet the superior Courts of this Sub-continent held that the consideration in Heba-bil-ewaj may be made at any time, be it in advance or afterwards.</u>

23. In the case of Peer Baksh vs Rabia Khatoon reported in 9 DLR 654 this Court held in the following manner

1: "A Heba-bil-ewaj in order to be a valid transaction must fulfil two conditions:

(1) actual payment of consideration on the part of the donee and

(2) a bonafide intention on the part of the donor to divest himself in praesenti of the property and to confer it upon the donee.

24. Adequacy of consideration is not the question. A consideration may be perfectly valid which is wholly inadequate in amount when compared with the thing given. But where there has been no payment of ewaj the documents cannot be Heba-bil-ewaj and is invalid in the eye of law."

25. The ratio decidendi of the above cases comes to that "a transfer of Heba-bil-ewaj shall be valid if the intention of the donee to divest itself from the property is manifestly clear and he received a consideration in any form either simultaneously or afterward. The time of payment of the consideration is not the essence of the transfer but absence of any of such elements will invalidate the transfer as Heba-bil-ewaj."

<u>26. Therefore, this Court has no hesitation to hold that the appellate Court correctly found that the payment of consideration at a later day i.e. handing over of Holy Quran after 4 days, did not make the Heba-bil-ewaj invalid.</u>

27. Now, turning to the 2nd set of argument advanced by MR Oziullah as to the question of probable invalidation of the deed of Heba-bil-ewaj executed by Hafizuddin Mallik to his wife defendant No.1, Nurjahan Begum, on the ground of its so-called false narration as to the payment of consideration, we propose to examine the decided cases to find out what Heba-bil-ewaj actually means.

28. In the case of Fazal Ahmad vs Mst. Rakhi reported in 10 DLR (WP) 36 their Lordships after examining the actual nature of the transaction involved in Heba-bil-ewaj decided it in the following terms:

"Heba-bil-ewaj of Muslim Law simply consists of two simple gifts, the only additional factor being that the first gift actually forms a consideration for the second. In a heba-bil-ewaj, the second gift is not, at the time when the first gift is made, in contemplation at all, that is, there is no condition attached to the first gift that the second gift is to be made. The second donor is at liberty to make or not to make a gift. The first gift has, therefore, to be completed by delivery of possession. The second gift too is an ordinary simple gift, with only this distinguishing factor that the first gift furnishes the reasons for it. In fact, there was no need to place the heba-bil-ewaj in a separate category at all, were it not for the fact that the revocability of a gift is affected once the donee has also made a gift in consideration for it, and the first donor has accepted the second gift. Having accepted the second gift, he is debarred from repudiating his own gift. When he is debarred, the donor of the second gift is for a similar reason also debarred.

The first transaction in a Heba-bil-ewaj is a gratuitous transfer and creates no obligation."

29. From a series of decisions of the superior Courts of this Sub-continent and also of this Court, it appears that the Heba-bil-ewaj if it does not fulfil the one or the other essential elements will be invalid as a Heba-bil-ewaj but will be valid as a simple gift. Reference may be made in this context to the case of Miaruddin Bhuiyan alias Chand Mia & another vs Saleh Meher Bibi & others reported in 11 DLR 445 wherein it has been held—

"If a document cannot be sustained as heba-bil-ewaj for want of consideration, it can be treated as simple Heba if the intention of the donor and the other necessary elements of a valid heba are present there."

30. In the case of Haji Aklema Khatun and another vs Shah Alam and ors reported in 33 DLR 62 it has been held—

"Under Muslim Law oral gift is complete with declaration and delivery of possession of the subject matter—subsequent written deed followed by registration will be, according to law valid."

31. From the decisions of the aforesaid cases, it appears that the Heba-bil-ewaj consists of two separate simple gifts under the Muslim Law. If the two gifts materialise by fulfilling its requirement then these two gifts turn into a Heba-bil-ewaj. If the requirement of Heba-bil-ewaj is not fulfilled but the requirement of Heba i.e. simple gift, is fulfilled then the deed of Heba-bil-ewaj may be considered as simple deed of Heba and, as such, will be treated as valid.

<u>32. In the case before this Court on apprising the evidence on record, it appears that the plaintiff challenged the genuineness of two deeds of Heba-bil-ewaj dated 14-7-1965 and 3-1-1978 respectively allegedly executed and registered by his father Hafizuddin Mallik in favour of his 2nd wife Noorjahan Begum, out of which one was executed on 14-7-1965 and finally registered under section 60 of the Registration Act on 2-9-1965 and the other was executed on 3-1-1978 and finally registered under section 60 of the Registration Act on 10-7-1982. The Courts below, it appears from the judgment, did not relate the assertion of PW 1 regarding payment of consideration after 4 days to any particular deed out of these two documents and on a wholesale consideration the Courts below came to a converse finding. But, on reassessing the evidence on record by this Court, it appears that the records of right of the suit property for an area of 12 bighas included in the Heba-bil-ewaj dated 14-7-1965 stands in the name of Nurjahan Begum, the defendant No.1 in the suit. The fact of this record when cross referred with the statement of the PWs it appears that the PWs in one voice has stated that there was a talk of gift of two bighas of land in favour of defendant No.1 by Hafizuddin Malik. But the case of the plaintiff is that in spite of intended two bighas of land the defendant No.1 managed to execute and register the said deed of Heba-bil-ewaj dated 14-7-1965 for an area of 12 bighas of land. It appears from the evidence on record that the plaintiff failed to prove by any direct evidence that this quantum of land was included in the Heba-bil-ewaj of 1965 as fraudulently. The factual position of the record of right ipso facto proved that the plaintiffs did not take steps against the record of right under which the defendant No.1 Noorjahan Begum asserting her title upon 12 bighas of land by paying rent to the appropriate authority and admittedly possessing the said land. On this factual backdrop, this Court has no hesitation to hold that the Heba-bil-ewaj of 1965 has been successfully proved by the defendant No.1 on the balance of probability as a genuine document through which the defendant No.1 became the owner of 12 bighas of land in the suit property.</u>

<u>33. But since the question raised that the narration in the deed as to the payment of consideration was not correct and, as such, the deed itself became a nullity, it transpires from the decided cases, as mentioned earlier, that if by the narration of the registered deed it manifests that all the elements of Heba-bil-ewaj has not been fulfilled, even then the deed may be considered as simple deed of Heba if all the elements of simple Heba is fulfilled in respect of its essential elements, i.e. the declaration of offer and its acceptance along with delivery of possession. Since this element is proved to be in existence in the gift made on 14-7-1965 the deed which is validly registered can also be treated as deed of simple gift transferring the title to the donee. Therefore, the argument advanced by Mr Oziullah, on the point of erroneous recital in the deed of Heba-bil-ewaj dated 14-7-1965 making it as invalid, gained no ground.</u>

<u>34. But so far the Heba-bil-ewaj allegedly executed on 3-1-1978 and finally registered under section 60 on 10-7-1982 is concerned, it appears from the evidence on record that the defendant No.1 could neither procure any mutation in her name nor could pay the rent for the property included in the subsequent Heba-bil-ewaj dated 3-1-1978. Moreover, it was an admitted fact that Hafizuddin Mallik, at the relevant time of alleged execution of this deed, was in the custody of his 2nd wife in a very sick condition. The plaintiff categorically framed his case of undue influence and by the PWs the plaintiff could successfully prove the question of influence upon the husband by the defendant No.1, as such, the appellate Court below correctly shifted the onus of proving upon the defendant No.1 as to the question of non-influence and also as to the genuineness of the 2nd deed of Heba-bil-ewaj. On browsing the evidence on record on this point, it appears that Hafizuddin Mallik was taken to Naogaon town by his brother-in-law i.e. the brother of defendant No.1 one Jasimuddin, who has identified Hafizuddin Mallik in the registered document before the sub-registrar Although this Jasimuddin deposed in the suit as DW and attempted to prove the document as genuine but under the facts and circumstances of the case this second deed of Heba-bil-ewaj dated 3-1-1978 has not been proved on the balance of probability as genuine. Such being the position, this Court holds that the shifting of onus upon the defendant No.1 in respect of proving the genuineness of 2nd deed of Heba-bil-ewaj dated 3-1-1978 was correctly done which the defendant No.1 miserably failed to discharge and, as such, the genuineness of the 2nd deed of Heba-bil-ewaj dated 3-1-1978 has not been proved. The appellate Court without considering this aspect allowed the appeal which needs interference by this Court.</u>

35. Prior to proceeding to the operative portion of this judgment, a subtle and important question need be resolved as to the framing of the suit. The plaintiff/respondent/ petitioner instituted Other Class Suit No. 188 of 1983 with a prayer for cancellation of aforesaid-two Heba-bil-ewaj deeds and also for partition. The former prayer as to the cancellation of document attracts section 39 of the Specific Relief Act which runs as follows:

Section 39 "When Cancellation may be Ordered— Any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, who has reasonable apprehension that such instrument if left outstanding, may cause him serious injury, may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable; and the Court may, in its discretion, so adjudge it and order it to be delivered up and cancelled.

If the instrument has been registered under the Registration Act, 1908, the Court shall also send a copy of its decree to the officer in whose office the instrument has been so registered; and such officer shall note on the copy of the instrument contained in his books the fact of its cancellation."

<u>36. From a bare reading of the section it transpires the decree of a suit framed under section 39 of the Specific Relief Act must contain indispensably a declaration as to the document, whether it is void or voidable and if the Court finds its void ability then only the further consequential relief by way of cancellation of the document would find its place in the decree. But, if the Court finds that the instrument is void no such consequential relief by way of cancellation will be needed and, if given, must be treated a superfluous one. Reference may be made in the case of Sufia Khatoon vs Faizunnessa reported in 39 DLR (AD) 46.</u>

<u>37. The trial Court found that the impugned Heba-bil-ewaj deeds were void for want of consideration, nonetheless the trial Court decreed the suit granting relief of cancellation of these two deeds of Heba-bil-ewaj. Since a void instrument does not require cancellation the relief as granted by the trial Court in its operative portion of the judgment was erroneous.</u>

<u>38. On the contrary, the appellate Court allowed the appeal and set aside the trial Court's judgment and decree without giving further direction as to the fate of the suit, whether it is dismissed or pending for passing a fresh judgment. This anomaly, as indicated by Mr Oziullah, merits consideration since the appellate Court framed the operative portion of his Judgment, which culminated in the decree, as follows:</u>

<u>“অত্র আপীল প্রতিদন্ধি রেসপনডেন্টেগণের বিরুদ্ধে দোতরফা সূত্রে ও অন্যদের বিরুদ্ধে একতরফাসূত্রে বিনা খরচে মঞ্জুর হইল।</u>

<u>বিজ্ঞ সাবজজ কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত বিতর্কিত ৩১-৭-১৯৮৬ইং তারিখের রায় ও ৬-৮-১৯৮৬ ইং তারিখের ডিক্রি রদ রহিত করা হইল। নিম্ন আদালতের নথীসহ রায়ের অনুলিপি অবিলম্বে প্রেরন করা হউক।</u>

<u>39. This operative portion of the judgment of the appellate Court is unintelligible, inasmuch as it did not indicate what would happen to the suit since the impact of setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court only will not culminate into dismissal of the suit rather, without such direction the suit will be treated as having no judgment and decree passed at any time and a probable implication may be understood that a fresh judgment would have to be passed in the suit. Such an implication being not improbable a duty is cast upon the Court to pass intelligible operative portion in the judgment and, as such, this Court feels it necessary to grant an appropriate relief by framing the operative portion of the judgment in correct perspective.</u>

<u>40. On the reasoning as discussed above, this Court holds the finding of the appellate Court is only partially correct and, as such, it requires interference by this Court.</u>

<u>41. Therefore, the finding of the appellate Court so far it relates to the deed of Heba-bil-ewaj dated 14-7-1965 is upheld and the finding of the appellate Court so far it relates to the deed of Heba-bil-ewaj dated 3-1-1978 is set aside.</u>

42. In the result the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court below is hereby set aside and the judgment passed by the trial Court be restored with modification as observed in the body of this Judgment as to the registered deed of Heba-bil-ewaj No. 152 dated 3-1-1978. The Other Class Suit (title suit) No. 188 of 1983 is decreed in part in preliminary form and the title by inheritance of the plaintiff/respondent petitioner is declared so far as it relates to properties included in the registered deed of Heba-bil-ewaj No. 152 dated 3-1-1978. The plaintiff /respondent/petitioner will get 14 annas share in the aforesaid property and shall get partition of his share in the said property in metes and bounds. The Other Class Suit No. 188 of 1983 so far it relates to the property included in the registered deed of Heba-bil-ewaj No. 6440 dated 14-7-1965, is dismissed. However, there shall be no order as to cost.

43. Let a copy of this judgment be sent down to the Courts below for their future guidance.

Send down the LCR at once. The stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.

End.

lawyer:
For the Appellant: Mr. N.H. Khondker, Advocate-on-Record. 
For the Respondent No. 2 : Mr. Sharifuddin Chaldader, Advocate-on-Record. Respondent Nos. 1,3 and 4 : Ex parte.
parties:
Mohan BashiNama ------ Defendant Appellant.
Versus
Golam Rashid and others  ------ Plaintiff- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Mr. A.T.M. Afzal, J : - This appeal by leave is from judgment and order dated 12 August 1990 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court Division (Session at Chittagong) in revision, Civil Revision No. 258 of 1986, making the Rule absolute. 
2. Appellant Mohan BashiNama was defendant in Other Suit No. 64 of 1985 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Patiya, Chittagong filed by Respondents No. 1 and 2 for specific performance of an alleged contract for sale of the suit land, claimed by the appellar: to be his only land which includes his homestead. He also claims that the alleged agreement is false and fraudulent. 

3. Admittedly, summons was served on the appellant but on the date of hearing he was not present and the suit was decreed ex parte on 30.9.1985. On the next day i.e., on 1.10.1985 he filed a verified application under Order 9 Rule 13 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for set-ting aside the ex parte decree, registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 134 of 1985, taking the ground, inter alia, that he being an illiterate person had entrusted his neighbor Modon MohonNama to take necessary steps in the case but unfortunately the said Nama failed to appear on the date of hearing because, he himself (Modon MohonNama) deposed in the Misc. Case that, his father-in-law had suddenly fallen ill. 

4. The learned Subordinate Judge upon considering the evidence on record disbelieved the appellant's plea for remaining absent but even then allowed the Misc. Case in the interest of justice on 29.6.1986 with a cost of TIC. 500/- to be paid by the appellant to respondent Nos. 1 and 2 by 2.8.1986.

5. Plaintiff-respondents being aggrieved by the said order filed aforesaid Civil Revision No. 258 of 1986 in which a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division (at Chittagong), as already noticed, by the impugned judgment and order dated 22 August, 1990, made the Rule absolute taking the view that the learned Subordinate Judge ought not to have allowed the Misc. Case when the appellant was found to have failed make out a case of sufficient cause for non-appearance within the meaning of Order 9 Rule 13 C.P.C. The learned Judge observed that "as the opposite party No. 1 failed to make out a case under Order 9, Rule 13 which is a specific provision provided in the Code the Court below should not have acted in exercise of its jurisdiction under Section 151 C.P.C." 

6. Mr. N. H .Khondker, learned Advocate-on-Record, for the appellant obtained leave to appeal from the impugned judgment submitting that an important fact had escaped the notice of the appellant, which, if brought to the notice of the High Court Division, would have been a determining factor for not exercising the discretion under Section 115 C.P.C. in favour of the respondents. The fact is that pursuant to the order of the learned Subordinate Judge, the appellant had deposited the amount of cost (Tk. 500/-) within two weeks of the order of the learned Subordinate Judge and the respondents' lawyer withdrew the money and granted receipt and the Court by order dated 13.7.1986 restored the suit to its original file and number in terms of its order dated 29.6.1986. 

7. Mr. Khondker has argued that the respondents having thus acquiesced with the order of the learned Subordinate Judge dated 29.6.1986 by accepting the cost could no longer move against the same on 28.7.1986 by filing the revision petition and the High Court Division, at any rate, if made aware of the said fact, would not have interfered with the order of the learned Subordinate Judge in the exercise of its discretionary jurisdiction. 

8. That the respondents withdrew the cost and the suit was restored to file and number before filing of the revision petition by them is borne out by the order sheet of the learned Subordinate Judge. It is not also disputed by Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, learned Advocate-on-Record for respondent No. 2. Indeed Mr. Chaklader appears to be so much convinced about the submission of the appellant that he has not filed any concise statement even thus precluding him from making any submission. 

9. Be that as it may, on the general principle that a person cannot and/or ought not to be permitted to approbate and reprobate at the same time, the respondents were not entitled to question the order of restoration of the suit after having accepted the cost which was made a condition for the restoration. The High Court Division, we are sure, would have taken a different view if it were made aware of the important fact as above coupled with the facts already on record that the ex parte decree was passed on the first date of hearing of the suit after receipt of the summons, that the application under Order 9, Rule 13 C.P.C. was made on the very next day of the passing of the ex parte decree and the restoration of the suit was made on payment of adequate cost. 

10. In the circumstances of the case, the appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division are set aside and those of the Subordinate Judge dated 29.6.1986 are restored. There will be no order as to costs. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. A.R M Amirul Islam Chowdhury, J:- This Rule was issued on the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 14.6.80 passed by the Additional District Judge. Kushtia in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 17 of 1979 reversing the judgment and order dated 29.6.78 passed by the Munsif, Ist Court, Kushtia Sader Miscellaneous Case No. 21 of 1971 should not be set aside or such other or further orders as to this court may be fit and proper. 

	2. The pre-emptor petitioners filed an application under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (hereinafter referred to as 'Section 96') for pre-emption of 13-i decimals of land of plot Nos. 1536 and 1537 i.e. subject matter of sale deed No. 12008 dated 22.12.70 alleging therein that Ahmed All the purchaser is a stranger as such the pre-emptor petitioners being co-sharers of the holding are entitled to preempt the case land. Ahmed Ali, purchaser resisted the application under Section 96 by filing a written objection stating therein that in substance the sale effected by registered deed being No. 12008 is an exchange deed and as such under Section 96(10)(b) the land in question cannot be pre-empted. The case purchaser Ahmed All is that on 22.12.70 by 3 consecutive deeds being Nos. 12006, 12007 and 12008 captioned as sale deeds transfers of some lands were affected. By deed No. 12006 Ahmed Ali, Belayet Ali, Arab Ali and Rajab Ali transferred .18 acres of land to Mokbul Hossain, Amzad Hossain and Afzal Hossain. By deed No. 12007 Mokbul Hossain, Amzad Hossain and Afzal Hossain transferred '04k decimals of land to Belayet Ali. Arab Ali and Rajab Ali. By deed No. 12008 Mokbul Hossain, Amzad Hossain and Afzal Hossain transferred 13i decimal of land to Ahmed Ali. the purchaser contended that these 3 deeds if construed together would clearly show that the intention of the parties was t o effect exchange rather than out and out sale. The learned Assistant Judge on consideration of the evidence on record allowed the prayer for pre-emption in respect of deed No. 12008 holding that these 3 deeds captioned as sale deeds are out and out instruments of sale and not of exchange. Thereafter Ahmed Ali the purchaser in deed No. 12008 preferred an appeal before the District Judge and the Additional District Judge who heard the appeal on consideration of the evidence on record same to the conclusion that if these 3 deeds are considered together then the subject matter of deed No. 12008 would be treated as Exchange and as such is not pre-emptable under Section 96 and set aside the judgment and order of the trial Court, allowed the appeal and rejected the application under Section 96. 3. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order passed by the appellate Court below the pre-emptor petitioners moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

	4. Mr. Abu Siddique, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor petitioners submits that the 3 deeds had been captioned as sale deeds. He submits that in the circumstances it was not proper for the appellate court below to come to a finding that these deeds are in sub-stance deeds of exchange and that the subject matter of deed No. 12008 is not pre-emptable being an exchange. In this connection Mr. Abu Siddique the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor petitioners referred to the consideration stated in each of the 3 deeds. The consideration in deed No. 12006 is stated to be Taka 500/-. The consideration in deed No. 12007 is stated to be Taka 250/-. The consideration in deed No. 12008 is stated to be Taka 800/=. He submits that if exchange is to be presumed then the consideration amount of Taka 500/- stated in deed No. 12006 should be equal to the aggregate amount of consideration stated in deed Nos. 12007 and 12008. But in deed Nos. 12007 and 12008 the consideration had been stated to be Taka 250/- and Taka 800/- respectively. The aggregate amount of consideration of the 2 deeds namely deed No. 12007 and 12008 is Taka 1050/-which is more than Tk. 500, the consideration stated in deed No. 12006. He further submits that these 3 deeds are to be treated as deeds of out and out sale, and not as deeds of exchange. 

5. Mr. Abdul Aziz, the learned Advocate for the purchaser opposite party submits that the deed No. 12006 covers an area of 18 decimals of land. On the other hand deed Nos. 12007 and 12008 in the aggregate cover an area of 18 decimal of land. The area of deed No. 12006 being equal to the aggregate quantum of land transferred by deed Nos. 12007 and 12008 these three deeds are to be treated as deeds of exchange. He further submits that all these deeds were executed in one sitting and registered on the same day and the numbers are consecutive. In the circumstances though the consideration amount as stated in deed No. 12006 may not be equal to the aggregate amount of consideration shown in deed Nos. 12007 and 12008 these three deeds are to be treated as deeds of exchange inasmuch as the quantum of land covered by deed No. 12006 is equal to the aggregate quantum of land covered by deed Nos. 12007 and 12008. 

6. The question before me is if the 3 deeds are considered together whether they could be treated as deeds of exchange or simple deeds of sale. The word exchange has not been defined anywhere in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Section 118 of the Transfer of Property Act is relevant for our purposes. Section 118 of the Transfer of Property Act reads as under: 	"Exchange defined. When two per-sons mutually transfer the ownership of one thing for the ownership of another. neither thing or both things being money only. the transaction is called an exchange." In Halsbury's Laws of England 4th Edition Vol. 5 page 860 the word 'exchange' has been stated to be as under:"-"Exchange must be made for the best consideration in land or in land and money that can reasonably be obtained." 

7. In the case of Ismail Saha Vs. Saleh Muhammad Shah reported in A.I.R. 1925 (Lahore) 326 it was observed that "if the parties in substance intended to make an exchange of properties, the mere fact that a small sum of money was paid by one to the other by way of adjusting their values, would not alter the nature of the transaction as an exchange." 

8. In the case of Ram Badan Lal and others Vs. Kunwar Singh and others reported in A.I.R. 1938 (Allahabad) 229 and in the case of Randhir Singh and another Vs. Randhir Singh and others reported in A.I.R. 1937 (Allahabad) 665 it was observed that-"Where consideration for a transfer of property is partly money and partly other property, and it is not possible to divide the transaction into separate transaction of sale and exchange, it has been held that the transaction would be an exchange and not a sale for the purpose of pre-emption and that this would be so even if the purpose of adding non-pecuniary portion of consideration is to defeat the right to pre-emption." 

9. In the case of Prabhu Dial and another Vs. Shadi Ram and another reported in A.I.R. 1919 (Lahore) 246 it was observed that-"the question whether a transaction is a sale or exchange must be decided having regard to all the circumstances of the case and that the value of the properties mutually transferred were fixed by the parties does not necessarily, make the transaction mutual sales of property." 

10. In the case of Kishen Lal V. Ram Lal and others reported in A.I.R. 1927 (Allahabad) 696 it was observed that "In our opinion extrinsic evidence was admissible for the purpose of showing that these two documents, though purporting to be separate sale deed, were in reality part and parcel of the same transaction, which was one of an exchange. We may refer of the case of Hanif-un-nisa V. Faiz-un-nisa reported in I.L.R. 33 (All) 340= 1 1. I.C.398 decided by their Lordships of the Privy Council. Such evidence which shows that two documents executed and registered on the same date are part and parcel of one transaction and in fact represented only one trans-action, does not amount to leading evidence so as to vary the terms of a document. It was, therefore open to the learned Judge to take into account such evidence. It therefore, follows that his finding that the transactions were not two separate sale transaction but only one transaction of exchange must be accepted. The plaintiff has, therefore, no right to pre-empt the transfer. In other words for this purpose Section 92 of the Evidence Act, 1872 does not preclude the admissibility or extrinsic evidence to show that these 3 documents purported to be separate sale deeds are in reality part and parcel of the same trans-action and the fact that the value of the properties mutually transferred were fixed by the parties does not necessarily make the transaction mutual sales of the property. Reference in this connection may be made to the cases, reported in AIR 1927 (All) 696: AIR 1938 (All) 229 and AIR 1919 (Lahore) 146. 

11. In the instant case the aforesaid 3 deeds were executed in the same sitting and registered on the same day bearing consecutive numbers. Deed No. 12006 is for 18 decimals of land on one side and on the other side deed No. 12007 and 12008 together (in the aggregate) are for 18 decimals of land. The transferees of deed No. 12006 except Ahmed Ali are the recipants (transferees) of deed No. 12007 (the reel-pants are Belayet Ali, Arab Ali and Rajab Ali). The recipant (transferee) of deed No. 12008 is Ahmed All alone who is one of the transferees of deed Nos. 12006. The transferees of deed Nos. 12006 are together the recipants under deed Nos. 12007 and 12008 and the transferees of deed No. 12006 are the transferees of deed Nos. 12007 and 12008. 

12. In the circumstances I think that these 3 deeds if considered together, then the transactions would be treated as exchanges and that the land transferred by deed No. 12008 cannot be pre-empted because of Section 96(10)(b). 

13. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the decisions referred to hereinbefore I am of the opinion that the Additional District Judge had correctly held that the land covered by deed No. 12008 being in the nature of exchange cannot be pre-empted. 

14. For the reasons stated above the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. 

	End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 888 of 2009
lawyer:
A. J. Mohammad Ali, Senior Advocate, instructed by Zainul Abedin, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Petitioners 
Kamal-ul-Alam, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md. Toufique Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ----- For Respondent Nos. 1-3,5,7-9
