case_source: (From the Judgment and decree dated 23.02.2009 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 324 of 1997)
full_judgment:
Shah Abu Nayeem Mominur Rahman J.:- Instant application under Article 103 of the Constitution is for granting leave to appeal against the judgment and decree dated 23.02.2009 passed in First Appeal No. 324 of 1997 by the High Court Division in allowing the appeal in part and thereby decreeing the Other Suit No. 370 of 1994 dismissed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong. 

2. The respondent Nos. 1-9 as plaintiffs filed the suit for confirmation of possession upon declaration of title over 1.91 acres of land and for recovery of khas possession after eviction and also for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from entering into the schedule land and not to disturb the plaintiffs' title and possession and for further declaration that the Deed Nos. 746, 743, 742, 740 and 739 dated 01.01.1979, 03.01.1979 and 04.01.1979 executed and registered in favour of the defendants and Deed No. 11152 dated 13.09.1978 and Deed No. 11337 dated 18.09.1978 are forged, null, void, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

3. The plaintiffs' case is that their predecessor Younus Miah purchased 1.43 acres out of the suit land from the legal heirs of Kabir Ahmed, the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 21-24, vide registered deed No. 16787 dated 13.11.1979 and said defendant promised to sell the remaining 0.48 acres to the plaintiffs' predecessor and that Kabir Ahmed died on 10.01.1970 leaving behind the defendant Nos.  21-24 as his legal heirs to inherit his properties including the suit land and that the defendant in particular defendant Nos. 6 and 7, on 16.09.1994 threatened the plaintiffs to forcibly take possession of the suit land claiming ownership thereon through sale deed dated 01.01.1979, 03.01.1979, 04.01.1979, 18.09.1978 and 13.09.1978 allegedly executed and registered by Kabir Ahmed. 

4. The defendant Nos. 6-7 contested the suit by filing joint written statement denying the alleged claim of the plaintiffs and contending, inter alia, that the Kabir Ahmed owned the suit land through auction purchase and that by registered kabala No. 11152 dated 13.09.1978 he transferred the suit land in favour of Md. Younus Mia who in turn transferred the suit land to Mosst. Mahmuda Khatun and others by registered sale deed No. 11337 executed on 18.09.1978 and registered on 19.09.1978 and that the said purchasers Mosst. Mahmuda Khatun and others in turn sold the suit land by registered sale deed dated 13.01.1979 to the defendant No. 1, which prior to purchase published legal notice in the daily newspaper on 01.01.1978 about the purchase of the suit land and did not receive any objection there-against and that after .purchase the defendant got its name recorded in the B.S. record and paying rent regularly in its name and that in an appeal filed under Section 31 of the State Acquisition Act by the plaintiffs predecessor the possession of the defendant's was found and. con-firmed through an enquiry held on 19.02.1985, resulting dismissal of the appeal and that the defendant lost the original sale deed from the chamber of the lawyer. 

5; The learned Subordinate Judge decided the case reframing the issues as under: 
১। বর্তমান আকার ও প্রকারে মাত্র মামলা চলিতে পারে কি? 
২। অত্র মামলার উচিৎ মূল্যায়ন করা হইয়াছে কি?
৩। বাদীর মামলা তামাদিতে বারিত কি না? 
৪। মামলাটি পক্ষ দুষ্টতায় দুষ্ট কি না?
৫। নালিশী সম্পত্তিতে বাদী পরে স্বত্ব স্বামীত্ব আছে কি না? 
৬। নালিশী সম্পত্তিতে বাদী পক্ষে বিষয়কূল সখল আছে কি না? 
৭। দলিল নং ৭৪৬, ৭৪৩, ৭৪২, ৭৪০, ৭৩৯ তারিখ ৪/১/১৯৭৯, ১/১/১৯৭৯, ৩/১/১৯৯৭ এবং দলিল নং ১১৩৩৭ তারিখ ১৮/১/১৯৭৮ ও দলিল নং ১১১৫২ তারিখ ১৯/৯/১৯৭৮ জাল ফেরবী ও যোগসাজসী সাবাস্তে রদ ও রহিত যোগ্য কিনা যে গুলি বাদীগণের উপর বায়া নহে কি না? 
৮। বাদীপক্ষ প্রার্থিত মতে ডিক্রী পাইতে হকদার কি না? 
৯। আইন ও ন্যায়মতে আর কি কি (যদি থাকে) প্রতিকার বাদীপক্ষ পাইতে পারে? 

6. Both the plaintiffs and the defendants adduced 4 witnesses each and the documents produced by the plaintiffs were marked exhibit 1-7 series and those of the defendant were marked exhibit 'K ' to 'Q' series. 

7. On consideration of the materials and evidence on record and the submissions of the learned Advocates of the contesting parties the learned Court observed that Kabir Ahmed was the admitted owner of 4the suit land and the plaintiffs claimed that since Kabir Ahmed died on 10.01.1970 the registered sale deeds of the defendants dated 13.09.1978 in favour of the defendant's predecessor-in-interest Younus Miah and registered sale deed dated 19.09.1978 executed and registered by Younus Miah in favour of Mosst. Mahmuda Khatun and others are forged and fabricated documents and have been made through impersonating the deceased Kabir Ahmed through fictitious person and consequently Younus Mia could not acquire any right, title and interest in the suit land and hence the alleged deed executed on 18.09.1978 and registered on 19.09.1978 by said Younus Mia has no validity in the eye of law and thus the defendants alleged claim of ownership on the basis of purchase from Mosst. Mahmuda Khatun and others has no legal basis and that the plaintiffs having purchased from the legal heirs of Kabir, Ahmed with the delivery of possession of the suit land their title and possession are to be confirmed. 

8. It appears from the depositions of P.Ws.1,2 and 3 that they have corroborated the death of Kabir Ahmed on 10.01.1970 and in the cross examination they could not be shaken and further the statement of P.W.3, while deposing in Court that Kabir Ahmed died on 10.01.1970, has not been challenged by the defendants while cross examining said P.W.3 and that the plaintiffs produced the supporting documents to prove their title as well as the P.Ws.2 and 3, being attesting witnesses to the registered sale deed; deposed in the Court proving the execution and registration of the said sale deed. It further appears that the D.Ws. 3 and 4, the witnesses supporting the claim of the defendants' purchase of and possession in the suit land, are the employees of defendants. The plaintiffs also produced the supporting documents relating to death of Kabir Ahmed marked as exhibit 1 series. The defendants in view of their alleged loss of the original sale deed produced the relevant register from the office of the Sub-Registrar to prove the certified copy of the sale deed relating to suit land and thereby to prove the existence of the sale deed but the defendants did not produce any evidence to prove that the Kabir Ahmed was alive on the date of execution and registration of the sale deed in favour of Younus Miah to contradict the specific assertion of the plaintiffs that Kabir Ahmed died on 10.01.1970. 

9. Being aggrieved there-against the plaintiffs filed appeal in the High Court Division and the High Court Division on consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case, evidence and materials on record allowed the appeal in part decreeing the suit, amongst others, declaring title of the plaintiffs on 1.43 acres of land observing, amongst others, that: "Admittedly the defendants' deeds were executed during 13th September, 1978, 18th September 1978 and 13th  January 1979, within a space of 4 months, within which period they brought into existence of seven deeds. The execution of successive deeds is having transfers of the suit lands from one person to another and in the absence of examining any of those vendor and attesting witnesses, on the face of the plaintiffs challenge about their identities, raises a genuine doubt that the defendants have created these fraudulent deeds by setting up some fictitious persons. The learned Subordinate Judge has not at all considered this aspect of the matter and over looking this vital aspect believed the defendants deeds as genuine ones. 

10. These deeds are collusive and fictitious will also be apparent from the fact that the defendants have not produced the original deeds they have filed the certified copies of the deeds. In paragraphs 5(Kha) and 5(Ga) of the plaint the plain-tiffs made positive averments that they failed to trace out the whereabouts of these persons and thus they were fictitious persons. The defendants in their written statement simply claimed that these persons transferred the land to the defendants and that they handed over the deeds to their learned Advocate for filing an appeal against the record of right and thereafter, the learned Advocate lost those deeds from his chamber. In course of his evidence D.W.1 stated that the original deeds were destroyed in the Sub-Registrar's office as they could not procure the same in time and again he said that the documents were lost in 1985. He made two different versions in Court. On a query about the date of missing, he failed to mention the correct date. He, however, admitted that about the missing of the deeds, he did not make any G.1) entry with the local police station. As regards destroying the deeds, Shankor Kumar Dey (I).W.2) stated in cross that there was no remark about the destruction of the deeds in respect of the certified copies issued on 27th September 1994 relating to the deeds nos. 739 to 744. Therefore, as regards the missing of the original deeds, in view of the two inconsistent versions; initially they stated that those deeds were lost from chamber of the learned Advocate in 1985, but in course of evidence D.W.1 said that the documents were Registrar's office; it deeds were created pious persons after Ahmed destroyed in the Sub-is apparent that these in the name of fiction-the death of Kabir 

11. The defendants did not examine any attesting witnesses of their deeds. In this regard D.W1 stated in cross that he was acquainted with Moqbul Ahmed and others in 1978, when they came to transfer the suit lands. He further said that he did not personally enquire about Kabir Ahmed, Younus Mia and others and that he had no personal knowledge about the registration of the deeds in 1978. These deeds were executed on cartridge papers and not on stamp papers as admitted by D.W.1. He further stated that he did not enquire about the witnesses of the deed dated 13th September 1978. This admission of this vital witness that despite the challenge about the identities he was unmoved to ascertain the identities of their vendors and the witnesses of the deeds land us to believe that the defendants have created these deeds collusively and there-after, they have destroyed them in order to avoid criminal prosecution and by producing the certified copies they are claiming title in the suit lands." and that: 
"Learned Advocate appearing for the defendants-respondents argues that since the defendants have not examined the attesting witnesses of their deeds and in the absence of original deeds, they may be afforded an Opportunity to examine them and accordingly, the suit may be remanded to the trial Court for fresh hearing for ends of justice. Learned Advocate further submits that the defendant No. 6 has already allotted lands to different allottees and if the suit is decreed, there would arise various complications and in that view of the matter, the defendants may also be afforded an opportunity to examine those allotees as well. A remand may not be allowed as a matter of course. A remand may be allowed if the suit is disposed of on a preliminary point or that if the appellate Court thinks it proper it may direct the suit to be remanded to decide on what issues the suit would be tried but this power should be used sparingly. On assessment of the evidence on record we find that the parties have adduced their evidence in support of their claim and the Court below has decided the suit on all the issues on' merit. We find that it is not a fit case for remand for, if after a full flagged trial of the suit, the suit is remanded again to the trial Court the ends of justice will be defeated. In that view of the matter, we find no ground to send the suit on, remand for fresh decision for enabling the parties to fill up the lacuna. On consideration of the evidence on record, we are satisfied that the plaintiffs evidence arc more stronger and consideration and therefore the plaintiffs convincing than those of the defendant are not entitled to get the decree as passed. As regards the title, as observed by the High Court Division and that the above, the plaintiffs have been able to plaintiffs cannot pray for declaration that prove their title by purchase.

12. The title deeds of the defendants are null admitted heirs. 

End.

caseno: S.M.A. No. 32 of 1974 with Civil Rule No. 1021 (sm)/74 and Civil Revision No. 345 of 1975.
lawyer:
B.N. Chowdhury ------- For the Appellant.
Tajibul Huq ------- For the Respondent.
parties:
Begum Sayada Murguba Khatoon ------- Petitioner.
Vs.
Dewan Shahifur Reza Chowdhury & another ------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Abdur Rahman Chowdhury J. - This appeal arises out of an order of remand pasted by the learned Additional District Judge setting aside the decree passed by the learned Munsif and remanding the suit for rehearing.

2. Facts leading to this appeal, in brief, are that the plaintiff appellant instituted a money suit for realization of arrear rent and compensation from the defendant who was a tenant under her. The defendant contested the suit by filing a written statement. His defense inter alia was that the plaintiff was not the exclusive owner of the premises in question and she was entitled to only proportionate rent and not the entire rental circuit. He also claimed set off for having paid Municipal and other taxes and for repairs, water connection, etc.

3. Both parties adduced oral and documentary evidence in support of their respective cases. The learned Munsif on a consideration of the evidence on record decreed the suit in part for taka 2349/-and disallowed defendant's claim for set-off. The defendant preferred an appeal which was heard by the learned Additional District Judge who set aside the decree passed by the learned Munsif and remanded the suit for rehearing. The plaintiff thereafter preferred this appeal against the order of remand.

4. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant has submitted that the learned Additional District Judge was not justified in remanding the suit since the materials available on record were sufficient to decide the issues before him. He has further argued that the defendant having accepted the plaintiff as the sole owner of the premises in question cannot now be allowed to reopen the same.

5. Mr. Tazibul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-despondent has submitted that the case was rightly remanded for rehearing and the plaintiff would have an equal opportunity before the trial Court at the time of rehearing and as such there was no ground for any grievance. He has further argued that the plaintiff having failed to establish her exclusive title, she was pot entitled to claim the entire rent but was only entitled to proportionate rent as a co-owner of the premises in question.

6. It appears from the judgment of the learned Additional District judge that he has sent the case back on remand on the findings that the trial Court did not decide the question as to whether the suit was maintainable a, the instance of the plaintiff alone without proof of her exclusive title to the suit premises and that the trial Court also did not take into consideration the defendant's claim for set off on the ground of payment of municipal taxes, repairs and other expenditures incurred by the defendant for the maintenance of the suit premises. It appeals that the trial Court did go into the question and decide the issues involved, and the finding that these issues were not gone into by the trial Court are not borne out by the materials on record and the judgment of the trial Court itself.

7. Apparently, the order of remand in the instant case was passed under Order 41, rule 23 of the Code. But, in the instant case the trial Court did not dispose of the suit on preliminary point alone, nor did the lower appellate Court frame issues and send it for re-trial on specific issues as contemplated under Order 41 rule 25 of the Code. The learned Additional District Judge has found that the trial Court did not go into the question whether the plaintiff was the exclusive owner of the suit premises whereas it appears from the judgment of the trial Court that the learned Munsif has elaborately discussed both the oral and documentary evidence relating to the plaintiff's title and has come to the positive finding that the plaintiff was the sole owner by virtue of a partition amongst The co-sharers and has further found that the defendant had also acknowledged the plaintiff as The sole owner of the suit premises. The learned Additional District Judge did not advert to any of the exhibits relied on by the final Court exempting Ext. 4 to which I shall revert later when I go into the merits of the case.

8. The lower Appellate Court has also found that the trial Court did not consider the defendant's claim of set-off to which he was legally entitled. Here again, it appeals that the trial Court had gone into the question of set-off very elaborately and has disallowed the same with its own reasonings.

9. I have had occasions in the past to remind the lower appellate, Courts of their duties as an appellate Court and once again I would like to remind them of the relevant provisions of law in remanding a suit for rehearing. Now, Order 41, rules 23, 24 and 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure (hereinafter called the Code) which deal with the remand of a case by an appellate Court read as follows:

Rule 23. "Where the Court from whose decree an appeal is preferred has disposed of the suit upon a preliminary point and the decree is reversed in appeal, the appellant Court may, if it thinks fit, by order remand the case and may further direct what issue or issues shall be tried in the case so remanded, and shall send a copy of its judgment and order to the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred, with directions to readmit the suit under its original number in the register of civil suits, and proceed to determine the suit and the evidence (if any) recorded during the original trial shall, subject to all just exceptions, be evidence during the trial after remand."

Rule 24. "Where the evidence upon the record is sufficient to enable the Appellate Court to pronounce judgment, the Appellate Court may, after resettling the issues, if necessary, finally determine the suit, notwithstanding (hat the judgment of the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred has proceeded wholly upon some ground other than that on which the Appellate Court proceed."

Rule 25. "Where the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred has omitted to frame or try any issue, or to determine any question of fact, which appears to the Appellate Court essential to the right decision of the suit upon the merits, the Appellate Court may, if necessary, frame issues, and refer the same for trial to the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred, and in such case shall direct such Court to take the additional evidence required, and such Court shall proceed to try- such issues, and shall return the evidence to the Appellate Court together with its findings, thereon and the reasons therefore."

10. Under Order 41 rule 23 of the Code, there can be no remand unless the following conditions exist: (a) that the entire suit and not a portion of it has been disposed of by the trial Court, (b) that the disposal must be on a preliminary point (c) and that the preliminary point on which the suit is decided has been reversed by the appellate Court.

Order 41 rule 24 of the Code lays down that where the evidence on record is sufficient the appellate Court is competent to determine the suit finally and there is no need for remand.

11. Under Order 41 rule 25 of the Code, only specific issues are sent to the trial Court for findings and not for re-trial of the entire suit. After the return of the findings by the trial Court the appeal is to be heard under Order 41 rule 26 of the Code.

12. The lower appellate Court had every right to accept or reject the findings of the trial Court and come to its own findings on the basis of the evidence already on record but instead of doing so the learned Judge has thought it appropriate to remand the case for re-hearing of the entire suit. Having gone through the judgment, I cannot help feeling that the learned Additional District Judge was shirking his own responsibility as the appellate Court in not deciding the issues when the evidence on record was sufficient to enable him to determine the suit finally. This unfortunate trend should be discarded in order to avoid unnecessary prolongation of litigation and multiplicity of proceedings. Mere disagreement with the findings of the trial Court is no ground for the appellate Court to send a case on remand when the evidence on record is sufficient to decide the matter finally. Order 41 rule 24 of the Code is a clear and standing bar in such cases. Under Order 41 rules 23 and25 the Code clearly lays down that there can be no remand unless the conditions laid down in those rules exist. I am, therefore, clearly of the view that the learned Additional District Judge as the final Court of facts was fully competent to decide the case himself as the evidence on record was sufficient to enable him to come to a final decision without entailing on the party’s unnecessary trouble and expenses of a de novo trial.

13. Having found that the order of remand by the learned Additional District Judge was not sustainable in law, I have given my anxious considerations whether to send it back to the lower appellate Court for re-hearing of the appeal. The learned Advocates appearing for the parties, who very ably assisted me during the hearing of the appeal, prayed that the matter be disposed of by this Court. Having regard to the provisions of Order 41 rule 33 of the Code, I propose to dispose of the matter to avoid further prolongation of the litigation and unnecessary expenditure.

14. Now, coming to the merits of the case, it appears that the trial Court found that the plaintiff became the sole owner of the suit premises by way of amicable partition with his other co-sharers. He has further found that the plaintiff was entitled to the arrear rent for 29 months from December, 1969 to April, 1972. But he disallowed the plaintiff's claim for compensation of Taka 1100/- for the period between May, 1972 to 18th August, 1972. The learned Munsif has further found that the defendant's claim to set-off was not legally maintainable in view of section 21 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 (hereinafter called the Ordinance).

15. On the question of title, the learned Additional District Judge has found that although the plaintiff admitted having an unregistered document of partition in the absence of that document the Court could not properly decide the claim of the plaintiff to be the sole owner of the suit premises. It is rather curious that the learned Additional District Judge has relied on the compromise arrived, at between the parties before the Conciliation Court (Ext. 4) for the purpose of finding that the defendant was entitled to set-off but has to any ignored the other important aspect of the compromise namely, the acceptance by the defendant of the plaintiff as the sole owner of the suit premises. Besides, the trial Court has referred to and relied on Exts. 5, 5A and 5B, the rent-receipts showing the payment of rent by the defendant to the plaintiff thereby admitting her as the sole owner of the suit premises. In his evidence also the defendant admitted his signatures on the back of the counterfoil of the rent receipts granted by the plaintiff. The learned Additional District Judge has not at all considered those exhibits in arriving at his finding on the question of title of the plaintiff. After having accepted and attorned the plaintiff as the sole owner of the suit premises, the defendant cannot now be allowed to turn back and take up a different plea with a view to defeat the claim of the plaintiff. One cannot be allowed to approbate and reprobate, at the same time. I am, therefore, inclined to agree with the trial Court that the plaintiff is the role owner of the suit premises and the defendant is a monthly tenant under her.

16. With regard to the defendant's claim to set-off it appears that the trial Court found that the claim was not legally maintainable in view of section 21 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 which lays down as follows:

“21. Making of repairs and taking of measures for the maintenance of Essential services by the Tenant on the failure or neglect of the landlord to do so-

(1) The controller shall, on application made to him in this behalf by any tenant in possession of any premises, cause a notice to be served in the prescribed manner on the landlord thereof requiring him to make any repairs which such landlord is bound to make to the premises or to take any measures for the due maintenance of any essential supply of service, such as, the maintenance of the supply of water or electricity, the maintenance of drainage service and the maintenance of any lift, which such landlord is bound to maintain in the premises under the condition of the tenancy or according to local usage. (2) If within thirty days from the date of the service of such notice the landlord fails or neglects to make such repairs or to take such measures, as the case may be, the tenant may submit to the Controller an estimate of the cost of such repairs or measures and may apply to him for permission to make such repairs or to take such measures himself and, thereupon, the Controller may, after giving the landlord an opportunity of being heard and after considering such estimate of cost and making such enquiries as he may consider necessary, by an order in writing, permit the tenant to make such repairs or to take such measures as the case may be, at a cost not exceeding such amount as may be specified in the order ant it shall thereafter be lawful for the tenant. to make such repairs or to take such measures himself and to deduct the cost thereof, which shall in no case exceed the amount so specified, from the rent or otherwise recover it from the landlord. Provided that the amount so deducted or recoverable in any year shall not exceed one sixth of the rent payable by the tenant for that year.

Provided further that if the repairs or measures though necessary in the opinion of the Controller, exceed in cost the said amount, and the tenant agrees to bear the excess cost himself, the Controller may permit the tenant to make such repairs or to take such measures.

(3) The repairs or measures mentioned in sub-section (1) shall not be deemed to include such repairs or measures without which the premises are not habitable or usable except with great inconvenience, like keeping them wind and water-tight. The landlord shall be bound to make such repairs or take such measures in any event. On his failure to do so the provisions of sub-section (1) and (2) shall apply without the limitation as to the amount deductable or recoverable as provided in the said sub-sections.

(4) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1) and (2) if the necessity for making any repairs or for taking any measures referred to in sub-section (1) is so urgent that any delay involved in the procedure referred to in the said sub-sections is likely to subject the tenant to personal loss, damage or serious inconvenience, the tenant may himself cause the notice referred to in sub-section (1) to be served in the prescribed manner on the landlord requiring him to make such repairs or to take such measures within seventy two hours of the service of such notice and shall in every such case submit, at the same time, a copy of such notice to the Controller together with an estimate of the cost of such repairs or measures to enable the Controller Jo make such enquiries as he may consider necessary about the necessity of such repairs or measures and correctness of the estimate so submitted, and if after the service of such notice, the landlord fails to make such repairs or to take such measures within the time mentioned in the notice, the tenant may himself make such repairs or take such measures, as the case may be, and, after completion of such repairs or measures, submit to the Controller a statement of the cost thereof and thereafter the Con toiler, after considering such statement and making such further enquiries as he may consider necessary, may, by an order in writing, determine the amount of the costs which the tenant is entitled to recover from the landlord., and the tenant may thereupon deduct the amount so determined from the rent or otherwise recover it from the landlord : Provided that the amount so deducted or recoverable in any year shall not exceed one-sixth of the rent payable by the tenant for that year :

Provided further that the provision of the first proviso shall not apply to any repairs or measures without which the premises are not habitable or unable except with great inconvenience, like keeping them wind and water-tight.”

17. A perusal of the relevant provisions of the Ordinance shows that a notice has to be served first on the landlord in the prescribed manner requiring him to make any repairs which the landlord is bound to make or to take such measures for due maintenance of any essential supply of service such as the maintenance of supply of water or electricity, the maintenance of drainage service etc. which such landlord, is bound to maintain in the premises under the conditions of the tenancy or according to local usage. If after service of the notice upon the landlord he fails or neglects to make such repairs or to take such measures as contemplated under section 21(1) of the Ordinance, the tenant may then submit to the Controller an estimate of costs of such repairs or measures and may apply to him for permission to make such repairs or to take such measures himself whereupon the Controller after affording the landlord an opportunity of being heard in the matter, permit the tenant to undertake such repairs or to take such measures and thereafter to deduct the costs thereof from the rent or otherwise recover it from the landlord,. In case of urgency, however, the tenant may serve a notice in the prescribed form under section 21(4) of the Ordinance requiring the landlord to make such repairs within 72 hours of the notice and at the same time submit a copy of the notice to the Controller together with the estimate of the costs of such repairs and of the landlord after receipt of such notice fans to repair the tenant may himself undertake such repairs and after completion of the same submit to the Controller a statement of the cost thereof and the Controller after considering the statement and after further enquiry may by an order determine the amount of costs that the tenant is entitled to recover from the landlord and the tenant may thereupon deduct the amount so determined from the rent or otherwise recover from the landlord.

18. Considering the eventuality and circumstances that may arise between a landlord and a tenant, the legislature has provided for a detailed and comprehensive procedure for the redress of any grievance that the tenant may have for any matter like repairs and maintenance of essential service in the tenanted premises.

19. Now, Order 8 rule 6 of the Code which deals with particulars of set off lays down as follows:

“Particulars of set off to be given in written statement (1) where in a suit for the recovery of money the defendant claims to set off against the plaintiff's demand any ascertained sum of money legally recoverable by him from the plaintiff, not exceeding the pecuniary limits of the jurisdiction of the Court, and both parties fill the same characters they fill in the plaintiff's suit, the defendant may, at the first hearing of the suit, but not afterwards unless permitted by the Court, present a written statement the particulars of the debt sought to be set off. Effect of set-off (2) The written statement shall have the same effect as a plaint in a cross-suit so as to enable the Court to pronounce a final judgment in- respect of both the original claim and of the set off; but this shall not affect the lien, upon the amount decreed, of any pleader in respect of the costs payable to him under the decree.

(3) The rules relating to a written statement by a defendant apply to a written statement in answer to a claim of set-off.”

20. The relevant provisions of the Cede dealing with set-off clearly lays down that the following conditions must exist for the applicability of the Rule : (a) the suit must be for recovery of money (b) the claim demanded to be set-off must be an ascertained sum of money (c) it must be legally recoverable from the plaintiff (d) it must not exceed the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Court (e) both parties must fill the same character as they fill in the plaintiff's suit (f) the claim must be made at the first hearing unless permitted by the Court to do so afterwards.

21. It was, therefore, evident that apart from the other conditions to be satisfied before the rule can be applied in a particular case, the claim demanded to be set off must be legally recoverable from the plaintiff. The sum claimed as set-off which is; barred by limitation or barred under some other law cannot be deemed- to be legally recoverable.

22. The defendant in his written statement claimed the following as set-off; (a) deduction of taka 1495/40 paisa paid by the defendant towards taxes (b) re imbursement of taka 2,000 for urgent repairs incurred by the defendant (c) deduction of taka 340/- for re-occupation of a portion of the tenanted premises by the plaintiff (d) re-imbursement of taka 1180/for the loss of water. The trial Court has negatived the claim of the defendant on the ground that the taxes were paid and the expenditures for repairs and other things were incurred by the defendant without the necessary permission- of the Rent Controller as required under section 21of the Ordinance. So far as the claims relating to Taka 2,000/- for repairs and Taka 1180/- for the loss of water are concerned, I am afraid, the deductions claimed cannot be deemed to be legally recoverable in view of section 21 of the Ordinance where a detailed and elaborate procedure has been laid down for service of notice upon the landlord and for obtaining necessary permission of the Rent Controller before such repairs can be undertaken or expenditures incurred by the tenant. Admittedly, no such notice as required under the law was served upon the plaintiff nor was any permission obtained from the Rent Controller for the repairs undertaken or the expenditures incurred and as such the amount so claimed as set-off cannot be legally recovered. Regarding the claim of Taka 340/- for the reoccupation of a portion of a tenanted premises by the plaintiff, I am afraid there is no evidence to substantiate the claim against the plaintiff. I am however not inclined Jo agree with Ike trial Court regarding the defendant's claim of taka 1495/40 paisa towards his payment of municipal taxes and WASA dues. The payment of taxes and other dues to the local, authorities, in my opinion, are legally recoverable-and can be claimed as set off by the tenant against the claim of the landlord, since they do not come within the purview of section 21 of the Ordinance and no permission from the Rent Controller is required for payment of the same by the tenant. The payment of the taxes amounting to Taka 1495/40 paisa by the defendant has not been disputed by Mr. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the appellant, who has categorically submitted that he had no objection to the amount being allowed as set off. In such view of the matter, I am inclined to allow the defendant to set off Taka 1495/40 paisa against the plaintiff's claim of arrear rent of taka 2349/.

23. One other point remains to be decided before I conclude and that is the question of payment of Court fees with regard to the set off claimed by the defendant. It appears that the defendant did not pay any Court fee till date on his claim to set-off. There is no doubt that Court fees must be paid on the full amount claimed as set-off but the question is whether the defendant can be allowed to put in the Court fees at this belated stage when the matter has travelled beyond two Courts. Section 149 of the Code lays down as follows:

“149. Power to make up deficiency of Court fees. Where the whole or any part of any fee prescribed for any document by the law for the time being in force relating to Court-fees has not been paid, the Court may, in its discretion, at any stage, allow The person, by whom such fee is payable, to pay the whole or part, as- the case may be of such Court fee; and upon such payment the document, in respect of which such fee is payable, shall have the same force, and effect as if such fee had been paid in the first instance”.

24. Under the aforesaid section where the whole or any part of Court fees prescribed for any document by the law has not been paid, the Court may in its discretion, at any stage, allow the person by whom such fee is payable, to pay the whole or part, as the case may be of such Court fee and upon such payment the document shall have the same force and effect as if such fee had been paid in the first instance. The discretion has, therefore, been given to the Court to allow Court fees to be paid at any stage by the person by whom such fee is payable. In view of my finding that the defendant is entitled to set-off a part of his claim; I am inclined to allow him to put in the requisite Court fees payable on the full amount claimed by him as set-off. In the result, the appeal is allowed. The judgment and order passed by the learned Additional District Judge is set aside. The decree passed by the learned Munsif is hereby affirmed subject to the modification that the defendant-respondent shall be allowed to set-off Taka 1495/40 paisa from the decretal amount of Taka 2349/-. As prayed for, the defendant- respondent is allowed 4 (four) weeks' time from the day to put in the requisite Court fees on the full amount of Taka 5015/50 paisa claimed as set-off, in default his claim for set-off shall stand dismissed and the plaintiff-appellant shall be entitled to recover the full amount of Taka 2349/- from the defendant respondent in accordance with law.

 In the facts and circumstance of the case, there will be no order as to costs.

The connected Civil Rule No. 1021 (sm) of 1974 arising out of this appeal is accordingly discharged without any order as to costs.

In view of the judgment delivered in the S.M.A. No. 32 of 1974, the rule in Civil Revision No. 345 of 1975 has become in fructuous and is accordingly discharged without any order as to costs. The order of ad-interim stay is hereby vacated. Let S.C.C. Suit No. 1 of 1973 now proceed in accordance with law and it is directed that the suit be disposed of within two months of the receipt of the records by The Court below, as prayed for by the parties.

Send down the records of the S. C. C. Suit at once.

End.

case_source: In the matter of an applicable is under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 for setting aside the order dated in 8-3-72 of the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dacca passed in Money Execution Cate No. 19/67.
full_judgment:
K. Hossein, J.-This Revisional case has been referred to the Special Bench of the instance of a Division Bench  by the Learned Chief Justice as interpretation of Article 3 of President's Order No. 12 of 1972 is involved, and which is a question of general importance.

2. Facts concerning the Revisional Case briefly stated are that National Bank of Pakistan, as it then was, obtained a money decree against the judgment-debtor, Sunil Kumar Basu on 12-9-62. The decree was put into execution, and a house property at Hatkhola of the judgment-debtor-was attached and put to auction sale on 1.8.70. Syed Maksud Ahmed the petitioner is the acting purchaser. Judgment Debtor Basu filed an application under Order 21 rule 90 of Civil Procedure Code on 29.8.70 for setting aside sale. It was registered as Misc. Case No. 354 of 1970. It may be noted that the judgment-debtor has started several other proceedings relating to auction sale but, we are in this revisional case, concerned with this case. During the Pendency of this case, the liberation war started, and on 15.5.71, the date fixed for decree-holder opposite party to file objection, the case was dismissed for default for the non-appearance of the judgment-debtor. On that day the auction-purchaser appeared by a vokalatnama, and the decree-holder prayed for further time for filing its objection. On 17.5.71 the Executing court passed another order ex parte vacating the stay order obtained earlier by the judgment on 31.8.70.: by the same order the sale was confirmed. The other relevant orders calling attention are that on 27.5.71 sale-certificate was granted to the auction Purchaser; on 31.5.71 order for the issue of writ of delivery of possession was made. On these occasions the judgment-debtor appeared through a lawyer, though not personally. On 11.6.71 the delivery of possession of the property was given to the auction purchaser then came the liberation of Bangladesh on 16th December, 1971. On February, 7, 1972 President's Order No. 12, 1972 was promulgated. The judgment-debtor on 18.2.72 filed an application for restoration of the Misc. Case No. 354 of 1970 which was dismissed for default on 15.5.71, and it was restored treating the dismissal order null and void. The judgment debtor thereafter filed two applications on 22.2.72 and 3.3.72 praying for setting aside the orders and actions dated 17.5.71, 27.5.71, 31.5.71 and the delivery of possession on 11.6.71. These two applications were heard in the presence of the parties on 8.3.72 on which day the learned Court below allowed the applications of judgment-debtor, and declared the aforesaid orders and actions null and void. The auction-purchaser has challenged this order in this application. Mr. Moinul Huq has appeared for the auction-purchaser-petitioner; Mr. B.B. Roy Choudhury for the judgment debtor opposite party; Mr. Aswarul Hossain for the decree-holder opposite party, though there is anomaly in his appearance inasmuch as National Bank of Pakistan has been Nationalised and its assets and liabilities vested in the Sonali Bank. Mr. Huq appearing for the auction-purchaser-petitioner has submitted that since in the court below there has not been any substitution and also that he entertains doubt on Sonali Bank being a successor to the National Bank of Pakistan he has consciously refrained from praying for substitution. A power was filed strangely enough in the name of National Bank of Bangladesh which, obviously, is not the Bank either before or after nationalization. We have, however, given liberty to Mr. Hossain to make this submission in view of the importance of the question involved.

We have heard learned arguments on either side and many questions have been debated

but first of all I want to deal with the questions as I see.

<u>3. Before entering into the questions it may be noted that the petitioner has formally challenged the order of 8.3.72. But Mr. Huq has also raised a question which impliedly raises a challenge to the validity of the order dated 18.2.72 passed by the court below, treating the order dated 15.5.71 null and void though that order is not formally under challenge. Mr. Huq citing the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Md. Swaleh Vs. U.G. & Fodder Agencies (964) 16 DLR (SC) 155 has submitted that earlier order can be challenged or, if the order is without jurisdiction, and the High Court can interfere suo motu. Since a question of law of great importance is involved, we think we should look into it inasmuch as the impugned order is dependent on the validity of the order dated 18.2.72 restoring the Miscellaneous Case. This question was raised very late on the third day of hearing. We have permitted Mr. Huq to argue the point. We, however, want to make it clear that this concession should not be taken as a precedent. A petitioner, in his revisional application under section 115 of the Code, should not be permitted to impugn earlier orders not formally challenged, unless the court thinks it absolutely essential so to do.</u>

4.  I can now proceed to deal with the question now before us. The broad question is what upon a true construction is the meaning of article 3 of President's Order No. 12 of 1972. And whether the impugned order dated 8.3.72 is a valid order. To appreciate the questions the material part of article 3 excluding the non-essential ones may be set out;

"Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force all Orders passed ex parte by any Court or orders disposing of matters due to default in compliance with any direction of any court in any legal proceeding at any time after the 1st day of March, 1971, and before the commencement of this Order, are hereby declared null and void, and the proceeding shall continue in accordance with the law."

5. The Article broadly speaking nullifies certain categories of decisions, passed within the stated period; 1st day of March 1971 and 7th February, 1972. It then provides for the continuance of the proceeding in accordance with law. The decisions are judgments, decrees and orders. These decisions must have been passed by any court or tribunal and in any legal proceedings. The conditions required to be fulfilled under Article 3 of President Order are: (1) there must be judgment, order or decree; (2) passed by a court or tribunal:(3) in a legal proceeding, (4) (a) passed ex parte or (b) disposal due to default in compliance with court's or tribunal's order, and (5) made between 1st day of March, 1971 and 7th February, 1972. If the aforesaid conditions are satisfied, the decision, to use a comprehensive term, is null and void.

Two expressions in the article require interpretation; first, ex parte and second, 'null and void'.

6. The expression ex parte governs three classes of decision; judgments, decrees and orders. The decision again must have been passed by any court or tribunal, and in any legal proceeding. "Legal proceeding" has been given an inclusive definition in the order to include suits, cases, prosecution, appeal, revision and review. Any decision made in any one of these diverse legal proceedings, and passed ex parte or disposed on default of compliance of court's direction comes within the mischief of Article 3 of the Order. The expression ex parte governs the diverse proceedings, civil, criminal, revenue and others. The common denominator is legal proceeding. The expression has not been defined in the Presidential Order. Since it governs devise decisions and proceedings, the expression is even though used in one of the procedural laws governing these diverse proceedings like the suit, cannot appropriately be applied to all proceedings. We are therefore, bound to give the word its plain meaning understood in common parlance. Dictionary meaning may give a guide; it means "upon, from or in the interest of one side only." Osborn's Concise Law Dictionary; Whartorn's Law Lexicon and Stroud's Judicial Dictionary, convey amongst others the dictionary meaning by one party in the absence of the other. I think, we are to construe the expression in a way as to govern all judgments, decrees and orders, and passed in all legal proceedings, inasmuch as the legislative authority has used it in article 3 in a comprehensive sense. That meaning is to be given as compehends all in order to give effect to the legislative intent. I think, we cannot profitably use the expression borrowing the meaning from one of the several procedural laws only.

<u>7. Though the expression can be found in the Civil Procedure Code, a closer examination reveals that its meaning, if at all is difficult to apply in the Article. The word has neither been defined, nor used in any uniform sense. The expression hardly finds place in criminal trial or appeal. In my opinion, we are left with no choice but to apply the general meaning. By so doing, the meaning appropriate to govern all decisions or proceedings, is to hold that any decision made in the absence of any of the, parties to the proceeding, be he the originator of the proceeding, or the person proceeded against. In either case it is to be taken as ex parte. This interpretation includes all and excludes none and so is to be adopted.</u>

<u>8. To turn to the expression 'null and void'. The word 'void' in Osborn is of no legal effect,' 'nullity'. That is also the ordinal meaning of the words null and void. I think, the words have been used in their primary sense. There are, of course cases where word void' or expression 'null and void' have been construed to mean voidable. The reasoning of those cases show that it was never doubted or disputed, that it does not mean nullity, but that, if the context so permits, then in score cases a restricted meaning of voidable be given. This restricted meaning is permissible to avoid absurdity or hardship, in case of third party bonafide purchaser for value will cut notice or not to allow a party to take advantage of his own wrong. No such condition is available here. On the other hand, Maxwell, 9th Ed. at page 221, says inter alia that when some object of public policy in view, the word receives its natural full force and effect. The preamble of the Presidential Order records, that due to the reign of terror of the Pakistan Occupation Army, people were not able to go to courts or tribunals either to institute legal proceedings or to defend them, to comply with direction and many legal proceeding have been disposed of ex parte or for default in compliance with direction of the court, that ends of justice demand their nullification. A public policy has been declared here. It is manifestly for the benefit of litigant public in general. The context, therefore, does not prohibit, but rather permits the construction of primary meaning, that of nullity. I would adopt it so.</u>

9. I get some indication to the meaning, I have sought to give to the expression null and void', if the last clause of this article is considered, which says that the proceeding shall continue in accordance with the law. How could the proceeding continue unless the contemplated decision is treated a nullity? The language of the Article gives a clear indication of construction to the expression in the manner I have done.

10. Another significant fact to be remembered is that the Legislative authority is declaring certain categories of decisions null and void, and has not left them to the choice of the party affected to apply to the court or tribunal for their reversal. It is legislative nullification, and can mean only nullity, void abs initio.

11. The manner chosen by the legislative authority is in the well-recognised from of declaration. Caracas's on Statute Law 6th Ed. page 59 says: `decelerating Acts are usually held to be retrospective; the effect is then a nullity.'

<u>12. The Article is dealing with decisions made within stated period, and the whole period is past. It, in clear language, is nullifying those past decisions. The operation of this Article is retrospective in clear language. The article says "all......orders passed between 1st day of March 1971 and the commencement of this Order" i.e. 7th February, 1972" are hereby declared null and void, 'Hereby' as the dictionary says, means 'by this' or 'from this'. What the Article says is that by this Presidential Order, the contemplated past decisions are declared null and void. The present indefinite tense has been used to nullify past transaction, which has effect of retrospective operation, and makes the decisions non-existent void ab initio.</u>

13. Turning to the order dated 15.5.71, I find that date was fixed for filing objection by the decree-holder-opposite party, and on that date both auction purchaser and decree-holder appeared and the latter filed an application for time. But the Judgment debtor did not appear, and so his Miscellaneous Case was dismissed for, default. The court, therefore, dismissed the case because of the absence of the judgment-debtor. He was the originator of the case and was seeking to set aside the auction sale. The dismissal order has adversely affected him. This order is within the meaning of ex parte order contemplated in Article 3 of the President's Order No. 12 of 1972, as I have understood. It is, therefore, null and void, a nullity.

14. I now take up the points raised by Mr. Huq for the petitioner and Mr. Asrarul Hossain who has substantially supported him. It has first been urged by the learned Advocates that the word ex parte does not include an order of dismissal for default. The basis of their submission is that the expression ex parte used in Civil Procedure Code is to be applied. It means an order passed where originator of the proceeding is present, and the person proceeded against is absent. The person in the first category is plaintiff, petitioner, or appellant; and that of the second, defendant, or opposite party, or respondent. In reply Mr. Roy Chowdhury submits that the word ex parte does not always bear this meaning, and in or der to give full effect to the Presidential Order, the ordinary meaning of the word; with one side only, is to be given. The word does not exclude an order passed in the absence, or for the default of the originator of be proceeding. He argues that Legislative Authority has sought to govern by the expression ex parte all diverse decisions passed not only under the Civil Procedure Code, but cut-side it, including proceedings like criminal where there is hardly any reference to this word. Abutter of decisions have been cited from the Bar. They are Mushtaq All Vs. Khushi. Muhamad. PLD .1961 Lahore 792, Hariram Rewachand Vs. Pribhdas Mulchand and others AIR 1945 Sind 98, Sangram Singh, Vs: Election Tribunal Kotah and another AIR 1955 (SC) 425. A detailed discussion of these decisions is uncalled for, as they are confined to the expression used in the Civil Procedure Code.

15. There is great weight in the submission of Mr. Roy Chowdhury when he says that' the word ex parte Used in Civil. Procedure Code in a peculiar special sense cannot to adopt in article 3 of the Order. It is true that in Civil Procedure Cede ex parte judgments or order indicates an order raised in favour of originator of the proceeding and against the person proceeded against in his absence, but this does not carry us far. The expression has not been defined in the Cede, nor is it been used in any uniform sense, in the Cede itself. To illustrate, lac the case of ex parte decree. It means that the defendant or the respondent was served with the notice and he, after the service of notice, has failed to appear in court and in terms of relevant rule the matter was set down for ex parte disposal, and when the suit or the appeal was called en for hearing, he was fetter absent and so the ex parte decree followed; But if the Order 41 rule (5)(4) is looked at, it is found that the court can, pending the hearing of application for stay of execution a the decree, pass an ex pane order of Here the expression has been used simply to mean in the absence of the other side. The use of the word is not uniform.

16. The problem becomes more complicated, if another illustration is taken. Suppose an ex parte decree has been passed. The defendant takes an appeal to the appellate Court against this decree, and thereafter his appeal is dismissed for default. What is the position an appeal is but the continuation of the suit. The defendant-appellant was no doubt prosecuting his appeal, but in fact he was defending the suit. According to the argument of Mr. Huq, the ex parte decree will be null and void, but not his appeal dismissed for default. The strict interpretation leads to attempt to deduce a general proposition from the cited decisions. The agreement of Mr. Hug does not commend to me. The illustrations indicate that the purported deduction is neither logical, nor serves the ends of justice. The Code has for different species of default, or dismissal provided for different and specific remedies. The Article under consideration comprehends all.

17. Then again Article 3 of the Order has used the expression with no qualifying words, restricting its meaning, nor has it been defined, or used any expression, to convey an intention to exclude the order passed in default of the originator of the proceeding. Rather it gets fuller meaning, if the word is interpreted to mean an order passed in the absence of any one of the contending parties. Take another illustration; according to Mr. Huq ex parte order passed under Order 41, rule (5) (4) though is an exparte order does not come within the contemplation of Article 3, as only when the appearance of the other side is either provided in rule, or is necessary, that exparte order is to be so treated. According to his submission the expression ex parte in the Code does not bear the same sense in all places. A generalization is not possible.

18. If this be the position of the expression in the Civil Procedure Code, where will it Idea us if we try to apply the suggested hypothesis to diverse proceedings envisaged in Article 3, Civil Procedure Code does not apply to most of them. Take the case of Criminal Appeal. Section 423 of the Criminal Procedure; Code says that the appellate court is to pronounce judgment, even if the accused appellant is absent, when the appeal is called on for hearing. There is no provision for dismissing the appeal for default; in the contrary the uniform judicial interpretation is that it prohibits such dismissal. Here we get a judgment in the absence of the originator of the proceedings. It does not fit in with the analogy of the Civil Procedure Code. The hypothesis suggested by Mr. Huq and Mr. Hossain breaks down.

19. Mr. Roy Chowdhury has rightly submitted by pointing to the preamble of the enactment that the word has a direct reference to persons who were not able to institute legal proceedings. This is a clear indication that the word 'exparte' cannot bear the restricted meaning sought to be given by Mr. Huq and Mr. Hossain Mr. Hug's reply that the expression 'to institute legal proceeding' does not include carriage of the proceedings, is so manifestly meaningless as calls for no answer.

<u>20. The foregoing discussion abundantly reveals that it is not possible to deduce a general definition of the word ex parte from the Civil Procedure Code. Even if it may be attempted, such an artificial meaning cannot be applied to cover all diverse proceedings contemplated in article 3 of the Presidential Order.</u>

21. Mr. Roy Chowdhury has submitted that the order dated 15.5.71 also cores within the ambit of the alternative clause of article 3, that is, an order disposing of the miscellaneous case for default in compliance with the court's implied direction of appearance of the judgment-debtor. Mr. Huq contends in reply that under Order 9, rule 8 of the Code, no discretion is left with the court, when the plaintiff does not appear on the day the case is called for hearing but to dismiss it. According to him the order takes effect more by the operation of law than by an act of the court. Such is not covered by Article 3. None of the submissions of Mr. Huq is tenable. A comparison of the language of Order 9, rule 8, with Order 22, rule 4(3) of Civil Procedure Code will reveal the distinction. Under the latter provision, if no application is made, the suit shall as against deceased accordant abate by operation of law, whereas under the former an order by the court is needed for dismissal. Then again this order of dismissal under Order 9, rule 8 could be passed only when the suit was called on for hearing. Hearing, of course, may be considered in its broadest sense to include any positive step in the carriage of the suit. Secondly, provisions of Order 9 do not in terms apply to miscellaneous case arising out of an execution proceeding. The executing court by reference to section 141 of the Code, and the Instruction contained in Manual of Practical Instruction for the conduct of civil case follows the procedure. The Manual in Chapter XIX, gives instruction to be followed in the execution proceedings. Rules 35 (3) and (14) indicate that the court, has been given wide discretion in dealing and disposing of a Miscellaneous Case arising out of execution proceeding. In miscellaneous cases all orders and directions are made or given primarily by the court. There is no scope for argument of automatic dismissal by operation of law. And so an order of dismissal for default of a miscellaneous case, which on the application by the judgment-debtor under Order 21, rule 90 was registered is Misc. case No. 354 of 1970, when dismissed for default, in my judgment, also covered by the clause orders, dismissing all matters due to the default in compliance with any direction of any court or tribunal in any legal proceeding provided in article 3 of the Order.

22. To turn to the impugned order dated 8.3.72, I find that the Executing Court has held that (1) order dated 17.5.71 vacating the stay order and confirming sale: (2) the order dated 27.5.71 granting the sale certificate to the auction purchaser; (3) the order dated 31.5.71 issuing writ of delivery of possession to the auction purchaser and (4) the delivery of auction purchased building to the auction purchaser under the orders of the court are null and void under article 3 of the Presidential Order and accordingly all those orders and delivery of possession are set aside and nullified and that it is ordered that the Execution Case be proceeded with as if there had been or such orders and the delivery of possession as referred to above.

23. Of the four items nullified by the Executing Court, items 2 and 4, the grant of sale certificate and giving delivery of possession, are acts rather than orders, and will be dealt with later on for the present, let me deal with items 1 and 3, the orders vacating the stay and confirming sale and issuing the writ of delivery of possession. Mr. Asrarul Hossain has submitted that Presidential Order 12 of 1972 is not retrospective in that it does not say that it shall be deemed to have taken effect from an earlier date.

<u>24. He further argues that the order dated 15.5.71 will be null and void from 7.2.1972 the day the Presidential Order came into operation and not from the day the order was made. It is to be observed that grant of retrospective operation to the statute in the manner suggested by Mr. Hossain, is not the sole method or the sole language employed by Legislature. We are to read an enactment as a whole to see the language employed, and the intent expressed therein. The same intent may be expressed in different language. Take the Presidential Order itself. The legislative authority took upon itself, first, the power to nullify certain decisions within stated period. It then in clear language, nullified these decisions. The language and intent of article 3 are plainly retrospective. I have already held the Article retrospective earlier and the reason need not be repeated here.</u>

25. Mr. Asrarul Hossain has next submitted that these two orders are consequential orders and the President's Order does not nulliffy consequential orders in terms, and it being a sequestrating enactment, should be given strict construction. Mr. Roy Chowdhury, conversely, says that it is a beneficial legislation bestowing the benefit of a hearing to the deprived party No. elaborate discussion on this point is called for. That it is a beneficial legislation cannot be doubted. Hence liberal interpretation giving effect to widest amplitude is called for.

26. Mr. Asrarul Hossain's next argument is that in any event, only the orders which in clear terms come within the mischief of the Presidential Order are nullified, and not the consequential orders. He says that orders under review are all consequential, flowing from the order of dismissal for default. This submission is linked with the question as to whether the order coming within mischief of the Presidential Order is (1) void order and (2) whether the other orders are dependent orders. If these two conditions are satisfied then there is no escape form the conclusion that these two orders shall fall, and must be deemed to be null and void.

<u>27. I have already held that article 3 is retrospective and that the nullification made therein makes the order void ab initio a nullity. The order dated 15.5.71 is a nullity. A nullity cannot give rise to a reality, nor a consequential order. Had the order dated 15.5.71 been a voidable order the submission of Mr. Hossain would have great force. The foundation of the hypothesis is wanting. The conclusion cannot stand.</u>

28. That these two orders are dependent orders will be manifest if Order 21, rule 92 is looked at. It says where no application is made under rule 89, rule 90 or rule 91 or where such application is made and disallowed, the court shall make an order confirming the sale, and thereupon the sale becomes absolute." Rule 94 says that where a sale has become absolute, the court shall grant certificate to the purchaser. Rules 95 and 96 provide for delivery possession of the auction-sold properly to the purchaser. It is to be noted that the judgment-debtor on filing the miscellaneous case also obtained an order of stay of further proceeding of the Execution case. Further proceedings could not have been made unless the bar of stay was removed. It was done ex parte on a subsequent day, on 17.5.71. This apart the language of rule 92 clearly says that when such a case has been filed, the execution court cannot proceed unless it is disposed of. The provisions set out clearly indicate that the two orders under consideration are dependent orders flowing from the order dated 15.5.71 when the miscellaneous case was disposed of though by a default order. Similar view has been expressed by the Madras High Court in the case of Varandarajan Vs. Muthu Venkatpathi Reddy and others; AIR 1953 Madras 567.

29. Mr. Roy Chowdhury citing Vendeateswarlu Vs. State of Madras AIR 1954 Madras 587 and 10 Moor's Indian Appeal 203 and Haji Abul Quasen Vs. Abdur Rahman (1970) 22 D.L.R. Dacca 822 has submitted that when the parent order is reversed, all dependent orders fall along with it, and no proceeding need be taken for setting aside these dependent orders. He mostly relied on Madras decision which has held that when the application under Order 21, rule (9) dismissed for default is restored, the orders of confirmation of sale and of delivery of possession being dependent orders stand automatically vacated. Mr. Huq in reply has cited Pyari Lal Vs. Hanifun Nissa I.L.R. 38 Allahabad 240, Rewa Mahton Vs. Ram Kishen Singh I.L.R 14 Calcutta 11, Queen Empress Vs. Wazir Jan I.L.R. 10 Allahabad 66 and submitted that the principle of automatic reversal of dependent orders does not apply in case of bonafide auction purchaser, which the petitioner is. I do not think it advisable to enter into a lengthy discussion of the rival contentions of the learned advocates. The question before us is not one under Civil Procedure Code, but article 3 of the Presidential Order. A reference to article 3 gives some indication as to how the dependent orders are to be treated. After nullifying ex parte orders and orders of disposal for default, the article provides the proceeding, on the commencement of the Order, shall continue in accordance with law. What is implicit is that dependent orders shall equally stand null and void. Unless they are so, the proceeding cannot continue in accordance with the law, which means the law under which the proceeding was being proceeded with. There is an additional reason for so holding, inasmuch an order which is a nullity cannot give rise to any effective or quasi-effective order. The two orders dated 17.5.71 vacating stay order and confirming the sale, and that dated 31.5.71 issuing writ of delivery of possession are null and void.

30. Mr. Huq has further argued that these two orders are in the nature of restitution. Restitution can follow only when an order giving rise to certain action has been reversed. He says that the judgment debtor's miscellaneous case has just been restored and it may not succeed on merits. If he succeeds and the sale is set aside, then only the question of the restitution will arise. The nullification of these two orders was premature. Apart from the fact that the point of prematurity was never raised in the court below, this submission cannot be accepted. The two orders are dependent orders as I have held, and they fall on the validness of the parent order.

31. Mr. Roy Chowdhury has also argued that on all the dates the orders were passed, the judgment debtor had a locus standi and his presence was necessary, and these two orders having been passed in his absence are also ex parte orders, nonetheless they are dependent orders. He has cited Aranuchai Chatting Vs. Vadla Koundmer and others A.I.R. 1952 Madras 871, and Mubarak Begum and another Vs. Sushi  Kumar and others. A.I.R. 1957 Rajshthon 154 in his favour. Mr. Huq however, said in reply that the sale set aside case having once been dismissed, the judgment-debtor has practically no role to play, and the other orders follow as a matter of course. The cited decision of Mr. Roy Chowdhury say otherwise. Mr. Huq however, could cite no authority in his support. I find little merit in the argument of Mr. Huq and accept that of Mr. Roy Choudhury.

<u>32. I now come to the two impugned actions nullified by the Executing Court. One is the grant of sale certificate, and the other the fact of delivery of possession to the auction purchaser. They are accomplished facts. The court below has made an anomalous order by declaring them null and void. You may say whatever you like, but it requires an act to undo another act. That has not been done. It requires to be done. The auction purchaser remains in possession in fact. Legally speaking the orders being null and void, the actions flowing therefrom cannot have any legal foundation the grant of sale certificate and delivery of possession lose their legal content, but exist de facto. The same view has been expressed in Begu and others Vs. The King Emperor -4 C.L.J. 439 and Jagrup Sahu Vs. Ramand Sahu I.L.R 39 Allahabad 635: The legal validity of the sale certificate and the delivery of possession having been lost the auction-purchaser cannot claim to have a legal title or a lawful possession. The court is at liberty to restore parties to status quo ante, think, it would be advisable to deal with this matter of restitution after the disposal of miscellaneous case. In any event the order of the court declaring the Acts null and void is inappropriate.</u>

33. Mr. Moinul Huq has alternatively submitted that the impugned order is premature and we should refrain from making any observation on the order dated 15.5.71 and the petitioner has not specifically challenged the order dated 18.2.72 by which the miscellaneous case has been restored. On this submission we have given our serious consideration and are unable to accept it. Mr. Huq submitted before the refereeing Division Bench that interpretation of article 3 of the President's Order was involved, and prayed for a larger Bench to consider the question and has obtained an order to that effect Before us on the third day of hearing be raised the question of dependent order, and that the order dated 15.5.71 being one for dismissal for default was not covered by Presidential order. Considering the importance of the question we allowed him to argue and he has so done. We have also dealt with his argument in full. He cannot be allowed to approbate and reprobate at the same time.

<u>34. In conclusion, I find that the order dated 1.5.71 was an exparte order in terms of article 3 of the Presidential Order. It is also an order dismissed for default in compliance with the implicit direction of the court for judgment debtor petitioner to appear on that date. It is null and void a nullity. The order dated 17-5-71 and 31.5.71 are dependent orders and are also nail and void. The actions, grant of sale certificate, and delivery of possession to the auction purchaser are without lawful authority and of no legal effect. With this modification of the impugned order, the Rule was discharged with-costs. Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J.-with great respect to my learned brother I could not persuade myself to the reasonings and conclusions adopted in his judgment.</u>

35. Facts giving rise to the proceedings have been sufficiently stated in the judgment of my learned brother. The judgment debtor filed the application under order 21 rules 90 C.P.C for setting aside the sale and it was registered as Misc. Case No. 354 of 1970. It was fixed on 15.5.71 for objection by the decree-holder opposite party and on that date the case was dismissed for non-appearance of judgment debtor and confirmed the sale. The sale certificate was granted to the auction purchaser on 27.5.71. The writ of delivery of possession was issued on 31.5.71 and thereafter on 11.6.71 delivery of possession of the property was given to the auction purchaser. On all these dates the judgment-debtor could not appear in court. On 18.2.72 on an application  under P.O. 12 of 1972 by the judgment-debtor the Misc. Case No 354 of 1970 was restored and on 8.3.72 on the application by the judgment-debtor the orders dated 17.5.71, 27.5.71, 31.5.71 and 11.6.71 were declared null and void in terms of President's Order No. 19 of 1912. The order dated 8.3.72 is under challenge in this revisional application. Considering the importance of the points the matter has been referred to the Special Bench.

36. The question is whether the dismissal order for non-appearance can be termed as ex parte order or orders due to default in compliance with any direction within the meaning of PO. 12. On perusal of P.O. 12 it seems the legislature took notice of the terror perpetrated by the Pakistan Occupation Army for which people were not able (1) to go to courts or tribunal to institute legal proceedings or (2) to defend them ; or (3) to comply with directions issued by the courts ; As a result (a) many claims and legal rights have become time-barred, (b) many legal proceedings have been disposed of ex parte (c)many legal proceedings have been disposed of in default of compliance with the direction of the court or tribunals.

Therefore, for ends of justice the legislature thought it necessary to provide;

(i)	for the saving of limitation for all legal proceedings &

(ii)	for the nullification of all judgments, decrees, and orders passed ex parte

(iii)	for nullification of orders passed in default of compliance with certain directions in certain legal proceedings.

37. In this view Bangladesh Legal Proceedings Order, 1972, was promulgated on 7.2.72 to commence at once. An inclusive definition of the expression legal proceeding has been given in Article 2 which includes suits, cases, prosecution, appeals, revision and review.

38. Article 3 stipulates that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force (1) All judgments or decrees or orders passed ex parte by any court or tribunal. (2) or orders disposing of matters due to default in compliance with any direction of any court or tribunal in any legal proceedings between 1.3.71 and 7.2.72 are declared null and void and the proceedings shall continue in accordance with the law.

39. Article 4 provides notwithstanding anything contained in any other law in computing the period of limitation prescribed for any legal proceeding period between 1.3.71 & 1.4.72 (both days inclusive) shall be excluded. As has been noted on 15.5.71 the Misc. case was dismissed for default. The executing Court recorded the following order:- O. P. files hazira. A.P. files hazira and fresh power. Petitioner files no hazira nor takes any step and found absent on repeated calls. Misc. case dismissed for default."

40. Mr. B.B. Roy Choudhury appearing for the O.P. Judgment debtor submitted that this dismissal for default amounts to an ex parte order because on the date the petitioner was absent and therefore Article 3 of P O. 12 makes the order null and void and the executing Court has correctly declared the orders null and void namely the order of vacating the stay and confirming the sale (on 17.5.71) granting the sale certificate (on 27.5.71), issuing the writ of delivery of possession (on 31.5.71) and delivery of possession to the auction purchaser (on 11.6.71).

41. Mr. Moinul Huq appearing for the auction-purchaser submitted that dismissal for default and exparte order are two distinct legal conceptions and throughout the procedural law this distinction was kept in view. The Misc. case, the learned advocate submitted, was dismissed for default. It was not dismissed by exparte order because the expression ex parte presuppose absence of the party against whom an order is made at the instance and for the benefit of the party present. Mr. Huq submitted that the Misc. case could not be restored by Article 3 of P.O. 12 and therefore subsequent four orders were set aside illegally.

Mr. Asrarul Hossain appearing for the decree-holder submitted that an ex parte order (cannot be paved against the plaintiff-petitioner appellant. It can only be passed against the defendant-opposite party-respondent. In course of debate both Mr. Moinul Huq and Mr. Asrarul Hossain submitted that the judgment-debtor had normal remedies under the law and for the purpose of limitation the legislature by Article 4 has excluded the period between 1.3.71 and 1.3.72.

42. Having given my anxious consideration to the contention raised by the parties the conclusion is that the contention of Mr. Moinul Huq and Mr. Asrarul Hossain appears to be the correct interpretation of P.O. 12 of 1972. In the preamble in the 2nd paragraph three things have been contemplated: (1) People were unable to go to courts to institute legal proceedings or (2) to defend them ; or (3) to comply with directions issued by courts.  As a result three circumstances have taken place ;

(1) Many claims and legal rights have become time barred;

(2) Many legal proceedings have been disposed of exparte;

(3) Orders have been passed disposing of matters due to default in compliance with any 	direction of any court or tribunal.

43. It seems the words "so" is a misprint. It ought to have been "or" between the words 'that' and 'to' in the 3rd line of the preamble.

44. Be that as it may, while enacting the section apart from the Articles 1 and 2 the legislature covered two things only in Article 3, namely; (1) ex-parte judgments decrees or orders (2) orders disposing of matters due to default in compliance with any direction of the court. In this Article no provision has been made for cases of dismissal for default for which a regulating procedure has been given under Order 9 of C P.C.
