The contention that the Civil Procedure Code is not applicable in interpreting the terms of the P O. 12 does not appeal to me because Article 3 enjoins that the proceedings shall continue in accordance with the law. Definitive Article "the" clearly points to the law that is applicable in the subject and since the Misc. case was the result of an application under Order 21 rule 90 C.P.C., the provisions of the Civil Procedure Code must apply. Otherwise in terms of the P.O the proceedings cannot continue after having declared the orders passed between 1.3.71 and 7.2.72 at null and void. Hence, guidance has to be taken from the Civil Procedure Code. Whether Order 9 will be applicable or not In the matter of execution proceedings will be dealt with at the appropriate stage but for the moment since the expression 'legal proceedings' includes suits it will be proper to consider the following circumstances:

(a) When neither party appears the suit is to be dismissed subject to rule 4 (Order 9, rule 3)

(b) When the plaintiff appears and the defendant does not appear and if the summons was duly served, the court may proceed ex parte (rule 6) It is not necessary to consider the question of necessity of second summons or postponement of the hearing for which provision has been made in rule 7.

(c) When the defendant appears and the plaintiff does not appear the suit is to be dismissed unless the defendant admits the claim (rule 8). If the suit is dismissed for default, rule 9 of Order 9 makes a specific provision to set aside the dismissal order. On the contrary if ex parte decree is passed as contemplated by rule 6, then the remedy is available under rule 13 for setting aside ex parte decree. Thus rule 9 provides one remedy when the defendant appears but the plaintiff does not and rules 13 deals separately for setting aside ex parse decree. It is true that the expression ex parte has not been defined by the code but the expression occurs in two sections, namely, in sections 96 and in the schedule it appears for the first time in rule 6 of Order 9. In rule 4 the expression is used for an order to set the dismissal aside. In rule 9 the same expression, namely, For an order to set the dismissal" aside" has been used. By section 2(2)(b) Any order of dismissal for default is excluded from definition of decree.

45. In order 41, rule 17(1) it is provided that if the appellant does not appear when the appeal is called on for hearing, the court may make an order that "the appeal by dismissed". But the rule 17(2) provides that if the appellant appears and the respondent does not appear, the appeal shall be heard ex parte". If the appeal is dismissed under rule 17(1) rule 19 provides for re-admission but in case of ex parse under rule 17(2) then rule 21 provides for rehearing of the appeal if the court is satisfied that he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing. Again when an application for stay of execution is filed Order 41 rule 5 (4) provides that Court may make an ex parte order for stay of execution pending the hearing of the application. This interim order operates against the respondent and passed in his absence affecting him prejudicially and this is an ex parte order.

46. Let us consider the question from another angle. In admitting an appeal beyond time, the court is required to given notice to the respondent as to show cause why the delay will not be condoned. If no such notice is given and the delay is condoned, the order is passed ex parte because it affects the respondent prejudicially. The Privy Council, it may be noted, disapproved the practice of hearing the point on limitation at the time of final hearing (Krishna Shamir Vs. Rajshahi A.I.R. 1971 P.C. 197).

47. Again, for example, in a suit the plaintiff himself is substituted as defendant on an application by a 3rd party (claiming himself to be an assignee) without giving the plaintiff any chance of hearing, the order of the court is passed ex parte and that order is revisable at the instance of the aggrieved original plaintiff (Tikait Ajant Singh Vs. F.T. Christian 17 C.W.N. 862).

48. It is unnecessary to multiply instances. Whenever an ex parte order is passed it is always passed at the instance of one party for his benefit against the other who was not present on the date when order was passed. In my humble research, I did not come across any case where the dismissal for default was treated as ex parte order. Mr. B.B. Roy Chowdhury frankly stated that he could not cite any case where any contrary view was expressed. In this view of the legal terms it cannot be said that an order for dismissal for default can be taken at par or interchangeably with an ex parte order. To hold otherwise and interpreting in the manner suggested by Mr. B.B. Roy Chowdhury means to lose sight of the distinction the legislature has so carefully kept in view and the legal decisions have followed consistently. My opinion is that the two terms ex parte and "dismissal for default" cannot be used interchangeably. (On 15th the opposite Party appeared but the petitioner did not). The executing court correctly recorded the order that it was dismissed for default. 49. In an execution case 3 parties are conceivable namely, (A) judgment-debtor, (B) decree-holder and (C) auction-purchaser'. We can think of t tree situations:

(1) Where none of the parties appear on the date. the court is to dismiss the application for non-appearance.

(2) When B and C appear but A does not-The application is to be dismissed for A's non-appearance.

(3) When alone appears at the hearing An ex parte order is made granting A's 	application and setting aside the sale.

50. It is now well settled that the Order 9 does not apply in a case for setting aside sale under Order 21, rule 90. Therefore, in the aforesaid first case dismissal of the application cannot be treated as dismissal under Order 9, rule 3 of C.P.C. and the provisions of rule 4 R. (B.H. Chowdhury, J.) 31 DLR (1979) of Order 9, C.P.C. do not apply, vide Namenda Vs. Rakhal A.I.R. 1925 Cal. 510. In that case after reviewing all the order and agreeing with the view of a full Bench of the Patna High Court it was held Order 9 C.P.0 does not apply to applications arising out of execution proceedings. It was further held that the effect of dis-missal of an application under rule 90 of Order 21 even for default is to confirm the sale under rule 92 and hence an appeal lies against the order under Order 43(1) (I) and the High Court has no jurisdiction to interfere with the order in revision.

51, In the second case the dismissal cannot be treated as a dismissal under Order 9, rule 8 and the provision of rule 9 did not apply: Chari Chandra Vs. Chandi Charon (19 C W.N. 25) where an application to set aside a sale under rule 90 of Order 21 C.P.C. having been dismissed for default the applicant applied for restoration of the case and it was held that no appeal lay against the order refusing to restore the case. The same view was expressed in Kaju Luri Shami Vs. Sooryanarayana in A.I,R. 1925 Mad. 126.

In the third case the ex parte order cannot be treated an order under Order 9, rule 6 and the provisions of rule 13 do not apply.

52. The reasons for the aforesaid view is that an order dismissing for default an application to have a sale set aside is the order under Order 21 rule 92 C.P.C. and as such an appeal lies against such an order under Order 43, rule 1(1). This view has been expressed in Kalikanta vs. Shyamlal, 25 C: L.J. 163. 53. If the above view is correct then the judgment-debtor in the present case could institute a legal proceedings, namely by way of an appeal under Order 43, rule 1(J) C.P.C. against the order of confirming the sale though his application has been dismissed for default.

The language of Order 43, rule I(J) is thus wide enough to cover a case where an application to have a sale set aside is dismissed for default.

The language of Order 43, rule 1(J) is as follows: The order under rule 92 of Order 21 setting aside or refusing to set aside a sale.

54. This expression is wide enough and obviously it means if the sale is confirmed the aggrieved party may file an appeal. Though in rule 92 the expression the court shall make an order confirming the sale" the corresponding change in Order 43, rule 1(J) has been noted in Asgar Ali Vs. Bhim Sarker, 33 CWN 392 as to why the words for confirming have been dropped out. It is thus clear that the judgment-debtor had his remedy amongst other by way of an appeal and for that Article 4 of P.O. 12 has come to his rescue for computing the period of limitation. Thus the persons who could not institute legal proceedings are given opportunity to institute legal proceedings and so far as limitation is concerned Article 4 has been enacted for their benefit. In article 3 only two cases are contemplated, namely, (a) ex parte judgments, decree and orders or (b) order disposing of matters due to default in corpulence with any direction of the court.

55. I have discussed so far as the expanse orders are concerned. Now let us consider the 2nd part of Article 3 that is order disposing of matter due to default in compliance with any direction of court. It has been canvassed by Mr. B.S. Roy Chowdhury that if the order of dismissal for default cannot be termed as ex parte it will in any case come under the 2nd part of Article 3, namely, due to default in compliance with any direction of the court. When questioned what orders were passed in default of compliance of which the court disposed of the matter, Mr. Chowdhury stated that date, namely 15th May, the petitioner was to be present in court and since he could not do so it was a default of compliance with the direction of the court. This argument does not appear to be sound.

56. Mr. Moinul Huq drew attention to the various provisions of the Code wherein directions are given by the court and failure to comply with such directions certain consequences to the peril of the person to whom the direction was given follow. This is what is meant In default of compliance with direction of the court.

57. The submission of Mr. Moinul Huq appears to be reasonable. There are a number of provisions in the code which authorise the milt to give directions and in default in compliance to take certain steps. To give few examples under Order 31, rule 2, the Court may as for security for appearance of a defendant shall bind himself in default of such appearance to pay any sum of money which the defendant may be ordered to pay to the suit. Another example can be had from rule 4 when the defendant fails to comply with an order under rule 2 or 3 the court may commit the defendant to civil prison. Order 25, rule 1 provides for security for costs and rule 2 provides for the consequences of failure.

58. Under Order 40, rule 4 when the receiver fails to submit his account as directed by the court the court may direct his property to be attached and may sell such property. To take another example Order 16, rule 10(2) the court may issue a proclamation requiring a person to attend and to give evidence or to produce document when such person without lawful excuse has failed to attend or to produce the document in compliance with such summons. Further, in sub-rule (3) the court may attach the property without issuing proclamation or issue warrant of arrest of such person. Thus, it is clear the second part of Article 3 contemplated different kind of default other than dismissal for default.

59. The distinction between ex parte order and the order of dismissal for non-appearance is highlighted by Order 17, rule 2 when on the adjourned date the parties fail to appear. The legislature has provided the court may proceed to dispose of the suit. The distinctive feature in each of the aforesaid 3 situations has been termed by legal expression namely ex parte order', 'dismissal for default', and disposal of the suit and they are thus brought in sharp focus and there is hardly any scope focusing these legal term interchangeably, when distinct legal connotations bad been attributed to each of them.

60. In R.V. Slator (1881) 8 Q.B.D. 267 Denman, J. rejected the connotation that the term indictment meant criminal proceeding and observed:

"It always requires the strong compulsion of other words in an act to induce the Court to alter the well-known, meaning of a legal term." Bowen. J. observed: "There is certainly no such popular use of the 'term' among lawyers and if there is among persons ignorant of the law, it is an incorrect use of the term. It has been observed: 'Where cases have been decided on particular form of words in courts on acts of paramount use those forms of words which have received judicial construction in the absence of anything in the act showing that the legislature did not mean to use the words in the sense attributed to them by the courts, the presumption is that parliament did so to use them Per Lord Coleridge C. J. In Barlow Vs. Teal (1885) 5 Q B.D. 403.

61. In my view the dismissal order for default is therefore not contemplated in Article 3 of P.O. 12 and since against the order of confirmation of sale the judgment debtor had his remedy by way of appeal amongst others the legislature has enacted Article 4 for saving the limitation is this view of the matter the opinion is that the Misc. case was not legally restored and therefore the subsequent' orders declaring confirmation of sale, issuance of sale certificate and the writ of delivery of possession as null and void under Article 3 of P.O. 12 was illegal.

62. A point canvassed that P. O. 12 covers all Courts in the civil, criminal and revenue. This question is not, however, necessary to decide since in the present case no such enquiry is called for, but in passing it may only be stated that in criminal prosecution trial of an accused can only be held in absentia provided there is a law making such provision otherwise the trial is always held in the presence of the accused if his presence is not dispensed with under section 540 Cr.P.C. In a criminal appeal the appellant is always within the season of the court either by being on bail or in custody therefore, the question of ex parte order does not arise in a criminal case. Only in section 144 Cr. P.C. and 488 Cr.P.C. an ex parte order has been contemplated.

63. Another argument has been advanced that the P.O. 12 has enacted as a beneficial legislation and ere fore, the widest meaning should be given to achieve the object of the legislation. The argument is attractive no doubt but it entails a dangerous consequence namely leading to a slippery path. Because by interpreting the court will be legislating where the legislature could expressly contemplate two situations in Article 3 it could easily include the case of dismissal for default and since it did not do So it would not be legitimate as to speculate for its non-inclusion. As has been mentioned that the legislature has not left the originator of the proceedings without remedy. The originator as a plaintiff petitioner-appellant could still pursue his remedy by taking resort to the normal law and by Article 4 of P.O. 12 such originator of the proceedings has been relieved of the mischief of the limitation. Now, it is up to him to initiate the proceedings if he chose to do so. Next question as to why the legislature has treated in such a different way the two categories of people namely, (1) Persons who have been affected by ex parte orders and (2) per-sons whose proceedings have been dismissed for default. The answer is, in the case of ex pane orders the legislature' have declared them null and void but in the second case the point of limitation has been saved if such persons desired to initiate proceedings because it is up to the initiator of proceedings whether to proceed with the proceedings or not.

64. In the result, therefore, in my view the Miscellaneous case No. 354 of 1970 was not validly restored under P.O. 12 and there-fore the impugned orders were passed illegally and without jurisdiction and in that view of the matter I would make the rule absolute without any order as to costs.

Abdur Rahman Chowdhury, 3:-I have had the advantage of hearing the Judgments delivered by my learned brothers,

K. Hossain, J and B.H. Chowdhury, J. Both are well-reasoned and learned ones. I would, however, like to add a few words of my own.

65. It may be pertinent to point out that the impugned order before us was the order dated 8.3.72 and not the order dated 18.2.72 by which the Miscellaneous case was restored. One of my learned brothers has found that the Misc. case was rightly restored while my other learned brother has held that the Misc. case was not legally restored. In my humble opinion, however, we are not called upon to decide that question under the terms of reference to us nor was that order dated 18.2.72 seriously Challenged before us. My impression is that Mr. Moinul Huq, the learned Advocate was urging this point more as a supporting fire from his armory than as a real firearm of attack. If the petitioner has chosen not to specifically challenge the order dated 18.2.72 he must have consciously dote so for reasons best known to him.

66. Be that as it may, the only question before us was whether the orders (a) confirming the sale, (b) granting sale certificate, (c) issuing writ of delivery of possession and (d) the delivery of possession to the auction-purchaser came within the purview of Article 3 of P.O. 12 of 1972 or to be more precise, can be called ex parte orders or disposal due to default in compliance with the court's order.

67. Admittedly, the aforesaid Orders were all passed during the period contemplated under the said Presidential Order in the absence of the Judgment-debtor who but for the circumstances mentioned in the preamble would have been present to prosecute the Miscellaneous Case. It is also not the petitioner's case that the judgment debtor deliberately alienated himself and willfully allowed the car to be dismissed for default.

68. Learned arguments have been advanced at the Bar as to the true interpretation of the word ex parte. The arguments have been elaborately discussed by my learned brother and I do not propose nor is it necessary to repeat them. The generally accepted and well-recognized principle of construction of a statute is to ascertain the intention of the legs nature as expressed in the words used in the statute and they should be given their ordinary and natural meaning. This rule relating to literal construction has been very lucidly expressed in Corpus Juries Vol. 59 Section 569 at 953-958.

Where the language of a statute is plain and unambiguous there is no occasion for construction, even though other meanings could be found and the court cannot indulge in speculation as to the probable or possible qualification which might have been in the mind of the legislature but the statute must be given effect according to the plain and ordinary meaning....

69. Then there is another rule of interpretation which has also gained wide recognition in England and in the Supreme Courts of this sub-continent known as the mischief rule enunciated by Lord Code in what is known as Haydon's case. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in following the said rule of construction in the case of Messers S.A. Haroon Vs. Collector of Customs reported in (1959) 11 D.L.R. (S.C.) 200 observed as follows: "All rules of interpretation have been devised as aids to the discovery of the legislative intent behind an enactment. Where the words are plain and unambiguous that intent can best be judged by giving full effect to the ordinary grammatical meaning of those words An in perpetration which is calculated to sundress 'mischief' and advance the 'remedy' is likely to be in accord with the intention of the legislature,"

70. There is yet another rule of interpretation equally well recognised and well known as the golden rule of construction enunciated by Lord Wensleydale. In applying the said rule Lord Chancellor Viscount Simon in Nooks Vs. Don caster Amalgamated Collieries Ltd. reported in 1940 A.C. 1014 at page 1022 observed: "The golden rule is that the words of a statute must prima facie be given their ordinary meaning. If the choice is between two interpretations, the narrower of which would fail to achieve the 434.1nifest purpose of legislation, we hold avoid a CCIIS1M-tion which would reduce the legislation to futility and should rather accept the bolder construction based on the view that the parliament would legislate only for the purpose of bringing about an effective result."

71. These rules of interpretation hew been widely accepted and followed by the supreme courts of this subcontinent in different cases; Applying these salutary and well-settled principles and keeping in view the beneficial object of the legislation and the mischief it aimed at to remedy, I am clearly of .11e opinion that the word 'ex parte' admits of no other interpretation than to mean an order passed in the absence of any one of the contending parties.

72. The Presidential Order in question in undoubtedly a beneficial legislation intended to give relief to persons who were deprived of their right to have recourse to the law of the land under circumstances beyond their control. If, therefore, a restricted meaning is given to the word exparte then the beneficial aspect of the legislation, I am afraid, will be completely lost. It cannot be imagined that under the same set of facts and circumstances, the legislature intended to provide relief to one group of affected persons while leaving others to find relief under the ordinary law of the land.

73. There is no denying that the order dated 17.5.71 confirming the sale and the order dated 31.5.71 issuing the writ of delivery of possession are dependent and consequential orders flowing from the order dated 15.5.71 when the Miscellaneous case was dismissed for default. The parent order dated 15.5.71 having been set aside and hashing remained unchallenged, the aforesaid orders dated 17.5.71 and 31.5.71 are in my opinion, null and void 'and have been rightly set aside by the learned Subordinate Judge. For the same reasons am also of the opinion that the order dated 27.5.71 granting the sale certificate and the order dated 11.6.71 delivering possession of the suit property to the auction-purchaser, although fait accompli, lack legal foundations in view of the parent order being void. Further appropriate steps, however, shall have to be taken in accordance with law to restore the parties to their respective status quo ante.

74. With these observations, I agree with the decision arrived at by my learned brother K. Hossain, J. and concur with the judgment delivered by him discharging the rule with costs.

ORDER

In accordance with majority view the rule is discharged with costs.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree Nos. 505 & 506 of 2000.
lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam with Md Mozammel Hossain and Md Sagir Anower, Advocates------ For the Appellant. 
Shafique Ahmed, Advocate------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Shamsul Haque ------ Appellant 
Vs. 
Luna Fahmida Rahman and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: We heard both appeals together and now dispose of them by this judgment as the issues raised therein between the same parties are the same.

2. First Appeal No. 506 of 2000 arises out of other Suit No.17 of 1997. Luna Fahmida Rahman and Dana Farzana Rahman, two full sisters, on 19-5-97 instituted the suit against their uncle, Md Shamsul Haque and 3 others in the court of Joint District Judge at Rangpur for a decree declaring their right, title and interest in the suit property and also for recovery of possession of said property by eviction of the defendants therefrom. The suit property was described to be a two-storied building with 5 rooms in the ground floor and 4 rooms in the first floor erected upon about 12 decimals out of 36 decimals of land of plot No. 5158 appertaining to SA Khatian No. 184 of Mouza Radhavallav in the District of Rangpur.

3. The plaint case, in short, is that Jadunath Sarker and Sitesh Chandra Biswas were owners in possession as 'Korfa' tenants in equal share in said 36 decimals of land under one rent receiver, Protap Chandra Das Gupta and said Korfa tenancy was finally recorded in CS Khatian No. 124/20 in the name of Jadunath Sarker. While they were thus in possession by a registered deed of sale being No. 1612/38 dated 10-8-38 they transferred 12 decimals out of said 36 decimals of land to one Swadesh Ranjan Sarker and delivered possession to him.

4. Thereafter, Swadesh Ranjan Sarker transferred said 12 decimals of land to Md Abdul Wahed minor represented by his father Abdul Majid Sarker and Mohammad Rafiqul Islam. minor represented by his father Raj Mohammad Sarker by registered deed of sale being 7902 dated 21-3-53 and delivered possession to them. They also purchased 17½ decimals of land from the said plot. Accordingly, the names of Abdul Wahed and Rafiqul Islam were correctly recorded in the SA Khatian No. 184.

5. As the Sarkers purchased the land in the benami of their minor sons and possessed jointly, by a registered deed of partition being No. 1965 dated 27-9-65, Abdul Majid Sarker and Raj Mohammad Sarker partitioned the joint land and Abdul Majid Sarker got the suit land of 12 decimals in his share.

6. While Abdul Majid Sarker was thus owner in possession he transferred said 12 decimals of the suit land to Most. Begum Farida Rahman, mother of the plaintiffs by a registered deed of sale being No. 42106 dated 13-12-67 and delivered possession to her. After purchase, Farida Rahman got her name mutated vide mutation Case No. 742/68-69 dated 20-1-69 and paid rents.

7. In 1963, father of the plaintiffs, Md Mokhlesur Rahman went to England and got a job there. Then in 1964, Farida Rahman followed him. Farida Rahman had a job in England.

8. Farida Rahman appointed her father, Hamiduddin Ahmed caretaker in respect of the suit land. She instructed her father to make a two-storied building on the suit land and accordingly, she time to time sent money to her father.

9. Hamiduddin Ahmed got a plan approved by the, local Municipality on 17-12-80. By a Power of Attorney dated 16-6-85, Farida Rahman again appointed her father Hamiduddin Ahmed as her duly constituted attorney for construction of a house as per approved plan and design. During the period of construction of the house, Farida Rahman used to come to Bangladesh once/twice a year to see the progress of the work. In 1989, the construction was completed at the direct supervision of said Hamiduddin Ahmed. Connection of electric line, water, etc was taken, in the name of Farida Rahman, to the house. Hamiduddin Ahmed then inducted monthly tenants in the house and out of the rents collected, he used to meet the expenditure of Government rents, Municipal taxes, electric and water bills and maintenance cost.

10. On 22-8-90 Farida Rahman met with a road accident in the USA and died instantaneously leaving behind her husband, Md Mokhlesur Rahman, father Hamiduddin Ahmed mother Momena Khatoon and the plaintiffs as her only legal representatives. According to Muslim Law of Inheritance, husband inherited to the extent of 3/15th share, father Hamiduddin Ahmed 2/15th share; mother 2/15th share and each daughter 4/15th share in the suit property left by Farida Rahman.

11. Then, by a registered deed bearing No. 4608 dated 25-3-91, said Mokhlesur Rahman, Hamiduddin Ahmed and Momena Khatoon jointly gifted their entire 7/15th share in said property to the plaintiffs and delivered possession, which the plaintiffs accepted.

12. While thus possessing the plaintiffs got their names mutated in Mutation Case No. 339/91-92 and mutation Khatian being No. 5661 was prepared in their names in respect of entire suit property. Since then the plaintiffs paid rent, municipality taxes and other rates regularly. The plaintiffs got their education in England and also had jobs there. As they were staying in England and their grandfather. Hamiduddin Ahmed became old they needed one to look after the property. In March, 1991, at the instance of their father Mokhlesur Rahman, they appointed their uncle Shamsul Haque caretaker of the suit property. Md Shamsul Hoque also gladly accepted the offer. It was decided that after paying necessary taxes, rents and rates for utility services and maintenance out of the rent. Md Shamsul Haque would deposit balance of the monthly rents collected from the tenants in the name of the plaintiffs in their bank account at the Sonali Bank at Rangpur. Shamsul Haque deposited money in the said account up to April, 1992 but thereafter he stopped depositing any amount in the account. In the month of March, 1994 Shamsul Hoque evicted the monthly tenants and occupied the first floor of the house and started living, there with his family members without any word to the plaintiffs. Shamsul Haque wrote a letter to the plaintiffs in England disclosing that he was living with his family members in the house and also requesting for Taka 1,29,446 which he claimed to have expended for repair and other works. He also expressed his desire to purchase the suit land.

13. Further case of the plaintiffs is that after the death of their mother their father took a 2nd wife. But the step-mother could not live happily with the plaintiffs and there was always quarrel ensuing between them. At the instigation of their step-mother, their father withdrew and appropriated a fat sum of money out of the insurance claim on the death of their mother without paying them any money out of their shares. Relation between the plaintiffs and their father gradually deteriorated, and Shamsul Haque was looking for such opportunity.

14. In the last part of January, 1997 the plaintiffs came to Rangpur from England. On 29th January, 1997 at about 10-00 AM the plaintiffs along with their maternal uncle AKM Mosharraf Hossain entered their house and found their uncle Shamsul Haque inducted the defendant Nos. 2 to 4 in the house. Leaving his house at Munshipara, uncle Shamsul Huque also started living in the house beyond the knowledge of the plaintiffs. They also found he started construction on the 2nd floor. Their uncle became annoyed at their presence. When the plaintiffs desired to stay in their house for some days the uncle denied them accommodation saying there was no room vacant. The uncle also claimed ownership of the house. Then, the plaintiffs demanded of their uncle to vacate the house within IS days and deliver back possession to them to which uncle Shamsul Haque declined.

15. The plaintiffs then decided to institute the suit against the defendants. As they were staying in England they appointed AKM Mosharraf Hossain as their new attorney and accordingly, their newly constituted attorney instituted the suit. The suit was on transfer renumbered as Other Suit No. 15 of 1998.

16. Pursuant to the summons of the suit on 14-6-98 said uncle Shamsul Haque instituted Other Suit No. 85 of 1998 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge at Sadar, Rangpur against said nieces. Luna Fahmida Rahman and Dana Farzana Rahman and their father. Mokhlesur Rahman and maternal grandmother, Momena Khatoon and other legal heirs of their grandfather, Hamiduddin Ahmed for a decree of declarations that the deed of sale being No. 42106 dated 13-12-67 is benami and Farida Rahman was mere a benamdar of Mukhlesur Rahman; that the deed of gift being No. 46,08 dated 25-3-91 was void, illegal, inoperative, collusive and bad in law and that said nieces acquired no right, title and interest in the suit property by such deed or otherwise and that the plaintiffs acquired absolute right, title and interest in the suit property by deed of Heba-bil-Ewaz being No. 3209 dated 25-3-97. The suit was then on 13-1-99 transferred by the District Judge to the Court of aforesaid Joint District Judge at Rangpur and renumbered as Other Class Suit No. 04 of 1999.

17. Case of the uncle. Shamsul Haque as averred in his plaint, in brief, is that in 1963, his elder brother, Mokhlesur Rahman with the nieces went to England and he got a job of high salary. In the last part of 1964, he then took his wife, Farida Rahman to England. When Mokhlesur Rahman decided to make a house at Rangpur he contacted his father-in-law, Hamiduddin Ahmed and sent money to him for purchase of land. Hamiduddin Ahmed purchased the suit land and got it registered in the name of his daughter, Farida Rahman by kabala being No. 42106 dated 15-12-67.

18. At that time, Farida Rahman had no separate and independent source of income of her own. Mokhleshur Rahman then decided to make a two-storied building upon the land and started sending money to his father-in-law, who was entrusted with the construction of the building as per plan. In 1989, Mukhlesur Rahman along with his wife came to Rangpur to see the progress of work and found the house was not yet completed though he was informed of completion of the building. Then Mukhlesur Rahman and Farida Rahman returned to England.

19. Afterwards, on 22-8-90 both of them met with a serious road accident in the USA and Farida Rahman died. Mukhlesur Rahman was seriously injured in the accident and he returned to Rangpur alone in a state of melancholy. Cunning Hamiduddin Ahmed got a deed of gift being No. 4608 dated 25-3-91 executed and registered in favour of his nieces defendant Nos. 1 and 2. Mukhlesur Rahman, defendant No.3, continued to possess the suit property through his caretaker father-in-law and returned to England.

20. Then Shamsul Haque went to England and his contract job ended in 1992. On 30-3-92 both brothers came to Rangpur together. As Mukhlesur Rahman lost faith in his father-in-law, Hamiduddin Ahmed, he appointed Shamsul Haque caretaker to finish the rest of work of the building. He also asked him to reside in one part of the building and let out other parts.

21. Shamsul Haque agreed and accepted the duty and within short time completed the remaining works and also made some extra work for which he had to incur some expenditure from his own money. In 1997 Mukhlesur Rahman sent money to Shamsul Haque for construction of 2nd floor and it was so completed.

22. After death of Farida Rahman, Mukhlesur Rahman took a 2nd wife. Non-cooperation of the nieces led to enmity with Mukhlesur Rahman. In the course of quarrel once said nieces asked their father Mukhlesur Rahman to quit the building.

23. It is further asserted that Farida Rahman had no right, title and interest in the suit property and, as such, upon her death her daughters did not inherit anything from her. Impugned deed of gift was not acted upon. The nieces became desperate and involved in quarrel with their father who ultimately, decided to transfer the suit property to his younger brother Shamsul Haque and on 25-3-97 transferred the suit property to Shamsul Haque by way of a Hiba-bil-Ewaz being No 3209 and returned to England. He also cancelled the gift in favour of his daughters by a registered deed of gift executed and registered on 25-3-91. Thereafter; Shamsul Haque prayed for mutation which was still pending. After construction of 2nd floor Shamsul Haque was living with his family members in the first floor and let out the ground floor and 2nd floor.

24. Cases of the plaintiffs as averred in their respective plaints of their suits were taken as defence in the suits brought against each other.

25. Mukhlesur Rahman submitted a written statement in the suit of his brother Shamsul Haque but supported his case.

26. Both the suits were tried together and disposed of by one judgment. One set of evidence was recorded in the subsequent suit with reference to the parties therein.

27. On the above pleadings of the parties, following issues were settled:

1. Whether or not the suit was maintainable in the manner and form as framed;

2. Whether the plaintiffs had cause of action in the suit;

3.Whether the valuation of Other Suit No. 15 of 98 and court fees paid thereon were sufficient;

4.Whether or not the suits were barred by limitation;

5.Whether or not Other Suit No. 04 of99 was barred by estopple, acquiescence and waiver;

6.Whether or not in Other Suit No.4 of 99, defendant No.3 Mokhlesur Rahman acquired the suit property in the benami of his wife Farida Rahman and after purchase Mokhlesur Rahman possessed the property;

7.Whether or not the deed of sale dated 13-12-67 being No. 42106 was a benami.

8.Whether or not the deed of gift No. 4608 dated 25-3-91 executed by Mokhlesur Rahman, Hamiduddin Ahmed and Momena Khatoon in favour of Luna Rahman and Dana Rahman was illegal, collusive, fraudulent, ineffective and not binding upon the plaintiffs;

9.Whether of not the plaintiff in Other Suit No.4 of 99 became owner in possession by the deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaz being No. 3209 dated 25-3-97;

10.Whether or not the plaintiffs in Other Suit No. 15 of 98 became absolute owners in possession by way of inheritance and gift dated 25-3-91;

11.Whether or not Shamsul Haque in Other Class Suit No. 15 of 98 was a caretaker on behalf of the plaintiffs in respect of the land as well as the house;

12.Whether or not Shamsul Haque in Other Suit No. 15 of 98 started living in the suit property as caretaker and denied title of the plaintiff since 29-1-97 and

13.If the plaintiffs were entitled to any decree.

28. Plaintiff Shamsul Haque in his subsequent suit examined 5 witnesses and adduced some documents, which were marked exhibits 1 to 8 and 9 and 9 (ka), while plaintiffs Luna and Dana of earlier suit examined 4 witnesses and adduced number of documents which were marked exhibits A, B, C to C(2); D to D(2), E to E(2), F to F(5), G to G(3). H to H(19). 1(1) to 1(2), J to J(1), K, L to L(2). Defendant No 3 also examined himself as DW 5 in support of his brother Shamsul Haque.

29. By impugned judgment and decree learned Joint District Judge decreed Other Suit No. 15 of 1998 on contest against defendant No.1 Shamsul Haque and ex parte against the rest declaring good title of the plaintiffs Luna and Dana Rahman. In the suit property as prayed for and directing defendant Shamsul Haque and others to hand over possession of the suit house to the plaintiffs within 60 days from date otherwise the plaintiffs would be entitled to get possession by eviction of the defendants Learned Joint District Judge dismissed Other Suit No. 15 of 98 on contest against said Luna and Dana Rahman, and ex parte against the rest.

30. Against the decree, Shamsul Haque presented two appeals, namely, FA No. 505 of 2000 arising out of Other Suit No. 04 of 1999 and FA No, 506 of 2000 out of Other Suit No. 15 of 1998.

31. On behalf of the appellant, Mr. Mahbubey Alam. learned Senior Advocate, took us through the record. and submitted that Mokhlesur Rahman actually first acquired the land in the 'Benami' of his wife Farida Rahman and then made the construction out of his own money. Farida Rahman had no independent source of income as borne out by the evidence on record. Learned Joint District Judge fell in error in shifting the onus upon Shamsul Haque to prove 'Benami' transaction and holding that Farida Rahman acquired the land and constructed the house by her own money.

32. Secondly, he submitted that by deed of cancellation dated 25-3-97 Mokhlesur Rahman already cancelled the gift to his daughters by deed of gift dated 25-3-91 and upon such cancellation of the gift the decree passed in respect of the entire property must be held to be not maintainable.

33. Lastly, he submitted that if the properties are ultimately found to be the property acquired by Farida Rahman even then after cancellation of the gift by a registered deed of gift dated 25-3-97 the share of Mokhlesur Rahman as husband of Farida Rahman stands vested in him and his daughters were not entitled to a decree of declaration of right and title in the entire property and without formal suit of partition are not entitled to part possession of the suit property.

34. Mr Shafique Ahmed, learned Senior Advocate on behalf of Luna and Dana Rahman, submitted that the onus was always upon the party who claimed Mukhlesur Rahman acquired the property in the 'Benami' which it miserably failed to prove.

35. He submitted that source of income is never crucial in the proof of 'Benami' transaction. He submitted that since purchase in 1967 Farida Rahman exercised her possession in the suit property to the knowledge of everyone and all papers stood in her name. Such long possession belied the case of 'Benami'. In support he cited Nurjahan Begum vs Mahmudur Rahman Mullick 34 DLR (AD) 61 and Hasan Ali vs Jytendra Biswas. 1984 BLD (AD) 307.

36. Lastly, he submitted that long before his suit Shamsul Haque admitted Luna and Dana Rahman as the owners in possession of the suit property in his letter dated 2-4-94, Exhibit B and plaint dated 25-1-97 in his Other Suit No. 02 of 1997, Exhibit C and after such admission. he cannot be allowed to say that the nieces were not the owners of the suit property,

37. We find two sisters Luna and Dana living in England are fighting their uncle. Shamsul Haque and, to some extent, father Mukhlesur Rahman for their rights in the suit property left by their mother, Farida Rahman. How greed and hunger for property and money can come in the way to natural love, affection and care and ultimately, spoils all beauties of paternal love, care and duty is one of the finest examples set in the instant appeals. For clarity, we shall describe the parties with reference to their relationship.

38. In their suit, Luna and Dana claimed their mother Farida Rahman first purchased the suit land and then got a house constructed thereupon by her own money through her father Hamiduddin Ahmed. Right from the sale deed dated 13-12-67 up to her death all documents of revenue tax and rates in respect of the suit property admittedly, stand in her mine and after her death in the names of said sisters. So, they claim absolute right and title by way of inheritance as well, as gift of the shares of their father, grandfather and grand mother.

39. On the other hand, their uncle Shamsul Haque claimed that his brother Mukhlesur Rahman purchased the land in the name of his wife Farida Rahman and then constructed the house by his own money. Mukhlesur Rahman possessed the suit property. After death of his wife, Mukhlesur Rahman transferred the suit property to Sham sul Haque by a deed of Hiba-bil-ewaz dated 25-3-97. Shamsul Haque has since then been possessing the suit land as his own property. His nieces Luna and Dana have got no interest or possession in the suit property.

40. So, the fate of the cases hinges squarely on the decision first as to whether or not the sale deed dated 13-12-67 was a 'Benami' transaction.

41. More precisely, whether or not Mukhlesur Rahman purchased the land by said deed in the 'Benami' of his wife Farida Rahman and then got the house built thereupon by his own money is the moot issue in these appeals.

42. In order to appreciate the conflicting submissions of the learned Advocates we need to place some facts before us, which admit of no controversy. In 1963, Mokhlesur Rahman went to England and started to work there. In 1964, he married Farida Rahman and in the later part of the year, took her to England

43. It is also in evidence that Farida Rahman took up a job and worked there. Shamsul Haque was in England from 1989 to 1992.

44. The sale deed being No. 42106 dated 13-12-67 purchasing 12 decimals of land stands in the name of Farida Rahman. The consideration appears to be Taka 5,000. There is no dispute about the title of the vendors. Then, by order dated 20-1-69 passed in mutation case No 742/68-69 the record of rights was mutated in the name of Farida Rahman and since then rents were paid in her name. After construction of the house, municipal holding was created and electric and water connections, etc were all taken in her name. All papers revenue, tax, rates, etc stand in the name of Farida Rahman.

45. After her death in 1990 in a fatal road accident in the USA, by a registered deed of gift being No 4608 dated 25-3-91 Mokhlesur Rahman along with his father-in-law Hamiduddin Ahmed and mother-in-law Momena Khatoon jointly gifted their respective shares in the land and the house to Luna and Dana.

46. Accordingly, the record of rights stands again mutated in the names of Luna and Dana. All records relating to revenue, tax and utility services were accordingly mutated in the names of Luna and Dana. At no point of time from 1967 to 2000 when he deposed, Mokhlesur Rahman ever claimed any right or interest either over the land or the house. These are not disputed.

47. A deed of sale prepared and executed after much thought and deliberation and finally concluded by registration is a solemn act transferring right and title to the person whose name appears as transferee in the deed. The presumption carries with the registration not only that it was duly and regularly so done but also the state of things as recited in the deed is the real state of things and it is the named transferee who purchased the land by his money. Such presumption is of course rebuttable.

<u>48. Now, it is well settled that the burden to prove such purchase was benami and the apparent purchaser was not the real purchaser always rests upon the person who claims so. He is required to strictly discharge the burden by adducing legal evidence which would prove directly the fact of Benami or the circumstances which would unmistakably and reasonably lead to the inference of that fact.</u>

49. In support of his case, Shamsul Haque deposed that Farida Rahman had no independent source of income of her own. Mukhlesur Rahman sent the sale price and construction price to his father-in-law late Hamiduddin Ahmed.

50. In cross-examination, he however, admitted that Farida Rahman had temporary jobs. Luna and Dana were born in England and educated there. He sent the letter dated 2-4-94 (Exhibit B) to Luna and Dana from Rangpur. He requested them to send the money he spent for construction and repair and also desired to purchase the house, which was popularly known as 'Farida Manjil. He also admitted instituting of Other Suit No. 2 of 1997 against Luna and Dana giving their address at Senpara for specific performance of a contract. In the plaint of the suit he stated that Farida Rahman was the owner in possession of the suit property and after her death. Luna and Dana became owners in possession. It was also averred in the plaint that Luna and Dana executed an agreement upon receipt of Taka 1,50,000.00. The suit was however dismissed for default on 29-5-97.

51. Corroborating his brother Shamsul Haque PW 2 Matlubur Rahman deposed that Mukhlesur Rahman purchased the land in the 'Benami' of his wife Farida Rahman and got the house built by his own money. He testified that Mukhlesur Rahman used to send money to his father-in-law Hamiduddin Ahmed. He also sent money to other relations. In cross-examination, he said that he was not present at the time of purchase of the land. Nor he had any idea about the vendors or the land. PW 3 Touhidul Islam, who became a 'Bhaira' of PW 1 Shamsul Haque in 1986, deposed that Shamsul Haque lived in the first floor with his family and let out ground floor and second floor.

52. PW 4 Nazrul Islam deposed on 21-7-99 that he was living in the house of Shamsul Haque for last one year and one month.

53. PW 5 Kazi Obaidul Haque, a deed writer, deposed that he wrote deed of cancellation of gift being No. 3202 and deed of Hiba-bil-ewaz being No. 3209 dated 25-3-97.

54. DW 5 Mukhlesur Rahman, father of Luna and Dana and elder brother of Shamsul Haque, deposed on 6-2-2000 that he purchased the land by his own money in the 'Benami' of his wife Farida Rahman through his father-in-law Hamiduddin Ahmed and got the house built by his own money also through him. After death of his wife when he came to Rangpur he was mentally shattered, his father-in-law and other relations got the deed of gift fraudulently executed and registered in favour of his daughters. In 1992, he married a second time. On 30-3-92 he appointed Shamsul Haque caretaker of the house and gave him the keys of the house. Since then Shamsul Haque lived in one part of the house and let out the rest. Shamsul Haque finished the work and he gave the money. He cancelled the gift to his daughters by a deed and by another deed of Hiba-bil-ewaz both dated 25-3-97 relinquished his right title and possession in favour of Shamsul Haque. Since then Shamsul Haque possessed the house and constructed the second floor by his own money. In October 1964, his wife went to England and after 1971 she worked. Before her job she had no source of income.

55. In cross-exam ination, he said that in 1989 Shamsul Haque went to England for job and never came back home before 1992. In England, one receives unemployment benefit if he does not work. He lived in Sheffield and his daughters lived separately. He owned the house there. He got insurance money of his wife but he could not remember the amount. In the written statement filed by him, it is started that Abdul Majid Sarker transferred the suit land to Farida Rahman by deed No. 42106 dated 13-12-67, after purchase her name was mutated and she paid rent. He denied that being angry with the daughters he made the deed of Hiba-bil-ewaz.

56. It may be mentioned here that Mukhlesur Rahman did not file any document in support of his claim. The documents filed by his brother Shamsul Haque also relate to a period after 1997 excepting five rent receipts of monthly tenants of the period from 1992 to 1996.

57. So, that is all the evidence that could have been adduced by Shamsul Haque in support of his case of 'Benami'. It should not however miss our attention that in 1998, Shamsul Haque for the first time claimed that in 1967 his brother Mukhlesur Rahman purchased the land in the 'Benami' of his wife Farida Rahman and got the house constructed thereon through his father-in-law Hamiduddin Ahmed, Mukhlesur Rahman for the first time in his written statement filed in Court on 13-8-98 and deposition recorded on 6-2-2000 claimed that he first purchased the land and then got the house built thereon by his own money. Consistent case of two brothers is that Mukhlesur Rahman sent money for the price of the land as well as the cost of building to Hamiduddin Ahmed. But none of them tried to tender any evidence whatsoever on such transfer of fund to said Harniduddin Ahmed. There is practically no evidence at all of sending any fund to Hamiduddin by Mukhlesur Rahman.

<u>58. It is settled long ago that the question of 'Benami' is essentially a question of fact. In determining such question of fact, there is no hard and fast rule to be applicable in all situations.</u>

<u>However. the Court may be profitably guided by the following circumstances:</u>

<u>a. the source of the fund to pay the price of the property:</u>

<u>b. the nature and possession of the property after purchase:</u>

<u>c. the motive, if any, for such purchase in the name of ostensible owner instead of real owner;</u>

<u>d. the position of the parties and the relationship. if any, between the claimant and alleged benamdar;</u>

<u>e. the custody of the deed after the sale; and</u>

<u>f. the conduct of the parties in dealing with the property after sale, Cf. Jaydaya Poddar vs Bibi Hazra, (1974) 2 SCR 90.</u>

59. Besides. the essence of such 'Benami' transaction is the intention of the party or parties concerned. The intention is always shrouded with a thick veil which is sometimes difficult to unveil, particularly when the real owner is not available.

60. But in the case at hand, Mukhlesur Rahman who claimed to be the real owner was available and deposed in support of the case of 'Benami'. But he could not say a word as to why he purchased the land in the name of his wife. Neither Shamsul Haque nor Mukhlesur Rahman could offer any motive for such 'Benami' transaction. They could not produce even the original deed of sale which was adduced by Luna and Dana from their custody. As stated here in above overwhelming documentary evidence stand in the name of Farida Rahman and after her death, in the names of Luna and Dana clearly exercising right of their possession.

61. Last, but not the least, the written admission of Shamsul Haque in his letter dated 2-4-94 addressed to Luna and Dana, Exhibit B and the plaint filed by Shamsul Haque in Other Suit No. 2 of 97 for specific performance of contract, exhibit- C that Luna and Dana were the owners in possession of the suit property demolish finally the entire case of 'Benami'.

62. In such circumstance and on the evidence on record, we do not have any hesitation to say that Shamsul Haque hopelessly failed to discharge the burden of proving the sale dated 13-12-67 was a 'Benami' and learned Joint District Judge therefore committed no error in rejecting the case of ' Benami'.

63. Now. let us see the possession of the suit property. Admittedly, Shamsul Hoque has been possessing the suit property since 1992. It is the case of Luna and Dana that, they asked him to look after the house as a caretaker but subsequently, he entered the house without their permission and started living with his family on the first floor and inducted new tenants of his choice by evicting the old ones in the rest of the house.

64. On the other hand, case of Shamsul Haque is that in 1992 he entered the house as a caretaker on behalf of his brother Mukhlesur Rahman and then, he possessed as of his own since 1997 on the basis of deed of Hiba-bil-ewaz dated 25-3-97.

65. But the nature of possession of Shamsul Hoque loses all its importance in the case the moment he fails to prove first title of his brother Mukhlesur Rahman and then, that of his own in the suit property. Consequently, he is obliged to vacate possession in favour of the persons who have got the title if the suit is not barred otherwise by law of limitation. As Luna and Dana, being the true owners, instituted the suit for possession on 19-5-97 well within the period of limitation, Learned Joint District Judge has rightly granted them a decree for possession.

66. When the deed of sale dated 13-12-67 is found to be not a 'Benami' transaction the deed of Hiba-bil-ewaz executed and registered by Mokhlesur Rahman dated 25-3-97 in favour of Shamsul Haque becomes un-effective and inoperative and must be held to be void as a product of collusion and without any consideration. By such deed Shamsul Hoque acquired no title or interest in the suit property. Similarly, the cancellation of gift dated 25-3-91 by a deed of cancellation dated 25-3-97 would be of no avail since the gift was long ago acted upon, and given effect to by way of mutation and exclusive possession. Once a gift is acted upon title passes absolutely and that cannot be cancelled by subsequent action of the donor.

67. In the circumstances, we find no merit in any of the appeals which are doomed to fail. Learned Joint District Judge committed no error calling for any interference.

68. In the result, both appeals are dismissed with cost and impugned judgment and decree are hereby affirmed in their entirety. Defendant No.1 Shamsul Haque in Other Suit No. 15 of 98 is directed to vacate the suit house within sixty days from date positively.

Send down the LCR at once.

End.

case_source: (From the judgement and order dated 7th of August, 2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 6698 of 2001).
full_judgment:
Md Imman Ali J : This civil appeal by leave is directed against the judgement and order dated 7-8-2006 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 6698 of 2001 discharging the Rule.

2. The appellants as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 117 of 1998 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Muladi, Barisal seeking declaration that the deed of heba-bil-ewaz dated 23-5-1966, as stated in the 'Ka' schedule of the plaint, is illegal, void and not binding upon them. They stated, inter alia, that the suit property described in schedule 'Kha.` to the plaint belonged to Saizuddin Sikder and his only daughter having predeceased him without any issue, after his death the suit property was inherited by his wife as well as full brothers Abul Hashem Sikder and Raham Ali Sikder, who used to live in the same mess. Then the wife of Saizuddin died without leaving any issue. Raham Ali died leaving behind sons, defendants Nos. 1 and 2 Abdul Malek and Shajahan and also defendant Nos. 4-13. Raham Ali, in order to cheat his younger brother Abul Hashern, just 10 days before the death of Saizuddin took Saizuddin to Barisal on the plea of his treatment and then he took him to Rahmatpur Sub-Registry Office and by inserting a fictitious property allegedly situated within Babugonj Police Station, fraudulently got the deed of heba-bil-ewaz dated 23-5-1966 executed and registered showing transfer of the suit property in favour of Afazuddin, Malek Sikder, Shajahan Sikder, his three sons, and Renu Bibi, the live-in daughter of Saizuddin. Then Abul Hashem also died leaving behind his sons, plaintiff Nos. 1-3 and widow, plaintiff No. 4. The plaintiffs on 16th Baishak 1405, for the first time came to know about the above deed of heba-bil-ewaz when the defendants claimed exclusive ownership over the suit property on the strength of the above deed of heba. Until then the above deed of heba was kept secret, and further, there was no ewaz and the plaintiffs have been in possession of the entire property of Saizuddin. Further, Saizuddin having remained ill and bed-ridden since three months before his death, was not capable of understanding anything, and hence the deed of heba-bil-ewaz is also void.

3. Defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 5 contested by filing written statement contending that Saizuddin and Abul Hashem were not full brothers and Saizuddin executed the deed of heba-bil-ewaz voluntarily; Abul Hashem misbehaved with Saizuddin Sikder and did not look after him; further the plaintiffs as heirs of Saizuddin are estopped from challenging the above deed on the ground of alleged fictitious land of Babugonj Police Station therein, and further that the possession of the suit property was delivered to the defendants and the suit is barred by limitation and the plaintiffs are also not in possession of the suit land.

4. The Assistant Judge, after hearing the parties and considering the materials on record decreed the suit. Then the defendants filed Title Appeal No. 203 of 2000 in the Court of District Judge, Barisal. On transfer to the Court of Subordinate Judge, Artha Rin Adalat the appeal was heard and allowed. Against the aforesaid judgement and decree of the appellate Court the plaintiffs filed Civil Revision No. 6698 of 2001 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule, which upon hearing was discharged. 5. Being aggrieved by the said judgement and order of the High Court Division, Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1680 of 2006 was filed by the plaintiffs-appellants and leave was granted to consider the following grounds:

"I. Whether the High Court Division committed error in affirming the judgement of the appellate Court and the finding of the High Court Division that the petitioners, as heirs of Saizuddin are precluded from challenging the deed of heba-bil-ewaj is erroneous as the petitioners are neither transferors nor transferees in the above deed and they being third party to the said deed, their right is not at all affected by the said deed.

II. Whether the High Court Division also committed error of law in finding exclusive possession of the defendants in the suit property and in not considering that the suit property is joint property and was never partitioned.

6. Mr Abdul Quayum, learned Senior Advocate appearing for the appellant submitted that the High Court Division did not consider that no evidence was lead as to the exchange of ewaz and the appellate Court misread the evidence of DWs 1 and 2 and exhibit K(1)-K(2) was not considered, and thus came to the wrong conclusion that the document was acted upon, and hence committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice. He further submitted that the finding that the document is binding upon the heirs of the parties to the documents and thus it is binding upon the plaintiff-petitioners who have challenged the documents as fraudulent, is based upon misconception of law, and thus the High Court Division committed error of law in affirming the same. The learned Advocate submitted that the appellate Court in finding that plaintiff-petitioners are precluded from challenging the document as heirs, although they are neither vendor nor vendee, being third parties to the document and affected by the document, thus committed error of law occasioning failure of justice. He finally submitted that the High Court Division committed error of law occasioning failure of justice in finding exclusive possession in favour of the respondents and failed to consider that the suit property is joint property and it was never partitioned.

7. None appeared for the respondents.

8. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Senior Advocate appearing at the request of the Court as amicus curiae, made submissions in support of the impugned judgement and order of the High Court Division. He submitted that section 28(a) of the Registration Act precludes a party to the deed from challenging its veracity and section 28(b) aids a third party, but the heirs of the transferor are not independent and derive their right from him. So, they cannot challenge the deed of heba-bil-ewaz as fraudulent. He submitted that the heirs stand on the same footing as the transferor and cannot take benefit of section 28 of the said Act. He further submitted that section 115 of the Evidence Act also provides that representative of the executant cannot deny the transfer, even though the executant may have acted fraudulently. In support of his contention, Mr Bhuiyan referred the decision in Bazlur Rahman vs Sadu Mia, 45 DLR 391.

9. Section 115 of the Evidence Act provides as follows:

"115. Estoppel—When one person has, by his declaration, act or omission, intentionally caused or permitted another person to believe a thing to be true and to act upon such belief, neither he nor his representative shall be allowed, in any suit or proceeding between himself and such person or his representative, to deny the truth of that thing.

Illustration: A intentionally and falsely leads B to believe that certain land belongs to A, and thereby induces B to buy and pay for it.

The land afterwards becomes the property of A, and A seeks to set aside the sale on the ground that, at the time of the sale, he had no title. He must not be allowed to prove his want of title."

10. We may firstly deal with the question of possession of the parties in the suit land since that was a ground upon which leave was granted by this Division. The land was conveyed to the defendant by Shaijuddin by the impugned deed of Heba-bil-ewaz on 23-5-1966, some 32 years before the filing of the suit. DW1 admitted that the land was not mutated in the names of the recipients. The trial Court considered the rent receipts adduced by the defendants and also the deposition of DW1 in cross examination that the money for the rent was paid by all the co-sharers in accordance with their shares. He also admitted that Aynal Hawlader had established his homestead on plot No. 563/615 of Khatian No. 267 and that Mostafa Sikder established his homestead on the plaintiffs' portion of the said Khatian. DW1 also admitted that he paid Taka 12,000 to the plaintiffs in respect of sale of trees from the land of the heba-bil-ewaz. After considering the above aspects and the evidence of the other witnesses, the trial Court concluded that the land was in ejmali possession.

11. The appellate Court, on the other hand did not discuss the possession of the parties in the suit land. It was simply stated that DW 2 deposed to the effect that the defendants possess the land transferred by Saijuddin and there was no reason to disbelieve his evidence. But the appellate Court did not advert to or reverse the findings of the trial Court with regard to the aspect of possession of the land in question.

12. The High Court Division noted that the appellate Court found the defendants in exclusive possession of the suit property. However, we do not find any such specific finding of the appellate Court. We also do not find any basis of the observation that "the appellate court properly held that the plaintiffs failed to prove that they had/have been in possession of the suit property in ejmali with the defendants." We note that the High Court Division also did not advert to or reverse the trial Court's assessment of the evidence with regard to possession. After assessing the evidence, the High Court Division came to a finding that "the defendants had/have been in exclusive possession of the Ghar which is situated in another Bhiti and the plaintiffs were never in possession thereto." This finding in no way indicates the exclusive possession of the defendants in the 2.11 acres of the property gifted by Saijuddin. Hence the finding of exclusive possession of the defendants in the suit property is not sustainable.

13. Now let us turn to the substantive issue of locus standi of the plaintiffs to challenge the validity of the impugned heba-bil-ewaz deed. Simply put, the argument on behalf of the defendants, as also supported by Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiya, is that Saijuddin, being the executant of the deed could not challenge its validity claiming its fraudulent registration as provided by section 28(2)(a) of the Registration Act, and the plaintiffs being heirs of Saijuddin have no locus standi to challenge the validity of the deed on the same ground. Mr Bhuiya has additionally put forward the argument that under section 115 of the Evidence Act the plaintiffs being in a representative capacity are estopped from denying the validity of the registration effected by Saijuddin, the executant of the deed.

14. Undoubtedly the deed of heba-bil-ewaz contains 01 decimal of land of plot No.120 within khatian No. 80 of Kedarpur Mouja under Babugonj Police Station which is within the jurisdiction of Rahmatpur Sub-registry Office. It was the inclusion of this 01 decimal of land which enabled the executant to register the land at the Rahmatpur Sub-registry Office in spite of the fact that the remaining 2.10 acres of land detailed in the schedule of the deed is situated within the jurisdiction of Muladi Sub-registry Office. It was alleged by the plaintiffs that Saijuddin in fact did not own the land of khatian No. 80 of Kedarpur Mouja and hence the registration of the deed in Rahmatpur Sub-registry Office was illegal being violative of section 28 of the Registration Act.

15. Section 28 of the Registration Act provides as follows:

"28. Place for registering documents relating to land (1) Save as in this Part otherwise provided, every document mentioned in section 17, sub-section (1), clause (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e), section 17, sub-section (2), and section 18, in so far as such documents affects immoveable property shall be presented for registration in the office of a Sub-Registrar within whose sub-district the whole or major portion of the property to which such document relates is situate :

Provided that where the, major portion of such property is not situate within one sub-district the document shall be presented for registration in the office of the Sub-Registrar within whose sub-district any portion of such property is situate.

(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1),—

(a) after a document is registered, no party thereto shall be entitled to question the validity of its registration on the ground that the property which purported to give jurisdiction to the Sub-Registrar to register it either did not exist or was fictitious or insignificant or was not intended to be conveyed; and

(b) a document the registration of which is secured by the inclusion of a non-existent, fictitious or insignificant portion or item shall not in any manner affect the rights of a person who was not a party thereto and acquired rights in the property without notice of the transaction to which such document relates."

16. The registration clearly falls foul of the provisions of the Registration Act. It is undoubtedly a case of fraud on the Registration Act. The defendants did not seek to deny the fact that the land of khatian No. 80 was not owned by Saijuddin. They took the stand that when any deed is registered in a sub-registry office which does not have the jurisdiction to register such deed, any party to that deed would not be entitled to cancel that deed. It was further contended that as the heirs of Saijuddin, the plaintiffs could not challenge the deed as provided by section 28(2)(a) and (b).

17. The trial Court rejected the contention of the defendants on the ground that the plaintiffs or their predecessors were not party to the deed in question.

18. We may point out at this stage that the finding of the trial Court that since two of the beneficiaries of the heba deed were minors, the deed in their favour was void. This is clearly a misconception of law and was rightly reversed by the appellate Court.

19. However, the live issue in this case is whether or not the heirs of the executant can challenge the deed which was registered by committing fraud on the statute. The plaintiffs are not party to the deed. The question is whether the heirs of the executant who registered the deed, and who stand to benefit from the fraud of the donor are contemplated by the provisions of section 28(2)(a) and (b).

20. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellants argued that the words of the statue are to be given their natural and ordinary meaning. In support of his contention he referred to the decision in Abdul Kader vs Secretary, Election Commission, 58 DLR (AD) 71. Hence, he submitted, the word 'party' to the deed would cover only the donor and donee since they are the persons who actively created the deed and would benefit from the execution and registration of the deed. Everyone else would be a third party as mentioned in section 28(2)(b). He submitted that had it been the intention of the statute to bar any heir or representative of the donor from challenging the deed then it would have been specifically provided in the statute. He also submitted that the plaintiffs' and donor's interests are conflicting and hence the provisions of section 28(2) are not applicable in the facts of the instant case.

<u>21. The provision of law in fact reflects the common law principle that no man shall take advantage of his own wrong. Having illegally registered the deed, which at the time suited his purpose, the donor would not be permitted by law to renege from his liabilities under it by claiming that what he did was illegal or that the deed was invalid. In these circumstances the law cannot impinge upon the rights of any other person who did not play any part in the fraud. Moreover, the tenor of section 28(2)(b) is that any third party who had no notice of the transaction is not precluded from challenging the validity of a deed to which he is not party and which was fraudulently registered.</u>

22. The learned Advocate for the appellants referred us to the decision in Corporation of the City of Victoria vs Bishop of Vancouver Island, AIR 1921 PC 240, where it was held, "In the construction of statutes their words must be interpreted in their ordinary grammatical sense, unless there be something in the context, or in the object of the statute in which they occur, or in the circumstances with reference to which they are used, to show that they were used in a special sense."

23. We are of the view that if the wording of a statute is not in any way ambiguous, then the natural meaning is to be given to the words used. We find no difficulty in understanding the meaning of the statutory provision before us. The intention of the statute is clearly to bar the parties to the fraudulently registered deed from challenging its validity when they themselves took the illegal path. However, the persons other than the actual parties are not precluded from challenging the fraudulently registered deed.

24. We find support for our view in the decision in Syed Kawsar Ali vs Gahar Kazi reported in 37 DLR (AD) 177. In that case also a fictitious plot of land was included in a sale deed in order to give jurisdiction to and enable registration in a particular Sub-registry office. The trial Court found the deed to be fictitious and the appellate Court held that the deed which included non-existent property only to give jurisdiction to the particular Sub-registry office was void under section 28 of the Registration Act. The High Court Division reversed the decision finding that there was no evidence that the transferee had any collusion with the vendor in including fictitious land and hence the transferee's right was not invalidated. This Division quoted the observation of the appellate Court as follows:

"It is only the parties to document be bound by kabala containing non-existent or fictitious land only to attract the jurisdiction of a Sub Registration office within meaning of sub-clause (a) of clause (2) of section 28 of the Registration Act. According to true interpretation of sub-clause (b) of section 28 of Registration Act as it stands now after the amendment in 1962 parties not being parties to the kabala for a fictitious or non-existent land can reasonably show that kabala like Ext A is invalid for all intents and purposes."

25. After analysing several decisions of the Subcontinent, their lordships of this Division held,

"The expression "no party" means defendant Nos.1 and 2 but not defendant No. 3 because he has not been mentioned here. In other words it was the vendor and vendee of Ext A namely, defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 2 who are precluded from questioning the validity of registration on the ground that the property did not exist or was fictitious or insignificant or was not intended to be conveyed and the registration was invalid."

<u>26. In the instant case the plaintiffs are not party to the deed in question and were totally unconnected at the time of the deed. Indeed, when it was created they were not the heirs of the donor. At the time of execution and registration of the deed the donor had a surviving wife and brothers who would have been his heirs. The plaintiffs were not even in contemplation of inheriting the property if the gift had not been made or the transaction had been invalidated at that time. They knew nothing of the heba-bil-ewaz. In hindsight it is seen that the fraudulent registration by inclusion of the fictitious land has affected the plaintiffs' interest. In our view the plaintiffs are third parties so far as the heba-bil-ewaz deed is concerned and their right to challenge the deed is not barred under section 28(2)(a) and has been protected by section 28(2)(b).</u>

<u>In view of the above discussion, we are of the opinion that unless there is evidence that the heirs were in collusion with the donor in the fraud committed upon the statute, they would not be precluded from challenging the validity of the deed in question. In this case there is no such evidence. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed and the judgement and order of the High Court Division is set aside. There will be no order as to casts.</u>

End.
