parties:
Nazera Bibi and another-----  Appellant
VS
Abdul Mazid and others -------- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 5-7-2010 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 5007 of 2004).
full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique J : This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 5-7-2010 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 5007 of 2004 affirming the judgment and decree dated 14-9-2004 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Rajshahi in Title Appeal No. 98 of 2001 affirming those dated 28-2-2001 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Tanore, Rajshahi in Other Class Suit No. 84 of 1996.

2. The relevant facts, for the disposal of this appeal, are that the appellant instituted the aforesaid suit for declaration that the kabala deed No. 15607 dated 17-10-1994 executed by Nazera Bibi, plaintiff No. 1 in favour of defendant No. 1 Abdul Mazid was forged, fraudulent, inoperative and the same was not binding upon the plaintiff stating, inter alia, that the scheduled land belonged to the defendant No. 1 who sold 0.66 acre of land to his second wife, the plaintiff No. 1, in lieu of dower money by registered deed No. 4925 dated 14-12-1992. The defendant No. 1 also sold 0.10 acre of land of the suit plot to the plaintiff No. 1 by another registered deed No. 4104 dated 31-10-1993 and handed over possession of those lands. Thus, the plaintiff No. 1 became the owner of 0.76 acre of land described in schedule to the plaint. Owing to extreme misbehaviour of the first wife of the defendant No. 1 with the plaintiff No. 1 she went to her father's house and, thereafter, gave birth to a son. The plaintiff No. I filed Mutation Case No. 242/18-1/95-96 for mutation of that 0.76 acre of land in her name. The defendant No. 1 raised objection in that mutation case stating that the plaintiff No. 1, after getting entire dower money, returned the said 0.76 acre of land to the defendant No. 1 by executing and registering sale deed being No. 15607 dated 17-10-1994 (the impugned deed). However, she got her name mutated in the khatian. Thereafter, she procured the certified copy of impugned sale deed No. 15607 dated 17-10-1994 and confirmed about the forged deed. She never executed any such sale deed in favour of the defendant No. 1, who forged the same beyond her knowledge in another Sub-Registrar's office within the jurisdiction of which the plaintiff No. 1 had no property at all. The further case of the plaintiffs was that being in need of money the plaintiff No. 1 sold 0.53 acre of land out of the suit land to the plaintiff No. 2 by two registered sale deeds dated 30-5-1995 and 7-7-1996 and handed over possession of the same. They have been possessing the entire 0.76 acre of land. The plaintiff No. 1 never executed the impugned deed and the defendant No. 1 had created the same by false personation.

3. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the plaint case contending, inter alia, that he never transferred the suit land to the plaintiff No. 1 and never executed the sale deeds dated 14-12-1992 and 31-10-1993. With a malafide intention to grab the suit land, the plaintiff- No. 2 with the help of the plaintiff No. 1, created those two deeds and also created the impugned deed dated 17-10-1994. The suit should be dismissed.

4. The trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the same was not maintainable without the prayer for cancellation of the impugned deed. The plaintiffs preferred appeal which was disallowed by the appellate Court and the same was upheld by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 5007 of 2004.

5. Thus, the appellant has preferred this appeal getting leave.

6. Mr Zainul Abedin, learned Advocate-on-Record appearing for the appellants, submits that they have challenged the genuineness of the impugned deed alleged to have been executed by the plaintiff No. 1 in favour of the defendant No. 1 making clear assertion that she did not execute any such deed and that the defendant No. 1, in order to grab the suit land, forged the impugned deed beyond the knowledge of the plaintiff No. 1 by false personation. He submits that since the impugned kabala deed was void abinitio the prayer for cancellation was not at all necessary, the High Court Division erred in law in discharging the Rule.

7. Mr MA Jabbar, learned Counsel appearing for the respondent No. 1, in his submission contended that the learned Courts below upon proper consideration of the pleadings and evidence on record, rightly dismissed the suit holding that the same was not maintainable.

8. It appears from the pleadings that the impugned deed was executed and registered on 17-10-1994 in respect of the land measuring an area of 0.76 acre of RS Khatian No. 160 and Plot No. 86 of Mouza Mohor, Police Station-Tanore, District-Rajshahi. It is evident that the said deed was executed in the Sub-Registrar's office of Nababgonj inasmuch as the suit land is situated within the jurisdiction of Tanore SR Office, Rajshahi. It is the case of the plaintiffs that the plaintiff No. 1 did not execute and register the said sale deed. In the plaint, the plaintiffs categorically stated,—

“১নং বাদিনী নাজেরা বিবির নালিশী মৌজা ভিন্ন অন্য কোন মৌজা বা থানায় কোন জমি নাই। জালিয়াত ১ নং বিবাদী ১ নং বাদিনীকে বহিত করা ও অন্যায় লাভের আশায় ভিন্ন মহিলাকে নাজেরা বিবি সাজিয়ে উক্ত জ্বাল দলিলের সৃষ্টি করিয়াছে । তানোর রেজিস্ট্রি অফিসে ভিন্ন মহিলাকে নাজেরা সাজিয়ে জ্বাল দলিল রেজিস্ট্রি করিলে হাতে-নাতে ধরা পড়ার ভয়ে জালিয়াত ১ নং বিবাদী নবাবগঞ্জ রেজিষ্টি অফিসে জ্বাল দলিল রেজি্ট্রি করিয়াছে। ১নং বাদিনী গত ইং ১৭-১০-১৯৯৪ তারিখে উক্ত দলিল রেজিস্ট্রি সম্পাদন ও করা দুরে থাক নবাবগঞ্জ রেজিস্ট্রি অফিসেই কোন দিন যান নাই।” In the written statement the defendant No. 1 did not claim that the impugned deed No. 15607 dated 17-10-1994 was a genuine one rather he stated that the plaintiffs created that deeds He has stated, “সুতরাং কথিত নালিশী সমস্ত দলিল বাদী দ্বয়ের যোগসাজসে ও জালিয়াতির আশ্রয়ে সৃজিত হইতেছে।”In his examination-in-chief as DWI he stated, প্রকৃত পক্ষে অত্র মোকদ্দমার বাদীনি জালিয়াত ও কথিত নালিশী দদিলের যোগসাজসীভাবে সৃষ্টি করেছে।”In cross-examination he said, “নালিশী দলিলটার সম্পর্কে (তারিখ ১৭-১০-১৯৯৪ নং ১৫৬০৭) আমি কিছুই জানি না।”The defendant No. 1 himself also did not say that impugned deed was a genuine one and the same was duly executed and registered. PW 5 Raisuddin, TC Assistant of Nababgonj District Registrar's office, was a examined for proving volume book of Nababgonj SR office who in his evidence has said, বাদীর দাখিলার ১৫৬০৭ তাং ১৭-১০-১৯৯৪ দলিলের জাবেদা কপি সহিত ভলিউমের দলিলের বিবরণ মিল আছে। দলিলের সনাক্তকারী হিসেবে উল্লেখ আছে আঃ মজিদ/গ্রহীতা নিজেই সনাক্তকারী এখানে । প্রদ-৭।”

9. Abdul Majid is defendant No. 1 who is recipient of the impugned deed as well identifier of the same. In mutation proceeding he supported the deed but strangely in this proceeding he stated that the deed was a collusive one. The executant denied the execution and recipient and identifier did not claim that the deed was duly executed rather he stated that the same was a forged and collusive one, in such circumstances, the Courts below, ignoring such pleadings and evidence, most illegally gave life of the said deed.

<u>10. Furthermore, the land as described in the schedule to the impugned kabala deed is situated within the territorial jurisdiction of Tanore SR office under Rajshahi District but the impugned deed was registered at Nababgonj SR office. In the pleading, the plaintiffs specifically stated that the plaintiff No. 1 has had no such land situated within the territorial jurisdiction of Nababgonj S.R. office as shown in the schedule to the impugned deed and the same was mentioned only for the purpose of avoiding the jurisdictional question to register the impugned deed at Nababgonj SR office. Every document mentioned in section 17 of Registration Act has to be presented for registration in the office of a Sub-Registrar within whose sub-district, the whole or some portion (before amendment) of the property to which such document relates is situated. Where a document is registered by including a property which is non-existent merely on conferring jurisdiction on the Sub-Registrar where it is registered, such a document is invalid.</u>

11. It is a suit for declaration that the plaintiff No. 1 was not a party to the impugned sale deed purported to have been executed by her alleging that her signature thereon was result of forgery. Such suit is maintainable if it is proved that said deed is a product of forgery and the same was created by false personation. It is apparent that the impugned deed was forged as well as fraudulent one and, thus, the same was void ab initio. When the document in question is a void one, the question of seeking its cancellation would not be necessary. It is only when a document is voidable, that is valid until it is declared as void, in that case the question of seeking its cancellation would arise. In the case of Sufia Khatun vs Faizun Nesa reported in 39 DLR (AD) 46 this Division has observed that if a written instrument is adjudged void and it is further declared that it has not affected the plaintiff's rights it need not be cancelled. It was further observed that where a document has been adjudged voidable, it will have to avoid both declaration and cancellation; and if the document is adjudged void or void ab initio it need not be cancelled.

12. In view of such facts and circumstances, the courts, below had committed error of law in holding that the instant suit was not maintainable without the prayer for cancellation. Accordingly, we find merit in the appeal.

Thus, the appeal is allowed. The judgment and decrees of the learned courts below are hereby set aside. The suit is decreed.

End.

parties:
HRC Properties Limited ------- Petitioner
Vs.

full_judgment:
Tariq ul Hakim J : Rule Nisi has been issued calling upon the respondent Nos. 1-5 to show cause why they should not be directed to record Deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 in the relevant Balam Book at the office of the Sadar Sub-Registrar, Chittagong and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts in brief is that on the application of the petitioner company the Respondent No. 6 sanctioned a loan of Taka 750 million to set up a Tea Processing Unit and for working capital loan on condition that its 57.42 decimals of land being Plot Nos. 64, 65 and 66 Agrabad Commercial Area, Chittagong vide Deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 would be provided as collateral security by registered and equitable mortgage. Thereafter, the Respondent No. 6 Bank made inquiries at the record room of the Sadar Sub-Registrar's office, Chittagong and found that the said registered deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 was not recorded in the concerned Balam Book of the Sadar Sub-Registrar's Office, Chittagong. After confirming the matter by making inquiries the petitioner wrote letters dated 17-4-2017 and 23-4-2017 to the Sub-Registrar, Sadar, Chittagong informing him that Hoechst Marin Roussel Limited sold the aforesaid land to the petitioner by registered deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 and that the same had not been recorded in the concerned Balam Book of the Sadar Sub-Registrar,. Chittagong and requested that it be so recorded. By letter vide Memo No. 447 dated 29-5-2017 (Annexure C) the Sadar Sub-Registrar, Chittagong informed the District Registrar, Chittagong that the registration of deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 was not recorded in the Balam Book of the said office though the matter of registration appeared to be evident from perusal of the Thumb Impression Book preserved at the said office. The Respondent No. 3 District Registrar, Chittagong thereafter brought the matter to the notice of the Respondent No. 2, Inspector General of Registration, Bangladesh under Memo No. 922 dated 22-9-2017 confirming that on perusal of the Thumb Impression Book kept at the office of Sadar Sub-Registrar, Chittagong it appeared that the aforesaid deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 was registered but for unknown reasons the deed in question was not recorded in the Balam Book kept at the Record Room of the Sub-Registrar, Sadar, Chittagong.

3. The petitioner getting no response from the Respondents sent a Demand for Justice Notice on 20-7-2017 through his learned Advocate to the Respondent No. 2 Inspector General of Registration, Bangladesh requesting him to take steps to get deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 recorded in the Balam Book of the Sadar Sub-Registrar's Office, Chittagong and not having received any satisfactory reply from him the petitioner has come to this Court and obtained the present Rule.

4. The Rule is being contested by the Respondent No. 2 Inspector General of Registration, Bangladesh by filing Affidavit-in-Opposition stating inter alia that the document in question was registered in the Sadar Sub- Registrar's Office, Chittagong and thereafter Balam Book and Index Book of the said year has been preserved in the Record Room of the said office. It is further stated that the respondents came to know about the non existence of above mentioned registered deed in the Balam Book when the petitioner applied to the record keeper of the said Sub-Registrar's Office for obtaining a certified copy of the same. On inquiry the vendor's signature was found in the Thumb impression book but the deed was not found in the concerned Balam Book. It is further stated that the respondents could not ascertain the reasons for the omission/absence of the petitioner's aforesaid deed in the Balam Book due to the death and retirement of the then officers and staff of the Sadar Sub-Registrar's Office, Chittagong and that at that time one Sirajul Moula was the Sub-Registrar at the said office but he has since passed away.

5. Pursuant to an order of this Court the Respondent No. 2 Inspector General of Registration, Bangladesh, Respondent No. 3 District Registrar, Chittagong and Respondent No. 4 Sadar Sub-Registrar, Chittagong appeared in person before this Court along with Thumb Impression Book and Balam Books of the year 1999 and submitted before this Court that they needed time to ascertain the reasons why the aforesaid deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 was not recorded in the concerned Balam Book. The Respondents however confirmed that the signatures of the vendors were present in the thumb impression book of the relevant time and it appeared to match the signatures of the vendors in the aforesaid Original Deed. The respondents however wanted time for verification of the aforesaid Deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 and on an application by the respondents one month time was allowed by this Court on 14-12-2017 for examining and verifying the said deed by the respondents. Subsequently by an application dated 14-12-2017 the respondents prayed for extension of time to obtain expert opinion from the CID on the matter and allegedly forwarded relevant documents to the Secretary, Ministry of Law for necessary steps in this regard.

6. The petitioner thereafter filed an affidavit-in-reply against the respondents' application for extension of time stating inter alia that the concerned officers of the registration department in their official correspondences dated 29-5-2017 Annexures B and C admitted that the vendor's thumb impression and signature was present in the thumb impression book maintained at the office of the Respondent No. 5 and therefore registration of deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 was genuine and that if the registering authority committed any error in the registration process it was a procedural defect which is curable under section 87 of the Registration Act and that there is no scope for obtaining expert opinion from the CID on the matter. It is further stated that the respondents are trying to shirk from their mandatory duty of recording deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 in the Balam Book maintained by the Respondent No. 5 by trivial excuses to harass the petitioner. It is further stated, that the petitioner produced the aforesaid deed at the office of the Sadar Sub-Registrar, Chittagong as per direction of this Court several times and without taking any final decision on the matter they are deliberately trying to deprive the petitioner of his legal right causing him unnecessary harassment and loss.

7. Mr. Syed Mahmudul Ahsan assisted by Mr. NM Ahsanul Haque, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the petitioner is a bonafide purchaser of the said land by providing valuable consideration to the vendor and the same was registered as deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 and the inaction of the respondents to record its contents in the relevant Balam Book is illegal and unlawful. The learned Advocate further submits that the petitioner is a commercial concern and is suffering irreparable loss and damage due to the Respondents' failure to record its deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 in the concerned Balam Book of the Respondent No. 4. The learned Advocate further submits that the respondents' failure to record the aforesaid deed No. 7216 dated 11- 11-1999 in the Balam Book has infringed the petitioner's right to property guaranteed under the Constitution. The learned Advocate further submits that the signatures of the vendor and purchaser are in the thumb impression book of the respondents which is evidence that the said deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 was presented for registration and subsequently since he obtained the original deed as well as a certified copy of the same, non recording the contents of the said deed in the concerned balam book is a fault and irregularity of the respondents for which they are liable and that a direction should be given to them to record the same in the concerned Balam Book.

8. Ms, Amatul Karim, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the Respondent No. 2 submits that Deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 appears to be registered at the Sadar Sub-Registrar's Office, Chittagong but its contents are not in the concerned balam book and index book at the Sadar Sub-Registrar's Office, Chittagong and that since other official documents of the said period have been destroyed and the concerned officers and staffs of the registration department are either dead or have gone into retirement it has not been possible to ascertain the reason why the contents of the aforesaid deed was not recorded in the balam book.

9. We have considered the submissions of the learned advocates, perused the writ petition, Affidavit-in-Opposition, Supplementary Affidavit and the other averments and Annexures.

10. It appears that Sale Deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 was executed on the 11th November, 1999 by the Managing Director of Hoechst Marin Roussel Limited, a multinational company in favour of the petitioner company. It is admitted by the respondents that the signatures of the said vendor is present in the thumb impression book of registration authority and preserved at the Sadar Sub-Registrar's Office, Chittagong. Furthermore, the word 'registered' together with a book number, volume number and page number of the book in which the document has been recorded i.e. Book No. 1, Volume No. 193 and page Nos. 10-179 have been stated on the aforesaid Deed No. 7216 of 1999 thereby indicating that section 60 of the Registration Act, 1908 has been complied.

11. Section 60 of the Registration Act states as follows:

"60. Certificate of registration—(1) After such of the provisions of sections 34, 35, 58 and 59 as apply to any document presented for registration have been complied with, the registering officer shall endorse thereon a certificate containing the word 'registered', together with the number and page of the book in which the document has been copied. (2) Such certificate shall be signed, sealed and dated by the registering officer, and shall then be admissible for the purpose of proving that the document has been duly registered in manner provided by this Act, and that the facts mentioned in the endorsements referred to in section 59 have occurred as therein mentioned"

12. The endorsement of the word `Registered' on the deed by the registering authority indicates that the said deed has been registered and the required formalities under sections 34, 35. 58 and 59 of the Registration Act has been complied with and is evidence of execution of the said document in accordance with the relevant laws. The respondents in their affidavit-in-opposition have in fact admitted that the document in question has been registered in the sadar Sub-Registrar's Office, Chittagong. The thumb impression and signatures of the parties are also present in the thumb impression book of the year 1999 preserved at the office of the Sadar Sub-Registrar, Chittagong which is further indication that the formalities for registering the said deed have been complied with.

13. On perusal of the Memo No. 2490 dated 4-4-2000 (Annexure F of the Supplementary Affidavit) a letter from the Executive Engineer, Public Works Department-1, Chittagong addressed to the petitioner it is stated:

এক্ষনে মন্ত্রণালয়ের সূত্রে উল্লেখিত একই স্মারক মুলে অনুমতি প্রাপ্ত হইয়া হোয়েকষ্ট ফার্মাসিউটিক্যালস কোম্পানী লিমিটেড বিগত ১১-১১-৯৯ ইং তারিখে সম্পাদিত ৭২১৬ নং হস্তান্তর দলিল মুলে আগ্রাবাদ বানিজ্যিক এলাকার ৬৪,৬৫ ও ৬৬ নং সহ মোট ৩ (তিন) টি প্লট আপনার সংস্থা এ এইচ আর,সি, প্রোপারটিজ লিমিটেড এর অনুকূলে হস্তান্তর কারায় নিম্নে বর্ণিত শর্ত পালন সাপেক্ষে পূর্বের মালিক হোয়েকস্ট ফার্মাসিউটিক্যালস কোম্পানী লিমিটেড  এর নামের স্থলে অত্র দপ্তরের সংশ্লিষ্ট নথি পত্রে আপনার সংস্থা এই,আর,সি, প্রোপারটিজ লিমিটেড এর নাম লিপিবদ্ধ করতঃ আপনার সংস্থাকে উক্ত ৩ (তিন) টি প্লটের ট্যানেন্ট হিসাবে স্বীকৃতি প্রদান পূর্বক আপনার সংস্থা এইচ,আর,সি, প্রোপারটিজ লিমিটেড এর অনুকূলে নামজারী করা হইল । শর্তঃ মুল লীজ দলিলের সকল ধারা উপ-ধারা আপনি মানিয়া চলিতে বাধ্য থাকিবেন ।

which indicates that the Government has acknowledged the petitioner owner of the concerned property executed and registered under the aforesaid deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999. There is nothing before us to show that either the vendor or any other party has disputed the ownership or title of the petitioner over the said land nor is there any scrap of paper before us to show that the aforesaid Deed No. 7216 of 1999 has not been executed and registered by the vendor in favour of the petitioner. In that view of the matter, we are unable to see any reason why the said Deed should not be recorded in the relevant Balam Book of the concerned Sub-Registrar's Office, Chittagong. In fact, Annexure C vide Memo No. 889 dated 29-5-2017 addressed by the Sadar Sub-Registrar, Chittagong to the District Registrar, Chittagong and Annexure B vide Memo No. 922 dated 29-5-2017 of the District Registrar, Chittagong addressed to the Inspector General of Registration, Bangladesh states that the aforesaid deed although was not entered in the relevant Balam Book its registration appears to be apparent by the presence of signature of the Vendor in the Thumb Impression Book preserved at the Office of Sadar Sub-Registrar, Chittagong and they prayed for direction from the Respondent No. 2 to record it in the Balam Book.

14. In view of the aforesaid matters it appears that the deed in question was duly presented to the registering authority for its registration but for reasons not known to this Court the contents of the said deed were not recorded in the balam book.

15. When the matter was brought to the knowledge of the Respondent No. 2 Inspector General of Registration in May, 2017 he should have made an inquiry into the matter and take appropriate steps in accordance with law but unfortunately he has shirked from his responsibility and after wasting several months filed an application to the Ministry of Law for taking steps for obtaining expert evidence on the signature of the parties. We find such action by the Respondent No. 2 Inspector General of Registration, Bangladesh inappropriate, as no one has complained about the genuineness of the signatures of the vendor or even disputed the ownership and title of the petitioner. The registering authority is vested with sufficient authority to cure any irregularity in the registration process under section 87 of the Registration Act. Section 87 of the Registration Act, 1908 states as follows:

"87. Nothing so done invalidated by defect in appointment or procedure—(1) Nothing done in good faith pursuant to this Act or any Act hereby repealed, by any registering officer, shall be deemed invalid merely by reason of any defect in his appointment or procedure.

(2) Any defect in or the want of authority of a person to present a document shall not by itself, render invalid the registration of the document or the transaction effected by it."

<u>16. Since the respondents have admitted that the deed in question was in fact registered they ought to have taken steps to inquire why it was not recorded in the concerned Balam Book and thereafter enter the contents of the said deed in the relevant Balam Book. If the respondents are suspicious of any matter about the deed they are always at liberty to make inquiries and take appropriate step in this regard but they should record the contents of Deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 in the relevant balam book without further delay since the petitioner company a commercial concern is suffering damage for every days delay by the Respondents.</u>

17. Accordingly, we find merit in this Rule and it is made absolute. The respondents are hereby directed to record the contents of Deed No. 7216 dated 11-11-1999 in the relevant Balam Book at the Sadar Sub-Registrar's Office, Chittagong within 2 (two) weeks of receipt of a copy of this judgment.

There will be no order as to costs.

End.

parties:

Vs

full_judgment:
Siddiqur Rahman Miah J: This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff, is directed against the judgment and decree dated 16-8-2001 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Additional Court at Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 279 of 1999, dismissing the suit.

2. The appellant as plaintiff instituted the suit No. 279 of 1999 against the defendants for specific performance of contract in respect of the suit property measuring 1 Bigha 13 Katha 14 chattaks and a pucca building standing thereon situated at Plot No. 6, Block No. NW(H), 159 Gulshan Avenue, Dhaka.

3. The plaintiff's case, in short, is that the defendant No. 1 Mrs Inge Flatz, who is originally an Austrian lady, and while she was living in the then East Pakistan, acquired the suit land by an indenture of lease deed executed on 14-9-1965 by the then Dhaka Improvement Trust and thus, the defendant No. 1 became the owner of the suit land by dint of the lease deed and got possession of the same. Subsequently, the defendant No. 1 constructed a pucca house thereon and she herself resided in the house and thus, she has been enjoying the suit property.

4. It is further stated in the plaint that after the liberation of Bangladesh, the suit property was wrongly treated as abandoned property and the same was vested in the government and that the defendant No. 1 applied to the government for releasing the suit property claiming her ownership and for the restoration of possession to her, and the Government in pursuance of the application of the defendant No. 1 transferred the suit property to her by a registered deed of sale dated 21-8-1980 and restored the possession of the suit property to her.

5. It is further stated that the defendant No. 1 Inge Flatz appointed Mohsin Darbar as constituted Attorney by executing a power of attorney on 25-6-1984 and conferred upon him the power, inter alia, to manage and look after the suit property realise the rent, let out the suit property, sell it and negotiate the sale and also execute and register the sale deed on her behalf; that the defendant No. 1 decided and proposed to sell the suit property through her constituted attorney and the plaintiff also agreed to purchase the said property and accordingly, the defendant No. 1 through her constituted attorney entered into an agreement for sale with the plaintiff on 10-8-1985 and the plaintiff also decided to purchase the suit property with his money earned in the United Kingdom; that the price of the suit property was fixed at Pound Sterling 60,000 which is equivalent to Taka 42,00,000 at the present rate of exchange and the plaintiff paid 20,000 Pound Sterling out of the total consideration as earnest money to the defendant No. 1 and the defendant No. 1 acknowledged the receipt of the said money and delivered the possession of the suit property in favour of the plaintiff and stipulated to pay the balance amount at the time of registration.

6. The further case of the plaintiff is that it was stipulated in the agreement for sale that the plaintiff would pay the entire consideration money to the defendant No.1 of his earning in the United Kingdom; that according to the terms of agreement for sale; the defendant No. 1 being the vendor, would obtain the permission from the Government or any other authority which might be required for transferring the suit property and would complete the sale as soon as possible; that if the defendant No. 1 caused any undue delay to effect the registration of the sale deed, the plaintiff would have the liberty to get the sale deed registered in accordance with law and that as the price of the suit property would be paid in foreign currency, the plaintiff applied to the Controller of Foreign Exchange through his appointed Lawyer vide letter dated 27-10-1986 and sought permission in respect of the sale of the suit property and subsequently, wrote another letter on 27-12-1986 and in pursuance of the aforesaid letters, Bangladesh Bank through its letter dated 17-2-1987 asked his lawyer to supply necessary papers in respect of the proposed sale. In pursuance of the letter, the plaintiff's lawyer supplied to the Bangladesh Bank the power of attorney in the name of Mr Mohsin Darbar, the UK passport of the plaintiff and the copy of agreement of sale.

7. It is further stated that subsequently, the Bangladesh Bank through its letter dated 9th August, 1987 informed the appointed lawyer of the plaintiff of the terms and conditions of the sale of the suit property by the defendant No.1. Among the terms and condition, there was a special conditions that the transactions shall be made in respect of the suit property through a nonresident account in the name of defendant No.1 Mrs Inge Flatz. As per the direction of the Bangladesh Bank, the plaintiff's lawyer informed the Bangladesh Bank of the opening of a nonresident account in the name of the defendant No. 1.

8. It is further stated that the constituted Attorney of the defendant No. 1 applied to the Chairman, Rajdhani Unnayan Katripakkha, seeking permission for the transfer of the suit property and in the said application, it was mentioned that the price of the suit property in foreign currency has been fixed at 60,000 Pound Sterling and the attested photograph of Mr Mohsin Darber and of the plaintiff Manzur Ahmed were attached with the application; that Rajdhani Unnayan Katripakkha through their letter dated 20-7-1989 informed the constituted Attorney of defendant No. 1 to the effect that the Attorney was permitted to perform all functions as mentioned in the-Power of Attorney executed by the defendant No. 1 in respect of the transfer of the suit property. The copy of the said letter was communicated to the address of the defendant No. 1 and thereafter, the constituted Attorney of defendant No. 1 had not taken any step in time to materialize the execution and registration of the sale deed in respect of the suit property.

9. It is further stated that although the defendant No. 1 entered into an agreement for the sale of the suit property at a consideration of Pound Sterling 60,000 and the said price was the highest market price prevailing at that time, the Rajdhani Unnayan Katripakkha issued Memo dated 25-7-1989 to the constituted Attorney of the defendant No. 1 and intimated him to the effect that the total price of the suit property would be Taka 83,12,680 which was much higher than what was agreed upon. In reply to the said Memo, Mr Mohsin Darber, the constituted Attorney of the defendant No. 1, wrote to the Secretary, Rajdhani Unnayan Katripakkha, on 3-8-1989 and requested him to revise the valuation of the property for the purpose of determining the transfer fee, although the defendant No. 1 is bound to execute and register the sale deed at the price as fixed in the agreement for sale, he requested Rajuk to reassess the valuation.

10. It is further stated that according to the terms of the agreement for sale, the defendant No. 1 herself or her constituted Attorney would execute and register the sale deed as soon as possible but the constituted Attorney of the defendant No. 1 failed to obtain the income tax and gain tax clearance certificate and also failed to obtain the permission for sale from the Rajdhani Unnayan Katripakkha and the Attorney caused an undue delay for effecting the registration of the sale deed, and consequently, despite the request made by the plaintiff, the defendant No. 1 or her constituted Attorney did not come forward to execute and register the sale deed. It is further stated that thereafter the plaintiff through his appointed lawyer tried to contact the constituted Attorney of the defendant No. 1 in order to pursue him to complete the sale but the appointed lawyer of the plaintiff could not trace out the Attorney and, finding no alternative, the appointed lawyer of the plaintiff wrote to the defendant No. 1 on 2nd March, 1991, requesting her take proper steps with regard to the execution and registration of the sale deed but the defendant No. 1 did not pay any heed to it; that the plaintiff is always willing to pay the balance consideration to the defendant No. 1 in order to get the kabala deed registered in his favour; that the plaintiff thereafter issued a letter dated 22nd May, 1991 through his appointed lawyer by registered post with due acknowledgement as the last chance and the letter was duly tendered to defendant No. 1 but the defendant No. 1 refused to take delivery of the letter and thereby refused to execute and register the sale deed in respect of the suit property and hence the plaintiff has been compelled to file the suit.

11. The defendant No. 3, Rajdhani Unnayan Katripakkha, appeared in the trial Court and filed written statement, denying all the material allegations contained in the plaint, inter alia, stating that the valuation of the suit property was not assessed correctly and that the suit was barred by law. It is further stated that the power of attorney given by the defendant No.1 on 10-8-1985 was forged, without consideration, collusive and concocted and that the constituted Attorney by virtue of the said power of attorney has no right to execute the agreement for sale and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

12. The defendant No. 2, the Government, did not enter appearance nor did it file any written statement in the trial Court.

13. Upon the said allegations the following issues were framed by the trial Court;

1. Is the suit maintainable in the present form?

2. Is the suit barred by limitation?

3. Is the agreement enforceable?

4. To what relief, if any, is the plaintiff entitled?

14. The plaintiff examined himself as PW 1 and PW 2 AM Mahbubuddin is one of the witnesses in the deed of agreement.

15. The plaintiff filed and proved the lease deed dated 15-9-1965 marked Exhibit 1, deed of sale dated 28-5-1980 marked Exhibit 2, general power of attorney marked Exhibit 4, an agreement for sale dated 10-8-1985 marked Exhibit 5 and confirmation letter dated 10-8-1985 regarding the receipt of the part payment of consideration money marked Exhibit 6. The plaintiff also filed the letter dated 20-7-1989 given by RAJUK which authorised Mohsin Darbar, the constituted attorney of Mrs Inge Flatz, to perform all works on her behalf which is marked Exhibit 9 and also filed the original application submitted by Mohsin Darbar addressing the Chairman praying for permission for transferring the suit property in favour of the plaintiff.

16. The defendants examined none nor did they file any document in support of their contention.

17. The learned Joint District Judge on consideration of the evidence on record, dismissed the suit by the impugned judgment and decree dated 16-8-2001 holding inter alia, that the agreement for sale dated 10-8-1985 was illegal and not enforceable.

18. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree dated 16-8-2001, the plaintiff preferred appeal before this Court.

19. Mr Azizul Hoque, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant, submits that the defendant No.1 Mrs Inge Flatz having title and possession over the suit property, appointed Mr Mohsin Darbar Attorney by executing a power of attorney on 25-6-1984 and conferred upon him the power to negotiate the sale, to sell and also to execute and register the sale deed on her behalf, that the defendant No.1 proposed to sell the suit property through her constituted attorney and the plaintiff agreed to purchase the same and that accordingly the defendant No. 1 through her constituted attorney entered into an agreement for sale with the plaintiff.

20. He further submits that the price of the suit property was fixed at pound Sterling 60,000 which is equivalent to Taka 42,00,000 out of which plaintiff paid 20,000 pound Sterling as earnest money to the defendant No. 1 and the constituted attorney, Mohsin Darbar, acknowledged the receipt of the earnest money received by Mrs Inge Flatz and delivered the possession of the suit property in favour of the plaintiff.

21. It is also submitted that as per the terms of agreement for sale the defendant No. 1 was lastly requested on 22-5-1991 to execute and register the sale deed but she refused to do so.

22. He further testifies that the power of attorney executed on 25-6-1984 is genuine; that Mohsin Darbar, the constituted attorney of Mrs Inge Flatz, executed the agreement for sale with the plaintiff on 10-8-1985 and that the plaintiff is legally entitled to get the decree.

23. It is further submitted that the agreement was not challenged by anybody but the Court below disbelieved the contract without assigning any cogent reasons that the learned Court has seriously failed to understand the proper aspect of things that in the absence of any evidence the learned trial Court on surmise and conjecture opined that the agreement for sale dated 10-8-1985 is illegal and not enforceable in law and that the learned Court below erred in not relying on the evidence, both oral and documentary, adduced by the plaintiff in support of his case.

24. No one appears on behalf of the defendant-respondent No. 3, RAJUK, in this appeal though this matter has been appearing in the list for a pretty long time and a written notice has been served upon the defendant-respondent No. 3 by the plaintiff appellant.

25. Mr Akbar Hossain, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of the Government, respondent No. 2, opposes the appeal contending, inter alia, that the plaintiff has failed to prove the case and that the judgment and decree dated 16-8-2001 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Additional Court, Dhaka, are quite justified which does not call for any interference by this Court.

26. The only point for determination in the appeal is, whether the learned Subordinate Judge was justified in passing the impugned judgment and decree dated 16-8-2001.

27. In order to appreciate the contentions raised by the learned Counsels of the contending parties and to judge the legality of the impugned judgment and decree, we are required to scrutinise the material evidence on record.

28. The learned Counsel for the appellant has placed before us that the lease deed, deed of sale, general power of attorney, the agreement for sale, the confirmation letter regarding the payment of the earnest money and other necessary papers and documents in support of his contention.

29. On perusal of the impugned judgment and decree, it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge decided the issues of maintainability and limitation in favour of the plaintiff and he opined that the agreement for sale dated 10-8-1985 was not genuine and the same was not enforceable.

30. Now let us see whether the agreement of sale is genuine or not.

31. Where a suit is brought for specific performance of contract. It is to be seen whether the plaintiff has been able to prove the contract between the plaintiff and the defendant and whether the plaintiff is ready and willing at all material dates to perform his part of the contract.

32. Law under section 101 of the Evidence Act is that the burden of proof lies with the party who substantially asserts the affirmative of issue. It is reasonable and just that the suitor, who relies upon the existence of a fact, should be called upon to prove his own case.

33. It is not disputed that Mrs Inge Flatz acquired the suit property by virtue of the lease deed No. 9110 dated 15-9-1965 marked Exhibit 1 and possessed the same, constructing a structure thereon; that after the liberation of Bangladesh the suit property was wrongly treated as abandoned and the same was vested in the government, that on her application, the Government transferred the suit property in her favour by virtue of a sale deed No. 22040 dated 21-5-1980 marked Exhibit 2.

34. It also appears from the report of the process server that both the plaintiff Mrs Inge Flatz and her constituted Attorney, Mohsin Darbar died and thus the suit property is vested in the government, as Mrs Inge Flatz had no heir in accordance with provision of law viz Bangladesh vesting of property and assets order 1972 and in accordance with Article 143 clause 1 (c) of the Constitution. As per this changed circumstances, on the application of the plaintiff, the plaint has been amended in accordance with the provision of law.

35. The plaint case is that the suit property belonged to defendant No.1 Mrs Inge Flatz who appointed Mohsin Darbar her attorney by executing a power of attorney on 25-6-1984, giving him power to manage, negotiate and sell the suit property; that defendant No.1 decided and proposed to sell the suit property through her constituted attorney and the plaintiff agreed to purchase the same and accordingly the defendant No. 1 through her constituted attorney entered into an agreement for sale with the plaintiff on 10-8-1985.

36. The plaintiff has filed the original power of attorney dated 25-6-1984 and original deed of agreement dated 10-8-1985 from his custody which have been marked Exhibit Nos. 4 and 5 respectively and also examined 2 (two) witnesses including himself in support of his contention.

37. The plaintiff, Manzur Ahmed, deposed that defendant No. 1, Inge Flatz, acquired the suit property from RAJUK defendant No. 3 by way of a lease deed No. 9110 dated 15-9-1965. He submitted the lease deed, getting the same from his power of attorney holder which is marked Exhibit No. 1. He further deposed that the suit property was wrongly treated as abandoned property and the same was vested in the government, that on the prayer of the plaintiff, she again acquired the suit property from the Government defendant No. 2 by virtue of sale deed No. 22080 dated  21-6-1980 which has been submitted from his custody receiving the same from Mohsin Darbar which is also marked exhibit No.2 and the challan through which the defendant No. 1 deposited consideration money is marked Exhibit 3. He further deposed that the defendant No. 1 Mrs Inge Flatz, appointed Mohsin Darbar her Attorney through a power of attorney dated 25-6-1986 which is marked Exhibit 4 and power of attorney came to Bangladesh through the Austrian Embassy. He identified the deed of agreement and also identified the signature of Mohsin Darbar in the power of attorney. He further stated that 60,000 (sixty thousand) Pound Sterling was fixed as the consideration money out of which 20,000 (twenty thousand) Pound Sterling was paid as part payment of consideration, that the constituted attorney gave a receipt of payment of part consideration and he identified the receipt and also identified the signature of Mohsin Darbar marked Exhibit 6 therein; that the terms of agreement were that Mohsin Darbar, obtaining gain tax and income tax clearance certificates from the concerned authorities, executed and registered the sale deed; that accordingly, Mohsin Darbar applied to RAJUK for permission and RAJUK gave him an indirect permission empowering him to do all works on the basis of power of attorney and he identified the letter marked Exhibit No. 7. He also deposed that Mohsin Darbar failed to execute and register the sale deed as per the terms of agreement for which he sent a registered letter to the defendant No. 1 and the receipt of which is marked Exhibit No. 8. He also deposed that he was ready to pay the rest consideration money; that he paid municipal tax and he identified the receipt book of tax marked exhibit No. 9 and that the defendant No. 1 delivered possession by virtue of the deed of agreement and he has been possessing the suit property with his family members. PW 1 further testified that as the defendant No. 1 failed to execute and register the deed of sale in spite of repeated reminders, he was constrained to file the suit.

38. He denied the suggestion that his papers were forged, that Mohsin Darbar was not given permission to sell the suit property; that the deed of agreement dated 10-8-1985 was without consideration and undervalued and that he was not entitled to get decree as prayed for.

39. In the cross-examination, he stated that he knew the suit property; that the deed of agreement was executed in the year 1985, that the terms of the agreement was to execute and register the sale deed obtaining gain tax and income tax clearance and that there was no specific time in the Bainapatra for executing sale deed.

40. He denied the defence suggestion that he would not get any relief by virtue of the deed of sale, that the suit property was undervalued, that the acknowledged receipt was not genuine, that the agreement for sale was forged and that Mohsin Darbar was a fictitious person. To a Court's question as regard the habitation/ address of Mohsin Darbar, this witness categorically stated that sometimes he resided at 159 Gulshan Avenue and sometimes at No. 5 Bangabandhu Avenue.

41. PW 2 is AM Mahbubuddin who is a lawyer. He on oath deposed that he was one of witnesses in the agreement of sale executed between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1. He identified his signature in the agreement for sale marked Exhibit 5/1, that there were some signatures of vendor Mohsin Darbar therein, that he was present at the time of execution of the deed of agreement.

42. He further deposed that he knew the plaintiff Mohsin Darbar and the suit property. PW 2 categorically deposed that now plaintiff Manjur Ahmed has been in possession of the suit property since the date of agreement for sale; that the price of the suit property was fixed at 60,000 (sixty thousand) Pounds; that 20,000 (twenty thousand) pounds out of total consideration was paid on that day; that Mohsin Darbar acknowledged the receipt of payment and his signature in the acknowledge ment receipt is marked Exhibit 6.

43. In the cross-examination, he deposed that Mohsin Darber had put initial in every page and also had put full signature in the last page of the deed of agreement; that he was present at the time of the talk of the deed of agreement which was executed in his presence on 10-8-1985 and that part payment of consideration money had been made earlier.

He denied the defence suggestion that he was deposing falsely.

<u>44. There is no denying the fact that the defendant No.1, Mrs Inge Flatz, wife of Mr Mohd. Ehsan, was an Austrian citizen. While she was in this country, she acquired the suit property. While she was in Austria, she appointed Mr Mohsin Darbar her attorney, giving him power to negotiate for sale and to sell the suit property and, with this end in view, she executed and registered a power of attorney before Dr Richard Talbot, Offentlicher Notar who registered the same the registration No. being 837/84 dated 25-6-1984, observing all official formalities and the said power of attorney was sent by the Austrian Government to M Motiur Rahman, First Secretary, Embassy of Bangladesh, 5300 Bonn 2, Federal Republic of Germany, who attested the power of attorney and sent the same to Bangladesh Government for validating the said power of attorney; the power of attorney has been filed from the custody of the plaintiff and the plaintiff as PW 1 has proved the power of attorney dated 25-6-1984 which has been marked Exhibit 4. It appears that observing all formalities as regards the execution and registration of the power of attorney by the Austrian and Bangladesh Governments, the power of attorney reached its holder Mohsin Darbar who handed over the same to the plaintiff and the plaintiff submitted the power of attorney to the Court from his custody and has proved the same and thus this power of attorney cannot be treated as fictitious without any cogent reasons. Rather, the evidence on record and circumstances behind execution, registration, authentication and validating of the power of attorney clearly speak of its genuineness. Moreover, the signature given by the defendant No.1, Inge Flatz, in the lease deed and her signature in the power of attorney clearly appear to be same by the naked eye. RAJUK also accepted this power of attorney through a letter dated 20-7-1989 marked Exhibit 7 permitting Mohsin Darbar to do all acts on the basis of the power of attorney. Thus, we are of the view that the power of attorney was actually given by Mrs Inge Flatz to Mohsin Darbar empowering the latter to sell the suit property and being empowered, her constituted attorney executed the deed of agreement for the sale of the suit property in favour of the plaintiff. The plaintiff as PW 1 proved the deed of agreement for sale which has been marked as Exhibit 5 and he stoutly deposed that he paid 20,000 (twenty thousand) Sterling pounds to Mrs Inge Flatz out of 60,000(sixty thousand) Sterling Pounds. Mohsin Darbar acknowledged the payment by giving a letter of confirmation which is marked Exhibit 6. PW 2 AM Mahabubuddim is one of the signatories of the deed of agreement for sale who identified his signature therein which is marked Exhibit 5/1. He deposed that he was present at the time of the execution of the deed of agreement for sale and that Mohsin Darbar signed the agreement in his presence. This witness knew the suit property and the parties. He testified that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit property since execution of the deed of agreement for sale. On the application of Mohsin Darbar for giving permission to execute the sale deed in respect of the suit property, RAJUK permitted him to do all acts. The signature of Mohsin Darbar appearing in the deed of agreement for sale and his signature given in the confirmation receipt of part payment marked Exhibit 6 are of the same hand. In the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record, we are fully convinced that the deed of agreement for sale is genuine and on the basis of this agreement, the plaintiff made part payment and got possession of the suit property. From the evidence on record, it is clearly proved that the plaintiff had requested Mohsin Darbar to execute and register the deed of sale on the basis of the deed of agreement but he deferred the matter and lastly, on 22-5-1991, he refused to do so.</u>

<u>45. A suit for specific performance is that in which the plaintiff claims relief under section 5 of the Specific Relief Act for directing the defendant to do the very act which he is under an obligation to do. When the plaintiff as per the terms of the deed of agreement performed his part, the defendant is also bound to perform his part, otherwise, the Court will act on behalf of the plaintiff.</u>

<u>46. In the instant case, it has been clearly proved that Mrs Inge Flatz empowered Mohsin Darbar by virtue of a power of attorney to sell the suit property and Mohsin Darbar accordingly, executed the agreement for sale in respect of the suit property and made part payment of consideration money and delivered possession of the suit property and thus, the part performance of agreement has been proved. Moreover, it appears that the plaintiff has done his part as per the agreement and is also willing to repay the balance consideration money with a view to getting the sale deed registered. In such circumstances, the defendant is duty bound to perform his part as per section 12 of the Specific Relief Act. What is required of the plaintiff is to show that he is ready to fulfil his terms of agreement. On perusal of the evidence on record, it appears that the plaintiff was always ready to fulfil the terms of agreement and he had been tendering Mr Mohsin Darbar to execute and register the sale deed, receiving the balance consideration money but the defendant No.1 did not comply with his request. So, there is no impediment on the part of the plaintiff for getting decree as prayed for.</u>

<u>47. Now we like to meet the findings put forward by the learned Subordinate Judge in the impugned judgment. The learned trial Court quoting section 18 of Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947 held that prior to make sale contract, the party is required to obtain permission from Bangladesh government and in the absence of such permission, the sale contract is illegal which is not tenable in law as that section does not apply in this case because the agreement for sale is not a complete contract which is merely a bainapatra;</u>

<u>48. The plaintiff is not a resident of Bangladesh.</u>

<u>49. In para 5 of the agreement, there is a term that the defendant will obtain necessary permission from the government or any other agency for the effective transfer of property. The plaintiff performed the terms of the agreement for sale in toto, so, he is also protected by section 21 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947.</u>

<u>50. It is not disputed that the suit property actually belongs to the government and the defendant No. 1, Mrs Inge Flatz took lease from the government. After the death of the defendant No. 1, Inge Flatz and her constituted attorney, now the suit property is vested in the government in accordance with the provision of Bangladesh (vesting of property and assets) Order, 1972 and Article 143 clause 1 (c) of the Constitution. As per Article 143 clause 1(c) while there is no rightful owner of the property that rests in the government. In the present circumstances, the suit land has been vested in the government. Thus, the question raised by the learned trial Court is not tenable in law.</u>

51. Though the defendant No. 3, RAJUK, filed a written statement at the trial stage, it did not adduce any witness in support of the contention. Rather, in reply to the application of Mohsin Darbar for permission for the sale of the suit property, RAJUK wrote vide Memo RAJUK estate/1892(1) dated 20-7-1989 admitting the contention of the plaintiff empowering the constituted attorney to do all acts on the basis of power of attorney and this memo clearly indicates that RAJUK had accepted the power of attorney and the agreement for sale.

52. The defendant No. 2, the government, did not contest in the trial Court nor did it file any written statement. In the appellate stage, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appeared to contest the appeal. As the government did not file any written statement in the trial Court nor did it file any counter-affidavit, the learned Assistant Attorney-General has nothing to say verbally in this Court. In spite of that he simply submits that the suit is barred by limitation; that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and that the suit is undervalued. His submission does not controvert the contention of the plaintiff-appellant rather, he indirectly admitted the main contention of the appellant.

53. The comment of the learned trial Court that the power of attorney in favour of Mohsin Darbar is false and the agreement for sale by Mohsin Darbar is not genuine, is absolutely wrong and contradictory and the learned trial Court has no basis of such comment. On perusal of the evidence on record it appears that on an application of Mohsin Darbar, RAJUK vide its letter dated 20-7-1989, marked Exhibit 7, recognised Mohsin Darbar authorising him to act and execute all relevant things contained in the power of attorney and thus, Mohsin Darbar was accepted as the proper person to deal with the property and thus, the conclusion drawn by the learned Subordinate Judge has no leg to stand and it is thus not sustainable in law and, as such, the learned Subordinate Judge erred in not relying on evidence, both oral and documentary, adduced by the plaintiff in support of this case.

54. From the scrutiny of the evidence discussed above, we find that the power of attorney dated 25-6-1984 Exhibit 4 and the agreement for sale dated 10-8-1985 Exhibit 5 have been convincingly proved by the evidence of PW 1 and PW 2 as well as by other documentary evidence. The defence has totally failed to shake the consistent and corroborative testimony of the plaintiff-appellant.

<u>55. The learned Subordinate Judge did not take pains to compare the signature of Mrs Inge Flatz in the lease deed marked 1 with the signature given in the power of attorney Exhibit 4 and also did not feel it necessary to compare the signature of Mohsin Darbar in the agreement for sale Exhibit 5 with the signature appearing in the letter of confirmation of part payment Exhibit 6. Section 73 of the Evidence Act clearly empowers the Court to do it as the Court, being the expert of all experts, and the Court itself is quite competent to compare the disputed signature with the admitted one. We have carefully compared the signatures of Mrs Inge Flatz and Mohsin Darbar with their available admitted signatures as mentioned above and we are fully satisfied that these are the products of the same hands. We are, therefore, inclined to find that the learned Subordinate Judge is quite wrong in holding that the power of attorney Exhibit 4 and the agreement of sale Exhibit 5 are not genuine. The defendants produced nothing before the Court to discard the corroborative and consistent evidence of PW 1 and PW 2 who have proved these documents.</u>

56. In the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, we have no hesitation in discarding the findings arrived at by the trial Court as the same are not based on sound and cogent reasons. It is found from the evidence on record that the plaintiff-appellant has successfully succeeded in proving the power of attorney and the agreement of sale.

57. The age-old maxim that he who seeks equity must do equity has been applied in full force in the present case. In the facts of the case and the evidence on record, we find that the plaintiff had made an agreement of sale with the constituted attorney of Mrs. Inge Flatz in good faith and paid part payment of the consideration money and he is also willing to pay the balance consideration money and also requested Mohsin Darbar to execute and register the sale deed on the basis of agreement but he refused. Hence the suit. The plaintiff has come to Court with clean hands, bonafidely performing his part and seeks equity for specific performance of contract and thus, he is entitled to get justice and equity.

58. We are, therefore, of the view that the plaintiff is entitled to a decree for specific performance of contract in respect of the suit property. It will be in the fitness of things and quite in consonance with the principle of justice, equity and good conscience to decree the suit. The learned Subordinate Judge was manifestly wrong in dismissing the suit without applying his judicial mind into the facts of the case and the materials on record. Consequently, we find substance in the appeal. The appeal succeeds.

59. In the result, the appeal is allowed. The judgment and decree dated 16-8-2001 dismissing the suit are set aside and the suit is decreed on contest against the contesting defendant and ex parte against the rest without cost. The respondent No. 2 is directed to execute and register a sale deed in favour of the plaintiff in respect of the suit property, receiving the balance consideration money in Bangladeshi Taka from the plaintiff within 60(sixty) days from the date. The respondent No. 3 is directed to accord necessary permission, receiving the legal transfer fee as per consideration money within the date for facilitating the execution and registration of the sale deed in default of which the plaintiff shall be at liberty to get the sale deed executed and registered through Court in accordance with law.

Send down the LCR at once.

End.

full_judgment:
A M Mahmudur Rahman, J: This appeal by leave at the instance of the appellant, Bangladesh Bar Council, is directed against the judgment and order dated November 5, 1997 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3450 of 1996 setting aside the judgment of affirmance of the courts below and thereby decreeing the suit.

2. The respondent filed Title Suit No. 35 of 1993 for declaration that the order of dismissal dated 21.12.1991 of the appellant No. 1, (defendant No. 2) the Bangladesh Bar Council is illegal, void and not binding Upon urn stating that he was a Lower Division 'Assistant of the erstwhile East Pakistan Bar Council and on independence of Bangladesh le was serving in the Bangladesh Bar Council as a section officer. In 1981 one Utpal Chaterjee was given admit card for viva-voce examination for enrolment as an Advocate after being satisfied on scrutiny of the relevant papers by one Maizuddin Ahmed who was in charge of Dhaka Division. Subsequently some written and unwritten answer papers and 2 written intimations were found in the locked drawer of Kazi Nurul Amin, Section Officer of Chittagong Division and M. Ali Akbar, Upper Division Assistant. As the respondent was in-charge of all these papers an explanation was called for from him and he gave the written explanation and he was suspended. An enquiry was held and he was asked to show cause and he showed cause. Appellant No. 2, asked him to submit a "better cause" which the respondent filed but he was dismissed on 21.12.91 on the charge of gross misconduct without giving any opportunity to defend himself.

3. The suit was dismissed on contest and the appeal against the decree of the trial court was also dismissed. The plaintiff against the judgment and decree of the lower appellate court moved the High Court Division in revision and the rule issued in Civil Revision No. 3450 of 1996 was made absolute by a Division Bench of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order, setting aside the judgments of the courts below and thereby decreed the suit.

4. Leave to appeal was granted to consider as to whether the High Court Division illegally went beyond the scope of the suit and the pleadings to enquire into the question whether the proceeding against the respondent or any past thereof was taken with the approval of the Bar Council as a body which was neither the case of the plaintiff nor any such issue was raised in the suit and thereby exceeded its jurisdiction in revision.

5. Mr. Amirul Islam, learned Advocate for the appellants, submitted that the High Court Division illegally went beyond the pleadings to enquire and decide the question as to whether the proceeding or any part thereof against the respondent was taken with the approval of the Bar Council and thereby exceeded its jurisdiction in exercise of its power under section 115 C.P.C. in that neither it was the case of the respondent nor any issue in this respect was raised and framed in the suit. Mr. Islam drawing our attention to the resolutions of the Bar Council dated 5/6.1.91, 9.11.91, 31.12.91, and 26.6.97 submitted that these resolutions amply prove that the order of dismissal although were approved by the Bar Council. He submits that the High Court Division fell in error in revision to interfere with the concurrent judgments of both the courts below.

6. The learned Advocate for the respondent submitted that the respondent was in-charge of Chittagong Section but the allegation relating to Utpal Chatterjee falls under a different section and as such he was not liable to be dismissed and as such the High Court Division rightly interfered with the concurrent judgments of the Courts below. He further submitted that the respondent was charged under 12 heads although the Enquiry Officer found all charges excepting charge Nos. 1 and 2 as false, frivolous and collusive but appellant No. 2 initiated office note stating that the respondent was guilty on all charges and recommended for his dismissal and the Chairman of the Executive Committee of the Bangladesh Bar Council signed the note which the Chairman, Bar Council approved. The learned Counsel for the respondent also submitted that Enquiry Officer was to initiate departmental proceeding only in respect of the irregularity in enrolment of one Utpal Chattedee buthe in collusion with the Taslimuddin Khan, Section Officer and D.W. 1 submitted enquiry report containing 12 charges to the Bar Council and as such the enquiry held was defective and illegal and appellant No. 2 assumed the power of the Bar Council in initiating the note holding the respondent guilty on all 12 Charges and as such the dismissal order is illegal, without authority and void ab-initio. The learned Advocate submitted also that question of jurisdiction was raised in the courts below but both the courts failed to consider the same and as such the submission of the appellant that the issue of jurisdiction was not raised earlier is not correct. He further submitted that the said concurrent judgments having been based on illegal proceeding and that the proceedings starting from the enquiry report ending with the dismissal order having been taken without the approval of the Bar Council as a body the High Court Division rightly interfered with the same for ends of justice. It was argued by him that unless the rules are made by the Bar Council the power of the Council under this Article shall be exercised by the Government as contemplated under Article 40(3) of Bangladesh Legal Practitioners and Bar Council Order and Rules, 1972 and in the instant case there being no rule framed by the Bar Council the Chairman of the Executive Committee and the Chairman of the Bar Council had no power to approve the order of dismissal passed by the respondent No. 2.

<u>7. This needs us to examine the relevant provisions of the Order and Rules. Article 40(1) of the Bangladesh Legal Practitioners and Bar Council Order and Rules, 1972 empowers the Bar Council to make rules to carry out the purpose of this Order and Article 40(3) provides that until rules are made by the Bar Council, the power of the Council under this Article shall be exercised by the Government. Article 10(j) empowers the Bar Council to perform all other functions conferred on it by or under this Order; and Article 40 (k) empowers to do all other things necessary for discharging the aforesaid functions. The expression 'to carry out the purpose of this Order' as employed in Article 40(1) includes power of appointment, removal, dismissal etc. of the employees of the Bar Council. The Rules be framed by the Bar Council would be certainly framed by delegation of rule making power and such rule can never be framed in derogation to the authority of the Bar Council as conferred by and under Article 40(1) of the Bangladesh Practitioners and Bar Council Order and Rules, 1972. No doubt Article 40(3) authorise the government in absence of framing of the Rules to exercise the power of the Bar Council but Article 40(3) does not oust the power of the Bar Council explicitly. The order of dismissal was approved by the Chairman of the Executive Committee as noted above. According to Article 10(1) of the Order the Bar Council is vested with the authority to perform function conferred on it by or under this Order. One of the functions of the Bar Council is to run the administration of the Council. Appointment of employees is a part of administration. Therefore, only for short of framing the Rules the order of dismissal cannot be held to be without legal sanction on the strength of the provision of sub-article (3) of Article 40 of the Order, 1972.</u>

8. The respondent having had accepted the appointment made by the Bar Council and continued his service up to promotion label the Bar Council, being the appointing authority has also power to dismiss him. This is in harmony with the principle that the authority which can appoint an employee has also authority to take action regarding his employment more so when the employee accepted the appointment. In this case before us nothing could be shown that the Bar Council had no authority to appoint the respondent and, thus, he cannot blow hot and cold in the same breath. He cannot approbate and reprobate. In this case the Enquiry Committee was duly appointed and its recommendation not being malafide the order impugned in the suit was wrongly set aside by the High Court Division acting in excess of its jurisdiction embarking upon an enquiry beyond the pleadings and upon an issue not raised in the suit without arriving at a finding that the judgments and orders of the courts below occasioned failure of justice. Mere illegality is no ground for the High Court Division for interference with the judgment and order of a court below in exercise of its power under section 115(1) C P C. On the facts of this case we do not find that the courts below dismissed the suit leading to failure of justice. Accordingly, we hold that the High Court Division fell in error in interfering with the impugned judgment and order of the courts below without reaching any finding of failure of justice.

9. For the aforesaid reasons, the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is set aside and the judgments and decrees of the courts below are restored and the suit is dismissed.

In the result, the appeal is allowed, without any order as to costs.

End.
